Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Taha

(p-3) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Ta-Ha﴾.

The most apparent of the opinions concerning it, in my view, is that it is among the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) at the beginnings of surahs. What indicates this is that the letters ta' and ha' mentioned at the opening of this surah occur in other places where there is no dispute that they are among the disjointed letters. As for ta', it occurs at the opening of Surat al-Shu'ara' ﴿Ta-Sin-Mim﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 1], at the opening of Surat al-Naml ﴿Ta-Sin﴾ [al-Naml: 1], and at the opening of Surat al-Qasas. As for ha', it occurs at the opening of Surat Maryam in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad﴾ [Maryam: 1]. We have already presented the discussion of the disjointed letters in full at the beginning of Surat Hud, and the best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

Some scholars said: His saying ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ means "O man" (ya rajul). They said: This is the dialect of the Banu 'Akk ibn 'Adnan, the Banu Tayy', and the Banu 'Ukl. They said: If you said to a man from the Banu 'Akk, "O man," he would not understand that you were calling him until you said "Ta-Ha." From this is the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah al-Tamimi:

"I called 'Ta-Ha' in battle, but he did not answer, so I feared for him that he would be a deserter."

It is also narrated as "muzayilan" (one who separates himself). 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr said: The meaning of (Ta-Ha) in the dialect of 'Akk is "O my beloved." This was mentioned by al-Ghaznawi. Qutrub said: It is in the dialect of Tayy', and he recited for Yazid ibn al-Muhalhal:

"Indeed, foolishness is 'Ta-Ha' in your dispositions *** may Allah not bless the accursed people."

It is also narrated as:

"Indeed, foolishness is 'Ta-Ha' in your natures *** may Allah not sanctify the spirits of the accursed."

Among those narrated from who said that the meaning of "Ta-Ha" is "O man" are Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', Muhammad ibn Ka'b, Abu Malik, 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abza, and others, as Ibn Kathir and others transmitted from them. Al-Qadi 'Iyad mentioned in al-Shifa' from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed, he would stand on one leg and raise the other, so Allah revealed 'Ta-Ha,' meaning: 'Set your feet upon the earth, O Muhammad.'" According to this view, the ha' is substituted from the hamzah, and the hamzah was lightened by replacing it with an alif, as in the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"They departed with Muslimah's mules in the evening, so pasture, O Fazarah, may that pasture not bring you comfort."

Then the matter was built upon it, and the ha' is for pausing. The weakness of this view and its remoteness from the apparent meaning are not hidden.

Among the other weak opinions concerning His saying ﴿Ta-Ha﴾ is the view that it is among the names of the Prophet (ﷺ). Also the view that the ta' is from purity (taharah) and the ha' is from guidance (hidayah), saying to His Prophet: "O one purified from sins, O guide of creation to the Knower of the unseen," and other weak opinions. The correct view, if Allah wills, regarding the verse is what we have stated at the outset, and it is indicated by the Qur'an in other places.

The Almighty's statement: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be distressed.﴾

Regarding His statement, the Exalted, ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be distressed﴾, there are two interpretations, and the Qur'an bears witness to both:

The first is that the meaning is: "We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be distressed," i.e., that you should exhaust yourself with severe toil, due to your excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and your anguish that they should not believe. Many verses have come in the sense of this interpretation, such as:

• His statement, the Exalted: ﴿So let not your soul expend itself in regret over them﴾ [Fatir: 8], and the verse continues.

• His statement: ﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself through grief over their traces if they do not believe in this message﴾ [al-Kahf: 6].

• His statement: ﴿Perhaps you will destroy yourself because they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 6].

Verses of this kind are very numerous, and we have already cited many of them in various places in this blessed book.

The second interpretation is that he (ﷺ) prayed during the night until his feet became swollen, so Allah sent down ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you that you should be distressed﴾, i.e., that you should wear yourself out with worship and make yourself suffer grievous hardship. "We did not send you except with the easy, tolerant Hanifiyyah (the pure monotheistic religion of Abraham)." The apparent meanings of verses from the Book of Allah support this interpretation, such as His statement: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His statement: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. The ruling is taken by the generality of the wording, not by the specificity of the occasion of revelation.

From His statement ﴿that you should be distressed﴾ it is understood that it was sent down to him so that he might be happy. This is also supported by the authentic hadith: "Whoever Allah intends good for, He gives him understanding in the religion." Al-Tabarani narrated from Tha'labah ibn al-Hakam, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed Allah says to the scholars on the Day of Resurrection: 'I did not place My knowledge and My wisdom in you except that I intended to forgive you for what you had done, and I do not mind.'" Ibn Kathir said: its chain is good. The meaning of the verse, according to this last view, resembles His statement: ﴿So recite what is easy of it and establish prayer﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and the verse continues (p-5).

The root meaning of shaqa' (misery, distress) in the language of the Arabs is hardship and fatigue. From it is the saying of Abu al-Tayyib:

"The man of intellect suffers in bliss because of his intellect, while the one of ignorance, in wretchedness, lives in ease."

From it also is His statement: ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, [for then] you would suffer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 3:

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except as a reminder for those who fear﴾.

The most apparent of the opinions regarding it is that it is a məf'ūl li-ajlih (object of purpose, i.e. an accusative of cause or reason), meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an upon you except as a reminder, that is, except for the sake of reminding those who fear Allah and dread His punishment. Al-tadhkira (reminder) is the admonition to which hearts are softened, so that they comply with Allah's command and avoid His prohibition. The reminder is specified for those who fear, to the exclusion of others, because they are the ones who benefit from it,

• like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So remind by the Qur'an whoever fears My warning﴾ [Qaf: 45],

• and His saying: ﴿You can only warn one who follows the Reminder and fears the Most Merciful unseen﴾ [Ya-Sin: 11],

• and His saying: ﴿You are only a warner for those who fear it﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 45]. So the specification mentioned in these verses, namely that the reminder benefits those people, who are the ones who benefit from it to the exclusion of others, is clear. And what he mentions here, that He did not send down the Qur'an except for reminding, He has explained in other than this place,

• like His saying: ﴿It is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾, ﴿for whoever among you wills to take a straight path﴾ [At-Takwir: 27–28],

• and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I do not ask you for any wage for it; it is nothing but a reminder to the worlds﴾ [Al-An'am: 90],

along with other verses.

As for the parsing of ﴿Except as a reminder﴾ as a badal (substitute) for ﴿to be distressed﴾, this is not valid, because the reminder is not distress. Its parsing as an absolute object (māf'ūl muṭlaq) is also not evident. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to be distressed﴾ ﴿except as a reminder for those who fear﴾:

We did not send down upon you this arduous hardship except so that it would be a reminder. On this reading, it is permissible for ﴿a reminder﴾ to be a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) and also a məf'ūl lahu (object of purpose).

﴿Tanzīlan min mamman khalaqa al-arḍa wa-al-samāwāti al-ʿulā﴾ (a revelation from Him who created the earth and the high heavens).

In His words ﴿tanzīlan﴾ there are many grammatical possibilities (i'rab, grammatical analysis) that the exegetes mentioned. The most apparent of them, in my view, is that it is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object, cognate accusative) governed by an implied verb, nazzala (He sent down), which is indicated by His words ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you to make you suffer﴾. The meaning is: Allah sent it down ﴿as a revelation from Him who created the earth﴾, meaning that it is not poetry, nor soothsaying, nor magic, nor "the fables of the ancients." This meaning is also indicated by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Nor is it the word of a poet; little do you believe. Nor is it the word of a soothsayer; little do you remember. It is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 41–43]. The verses that explicitly state that the Qur'an is sent down from the Lord of the worlds are very many and well known, such as His words:

• ﴿And indeed, it is a revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 192],

• His words: ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Zumar: 1],

• and His words: ﴿A revelation from the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 2].

The verses of this kind are exceedingly numerous.

Allah's saying: ﴿The Most Merciful (al-Raḥmān) is established upon the Throne (al-ʿArsh) [istawā]﴾.

The verses that clarify this verse and its like in the Qur'an were already explained fully in Surah al-A'raf, so there is no need to repeat them here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 7:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is yet more hidden.﴾

Allah addressed His Prophet ﷺ in this noble verse, saying: if he speaks aloud, that is, says it openly without concealment, then indeed He, Mighty and Exalted, knows the secret and what is even more hidden than the secret. This meaning, to which He alludes here, He mentions in other places, such as:

• His saying: ﴿And keep your speech secret or declare it aloud; indeed, He is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾ [al-Mulk: 13],

• and His saying: ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare﴾ [al-Nahl: 19],

• and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah knows their secret conferences﴾ [Muhammad: 26],

• and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say, "It was sent down by He who knows the secret within the heavens and the earth"﴾ [al-Furqan: 6], and so on, along with other verses.

Regarding the meaning of His saying in this verse, ﴿and what is yet more hidden (akhfa)﴾, there are well-known opinions, all of which are true and are supported by the Qur'an. Some scholars said: ﴿He knows the secret﴾ means what the servant says secretly, ﴿and what is yet more hidden﴾ means and He knows what is more hidden than the secret, which is what the soul whispers to itself, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And We have certainly created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16]. And some scholars said: ﴿then indeed He knows the secret﴾ means what the soul whispers to itself, ﴿and what is yet more hidden﴾ than that, which is what Allah knows the human will do before the human knows that he will do it, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And they have deeds other than that which they are doing﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 63], and as He, Exalted, said: ﴿He is most knowing of you when He produced you from the earth and when you were fetuses in the wombs of your mothers. So do not attribute purity to yourselves; He is most knowing of who fears Him﴾ [al-Najm: 32]. So Allah knows what a person conceals today and what he will conceal tomorrow, while the servant does not know what is in tomorrow, as Zuhayr said in his mu'allaqa:

؎ And I know the knowledge of today and of yesterday before it, but as for the knowledge of what is in tomorrow, I am blind to it.

His saying, Exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿akhfa﴾ is a comparative form (ism tafdil), as we have explained, that is, (p-7) and He knows what is more hidden than the secret. As for the saying of one who said that "akhfa" is a past-tense verb, meaning that He knows the secret of creation and concealed from them what He Himself knows, like His saying: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, but they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 110], this is clearly weak, as is not hidden.

His saying, Exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret﴾ means: you have no need to raise your voice in supplication or the like, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾ [al-A'raf: 55], and He, Exalted, said: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself in humility and fear, and without loudness of speech﴾ [al-A'raf: 205]. This meaning is clarified by the authentic hadith, when the Prophet ﷺ heard his companions raising their voices with takbir, he ﷺ said: "Be gentle with yourselves, for you are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; rather you are calling upon One who is All-Hearing, All-Seeing. Indeed, the One you call upon is closer to one of you than the neck of his mount."

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that He alone is the one worshipped, and that to Him belong the most beautiful names. He made clear that He alone is the one worshipped in verses too numerous to be counted, such as His saying: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and His saying: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾ and the rest of the verse [Muhammad: 19].

In other places He made clear that to Him belong the most beautiful names, and in some places He added the command to call upon Him by them, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180], and His saying: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ [al-Isra': 110]. In another place He added a warning against those who deviate concerning His names, namely His saying: ﴿And leave those who deviate concerning His names. They will be recompensed for what they used to do﴾ [al-A'raf: 180].

Some scholars said: Among their deviation concerning His names is that they derived al-'Uzza from the name al-'Aziz (the Mighty), and al-Lat from the name Allah. And in the authentic hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, Allah has ninety-nine names, one hundred less one. Whoever enumerates them enters Paradise." Some hadiths also indicate that among His names, majestic and exalted is He, are those that He has kept to Himself and did not teach to His creation, such as the hadith: "I ask You by every name that belongs to You, by which You named Yourself, or sent down in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept to Yourself in the knowledge of the unseen with You," and the rest of the hadith.

His saying: ﴿al-Husna﴾ is the feminine form of al-Ahsan (the most beautiful). He described His names, majestic and exalted is He, with the feminine singular form only because the broken plural (jam' al-taksir) in general and the sound feminine plural (jam' al-mu'annath al-salim) function in the manner of a singular feminine noun with metaphorical feminine gender, as he indicated in al-Khulasah (Ibn Malik's versified grammar) with his saying:

"The ta' together with a plural other than the sound masculine plural, [and the plural] of a masculine noun, is like the ta' in 'iḥdā al-labin."

A parallel to His saying here, ﴿al-Asma' al-Husna﴾, in describing a plural with the singular feminine form, is His saying: ﴿of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 23], and His saying: ﴿other uses﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ and the verses that follow [Ta-Ha: 9].

We have already explained the verses that clarify this in Surah "Maryam," in the discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We called him from the right side of the mount and brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam: 52]. That explanation suffices, so there is no need to repeat it here.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 15:

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-335) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah Ta-Ha

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I almost conceal it﴾.

This noble verse may give the impression that He, exalted and high, has not actually concealed it, but that He came close to concealing it, because kāda (to be about to) is a verb of approximation.

Other verses have explicitly stated that He has concealed it, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them but He﴾ [al-An'am: 59].

It is also established from the Prophet ﷺ that the intended "keys of the unseen" are the five mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ and the verse [31].

And like His saying: ﴿Say, "Its knowledge is only with my Lord"﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], and His saying: ﴿About what are you [concerned] to mention it?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 43], and others besides these verses.

The answer is from seven aspects:

The first, which is the preferred view: the meaning of the verse is "I almost conceal it from myself," i.e., if that were possible. This is according to the custom of the Arabs, since the Qur'an was revealed in their language. When one of them wants to emphasize concealing a matter, he says, "I concealed it from myself," meaning he does not disclose it to anyone. From this is the saying of the poet:

Days when Hind accompanies me, and I inform her of news that I almost concealed from myself.

A similar exaggeration is the Prophet's ﷺ saying in the hadith of the seven whom Allah will shade: "A man who gave charity and concealed it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." This view is narrated from most of the exegetes, and among those who said it are Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and Abu Salih, as Ibn Jarir transmitted from them, and Ja'far al-Sadiq, as al-Alusi transmitted from him in his tafsir. This view is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ubayy: "I almost conceal it from myself," (p-336) as al-Alusi and others transmitted.

Ibn Khalawayh transmitted that it is in the codex of Ubayy likewise, with the addition: "How then shall I make it apparent to you?" and in some readings with the addition: "How then shall I make it apparent to you?" and in the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud with the addition: "How then would a created being know it," as al-Alusi and others transmitted.

The second aspect: the meaning of the verse "I almost conceal it" is "I conceal the information that it is coming," and the meaning is closer to: I almost abandon informing about its coming altogether, due to the intensity of my concealing the determination of the time of its coming.

The third aspect: the hamza in His saying "uhfīhā" is the hamza of negation (hamzat al-salb), because the Arabs often make the hamza a tool for negating the verb, as in their saying: "So-and-so complained to me, so I removed his complaint (ashkaytuhu)," i.e., I removed his complaint, and their saying: "He tied the camel, so I untied it (a'qaltuhu)," i.e., I removed its tether.

Based on this, the meaning is: "I almost conceal it," i.e., I remove its concealment by making it manifest, due to the nearness of its time, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ and the verse [54]. This view is transmitted from Abu 'Ali, as al-Alusi transmitted from him in his tafsir, and al-Nisaburi transmitted it in his tafsir from Abu al-Fath al-Mawsili.

From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Abis al-Kindi:

If you bury the disease, we will not conceal it, and if you stir up war, we will not sit idle.

According to the narration with a damma on the nun in "lā nukhfihi" [we will not conceal it]. Ibn Jarir, in his tafsir of this verse, transmitted from Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna that he said: Abu al-Khattab recited it to me, from his people in his town, with a damma on the nun in "lā nukhfihi," and its meaning is: "we will not make it manifest."

As for the well-known narration with a fatha on the nun in "lā nakhfihi," there is no evidence in the verse except according to the reading of one who reads "akādu akhfīhā" with a fatha on the hamza. Among those who read thus were Abu al-Darda', Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Humayd, and the like is narrated from Ibn Kathir and 'Asim. The usage of khafāhu yakhfīhi with a fatha on the ya' in the sense of "he made it manifest" is a well-known and sound usage, except that reading with it is not free from irregularity (shudhudh).

From this is the aforementioned line according to the narration with a fatha on the nun, and the saying of Ka'b ibn Zuhayr or another:

Persisting two months, then a third month, dimly visible, between two thrones, they reveal it.

I.e., they make it manifest. And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Concealed from their spending, as if what concealed them was a rain-cloud from an evening, drawn out.

The fourth aspect: the predicate of kāda is omitted, and the meaning according to this view is: "The Hour is coming; I almost make it manifest." So the predicate was omitted, and then the speech began with His saying: ﴿I conceal it so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾ [Ta-Ha: 15]. A parallel to this in Arabic speech is the saying of Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Burjumi:

I intended but did not do, and I almost did, and I wish that my wives had left Uthman weeping.

Meaning: "and I almost did."

The fifth aspect: kāda comes in the sense of arāda (to intend). Accordingly, the meaning of "akādu akhfīhā" is "I intend to conceal it." This view was held by al-Akhfash, Ibn al-Anbari and Abu Muslim, as al-Alusi and others transmitted from them.

Ibn Jinni said in al-Muhtasab: Among the instances of kāda used in the sense of arāda is the saying of the poet:

She intended and I intended, and that is the best intention, if the past pastime of love would return.

As al-Alusi transmitted. Some scholars said: among the instances of kāda in the sense of arāda is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus We planned for Joseph﴾ [Yusuf: 12], i.e., We intended for him, as al-Nisaburi and others mentioned.

From this is the saying of the Arabs: "I will not do such-and-such, nor do I almost," i.e., "I do not intend," as some transmitted.

The sixth aspect: kāda from Allah indicates certainty (wujub), just as 'asā indicates it in His speech, exalted is He, such as: ﴿Say, "It may be that it is near"﴾ [al-Isra': 51], i.e., it is near.

Based on this, the meaning of "akādu akhfīhā" is "I [certainly] conceal it."

The seventh aspect: kāda is a redundant particle (ṣilah). Accordingly, the meaning is "Indeed, the Hour is coming; I conceal it" ﴿so that every soul may be recompensed﴾ and the verse. The proponent of this view cited the saying of Zayd al-Khayl:

Swift toward the battle, his weapons armed, so that his opponent hardly breathes.

I.e., his opponent does not breathe. They said: from this category is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He almost could not see it﴾ [al-Nur: 40], i.e., he did not see it, and the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

When distance changed the lovers, the lingering trace of passion for Mayya did not almost depart.

I.e., it did not depart, according to this speaker's view.

They said: from this meaning is the saying of Abu al-Najm:

If news of a death reaches you, then lament a father, for the enemies have almost appeared and the sermons.

I.e., the enemies have appeared.

We have already stated that the most preferred of these views is the first, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 27:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue﴾ ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾.

Some scholars said: His saying ﴿a knot from my tongue﴾, with the indefinite noun and the singular, and his following it with ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾, indicate that he did not ask for the removal of all the knots in his tongue, but asked for the removal of a part of them, by which the understanding of his speech would be achieved while some of them remained. This meaning is indicated by other verses, such as His saying about him: ﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in speech than I, so send him with me as a helper﴾ [al-Qasas: 34], and His saying about Pharaoh: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly make himself clear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52]. The argument from Pharaoh's saying about Moses indicates that Pharaoh was known for lying and slander. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Dafʿ Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech﴾.

It is not hidden that this is from the request of Moses, which his Lord told him He had granted, by His saying: ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 36]. That is explicit in the loosening of the knot from his tongue. But some verses have come indicating that something of what was in his tongue remained, such as His saying about Pharaoh: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible and can hardly make himself clear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52], and His saying about Moses: ﴿And my brother Aaron, he is more eloquent in speech than I, so send him with me﴾ [28].

The answer is that Moses, upon him and upon our Prophet be blessings and peace, did not ask for the complete removal of what was in his tongue, but asked for the removal of the amount that prevented them from understanding his speech, as His saying ﴿that they may understand my speech﴾ indicates.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir (exegesis) of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue﴾, the following text: "He did not ask that this be removed entirely, but rather to the extent that the impediment (al-'iyy) is removed and they achieve an understanding of what he means, which is the amount needed. Had he asked for all of it, it would have been removed. But the prophets only ask according to need, and for this reason a remnant remained. Allah, the Exalted, said, reporting about Pharaoh that he said: ﴿Am I not better than this one who is contemptible﴾ ﴿and can hardly make himself clear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 52], meaning he cannot express himself clearly in speech." End of Ibn Kathir's words, verbatim.

al-Hasan al-Basri said regarding ﴿And loosen a knot from my tongue﴾: "He loosened one knot. Had he asked for more than that, he would have been given it."

Ibn Abbas said: "Moses complained to his Lord of what he feared from the family of Pharaoh regarding the man he had killed, and of the knot in his tongue, for there was in his tongue a knot that prevented him from much speech. He asked his Lord to support him with his brother Aaron, who would be a helper (ridʾ) for him and would speak on his behalf about much that his tongue could not express clearly. So He granted him his request and loosened a knot from his tongue."

Ibn Abi Hatim said: It was mentioned from Umar ibn Uthman, narrated to us by Baqiyyah, from Artah ibn al-Mundhir, narrated to me by one of the companions of Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from him, who said: A relative of his came to him and said: "There is nothing wrong with you, except that you make mistakes (talhan) in your speech, and you do not apply i'rab (case endings) in your recitation." Al-Qurazi said: "O my nephew, do I not make you understand when I speak to you?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Moses, peace be upon him, only asked his Lord to loosen a knot from his tongue so that the Children of Israel would understand his speech, and he did not ask for more than that." End of Ibn Kathir's words, verbatim.

From this, the answer given has been transmitted from al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, as we have mentioned. It is also possible to answer that Pharaoh lied about him in his saying ﴿he is more eloquent in speech than I﴾ [28], which indicates that he shared eloquence with Aaron, so both were eloquent, except that Aaron was more eloquent. On this basis there is no difficulty. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

(p-339)

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time﴾ ﴿When We inspired to your mother that which is inspired﴾ ﴿Saying: "Cast him into the chest, then cast it into the river, and let the river throw it onto the bank, and there will take him an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his."﴾.

He, exalted and majestic is He, mentions in this noble verse that He bestowed favour upon Musa another time, before His favour upon him with prophethood and with his brother Harun being sent with him. This was by delivering him from Pharaoh while he was still an infant, when He inspired to his mother, that is, He inspired her (ألهمها) and cast it into her heart. Some have said: it was a dream seen in sleep. Others have said: this inspiration to her was through an angel who spoke to her with that. Inspiration concerning a specific matter does not necessarily mean that the one to whom it is inspired is a prophet. The "an" in His saying ﴿that cast him﴾ is the explanatory (al-mufassirah), because inspiration contains the meaning of speech without its letters. The use of the relative (al-mawsul) in His saying ﴿that which is inspired﴾ is to indicate the magnification of the matter mentioned.

Like His saying: ﴿So there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 78], and His saying: ﴿Then He inspired His servant that which He inspired﴾ [An-Najm: 10]. The chest (al-tabut) is the box. The sea (al-yamm) is the large body of water. The shore (al-sahil) is the bank of the sea. The sea mentioned is the Nile of Egypt. And al-qadhf is casting, placing, and from it is His saying, exalted: ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26]. The meaning of ﴿cast him into the chest﴾ is: place him in the box. (p-9) The pronoun in His saying ﴿that cast him﴾ refers to Musa without disagreement. As for the pronoun in His saying ﴿then cast him into the river﴾

and His saying ﴿then let the river throw him﴾, it was said that it refers to the chest. The correct view is that it refers to Musa inside the chest, because separating pronouns is not good. And His saying ﴿there will take him an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾ [Ta-Ha: 39] is Pharaoh. The imperative form in His saying ﴿then let the river throw him onto the bank﴾ has two well-known views among the scholars:

The first: that the imperative form means a report (khabar). Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr al-Muhit: "﴿Then let it throw him﴾ is an imperative whose meaning is a report, and it came in the imperative form for emphasis, since the imperative is the most decisive and most binding of verbs."

The second view: that the imperative form in His saying ﴿then let it throw him﴾ is intended as the imperative of creation and decree (al-amr al-kawni al-qadari), like His saying: ﴿Indeed His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it "Be," and it is﴾ [Ya-Sin: 82]. So the river must throw him onto the bank, because Allah commanded it so by creation and decree. We have already mentioned views resembling these two in the discussion of His saying, exalted: ﴿let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension﴾ [Maryam: 75].

What He, exalted and majestic, mentioned in these verses He clarified in another place, like His saying in al-Qasas: ﴿And We inspired to the mother of Musa: "Nurse him, and when you fear for him, then cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve; indeed We will return him to you and make him among the messengers."﴾ ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [al-Qasas: 7-8]. He, exalted, has also explained the intensity of his mother's distress over him when she cast him into the sea, and the sea threw him onto the bank, and his enemy Pharaoh took him, in His saying: ﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty; she would have almost revealed it, had We not fortified her heart so that she would be among the believers﴾ [al-Qasas: 10].

His saying, exalted, in this noble verse ﴿will take him﴾ is in the jussive mood as an answer to the demand which is ﴿then let the river throw him onto the bank﴾. If it is taken to mean the imperative of creation, the matter is clear. If it is taken to mean a report, then the jussive is observance of the verbal form. And Allah knows best. It is mentioned in her story that she made for him the chest and coated it with pitch (al-qar), which is tar, so that water would not seep through to Musa inside the chest, and she stuffed it with carded cotton. It was also said that the chest mentioned was made of sycamore wood (al-jummayz), and that the one who carpentered it for her was a believer of the family of Pharaoh, said to be named Hizqil. She had tied a rope to the chest, and when she feared for Musa from the eyes of Pharaoh she would send him into the river and hold the end of the rope with her; when she felt safe, she would pull him back to her by the rope. Once she went to tie the rope in her house, it slipped from her and the river carried away the chest in which Musa was, and this caused her such grief and worry as Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿And the heart of the mother of Musa became empty﴾ and what follows [al-Qasas: 10].

(p-10) What He, exalted and majestic, mentioned in this noble verse of His successive favours upon Musa, where He said ﴿And We had already bestowed favour upon you another time﴾ [Ta-Ha: 37], He pointed to something similar in His saying: ﴿And We had already bestowed favour upon Musa and Harun﴾ and what follows [as-Saffat: 114].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 39:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾.

Among the effects of this love which Allah placed upon His servant and prophet Musa, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, is what He, glorified and exalted, mentioned in "al-Qasas" in His saying: ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said, "[He will be] a comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him"﴾ [al-Qasas: 9]. Ibn 'Abbas said regarding ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾: that is, Allah loved him and made him beloved to His creation. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: He placed upon him a radiance of beauty such that whoever saw him could hardly hold back from him. Qatadah said: There was in the eyes of Musa a comeliness; no one saw him without loving him and being enamoured of him. Al-Qurtubi said:

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When your sister went along and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve.﴾

There is disagreement about the governing element (al-'amil al-nasib) of the adverbial time-noun "idh" (when) in His words ﴿when your sister went along﴾. It was said: it is "alqaytu" (I cast), i.e., "I cast upon you love from Me when your sister went along." It was also said: it is "tuṣna'a" (you be raised), i.e., "you were raised under My eye when your sister went along." And it was said: it is a substitute (badal) for the "idh" in His words ﴿when We inspired to your mother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 38].

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you say, how can the substitution be valid when the two times are different and distant? I say: just as it is valid, even though the time is extended and its two ends are far apart, for a man to say to you, "I met so-and-so in the year such-and-such," and you reply, "I met him at that time too," though perhaps he met him at its beginning and you at its end.

What Exalted and Most High mentions in this noble verse, namely that his sister walked up to them and said to them ﴿Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?﴾, He, Exalted and Most High, clarified in Surah al-Qasas. There He made clear that this sister was sent by his mother to learn his news after his departure into the sea, and that she had seen him from afar while they were not aware of it. And that God had forbidden him the wet-nurses other than his mother, a prohibition that was cosmic and decreed (tahrim kawni qadari). So his sister said to them ﴿Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?﴾, meaning, to a nursing woman whose breast he would accept, and who would nurse him for you with sincerity and trustworthiness. This is in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Moses's sister said, "Follow him up," so she watched him from a distance, while they did not perceive it. And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses before that, so she said, "Shall I direct you to a household who will rear him for you while they are sincere to him?" So We returned him to his mother, that her eye might be comforted and she not grieve, and that she might know that the promise of God is true, but most of them do not know.﴾ [Al-Qasas: 11–13]

So His saying in this verse of al-Qasas, ﴿And she said to his sister﴾, means: Moses's mother said to his sister, who was her daughter, ﴿Follow him up﴾, i.e., follow his trail and seek out his news until you learn the truth of his situation.

His saying ﴿so she watched him from a distance﴾ means: she saw him from afar, as one who turns away from him, looking at him while seeming not to want him, ﴿while they did not perceive it﴾, that she was his sister who had come to learn his news. She found him refusing to accept the breast of any nursing woman, because God says: ﴿And We had forbidden him the wet-nurses﴾, i.e., a cosmic, decreed prohibition, meaning We prevented him from them so that his return to his mother would be made easy. For if he had accepted another, they would have given him to that other who accepted him, to nurse and rear him, and he would not have returned to his mother.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that when she said to them ﴿Shall I direct you to a household who will rear him for you while they are sincere to him?", they seized her, doubted her matter, and said to her: "What makes you know of their sincerity to him and their compassion for him?"

She said to them: "Their sincerity to him and their compassion for him is out of desire for the king's pleasure and hope for his benefit." So they let her go. When she had said that to them and escaped their harm, they went with her to her family's home, and they entered with him to his mother. She gave him her breast, and he took it. They rejoiced greatly at that, and the messenger went to the king's wife, who summoned Moses's mother, treated her well, and gave her a great gift, though she did not know that she was his mother in reality, but only because he had accepted her breast. Then Asiya asked her to stay with her and nurse him, but she refused and said: "I have a husband and children, and I cannot stay with you. But if you wish, I will nurse him in my house." The wife of Pharaoh agreed to that and allotted her maintenance, gifts, clothing, and generous kindness. So Moses's mother returned with her son, whom God had replaced her fear with security, in honor and dignity, and provision of a home. End of quotation from Ibn Kathir.

His saying in the verse of al-Qasas: ﴿and that she might know that the promise of God is true﴾ [al-Qasas: 13]. The promise of God mentioned is His saying: ﴿Do not fear and do not grieve; We will surely return him to you and make him among the messengers﴾ [al-Qasas: 7]. The historians say that the name of Moses's sister mentioned is "Maryam."

As for His saying ﴿so that her eye might be comforted﴾: if we say that "kay" in it is a verbal particle (masdariyya), then the lam is elided, meaning "in order that her eye be comforted." If we say that it is causal (ta'lil), then the verb is in the subjunctive governed by an implied "an." As for His saying ﴿her eye be comforted﴾, it was said: its root is from "qarar" (settling), because the eye of a person settles upon what he loves and does not look at anything else, as Abu al-Tayyib said:

A slender figure on which the eyes rest, as if a girdle of pupils were upon it.

It was also said: its root is from "qurr" with a damma on the qaf, which is cold. The Arabs say: "yawm qarr" with a fatha, meaning a cold day, and from it the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

Tamim ibn Murr and its partisans, and Kinda around me, all patient,
when they mount horses and don armour, the earth burns and the day is cold.

And from it also the saying of the generous Hatim al-Ta'i:

Kindle, for the night is cold, and the wind, O kindler, is a biting wind.
So that someone passing may see your fire; if he brings a guest, you are free.

According to this view, the comfort of the eye is from its coolness, because the eye of one who is pleased is cool, and tears of weeping from joy are very cool, unlike the eye of the grieving, which is hot, and tears of weeping from grief are very hot. Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "More burning than the tears of the muqillat." These are women whose children do not survive, so their grief intensifies at the death of their children and the heat of their tears intensifies accordingly.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you killed a soul, and We delivered you from distress and tested you with a testing.﴾

Exalted and Most High did not explain in this noble verse the cause of his killing of this soul, nor whose soul it was, nor the means by which He delivered him from that distress, nor the trial with which He tested him. But He explained in Surah al-Qasas the story of the slain man mentioned in His saying: ﴿And he entered the city at a time of heedlessness of its people, and found in it two men fighting, one from his party and the other from his enemy. The one from his party sought his aid against the one from his enemy, so Moses struck him and killed him. He said, "This is of Satan's work; indeed he is an enemy, a misleading, manifest one." He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me." So He forgave him; indeed He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ [al-Qasas: 15–16]. He pointed to the slain man mentioned in His saying: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I have killed a soul among them, so I fear they will kill me."﴾ [al-Qasas: 33]. This is what is meant by the "sin" in His saying, exalted is He, about Moses: ﴿So send to Harun. And they have a charge against me, so I fear they will kill me.﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 13–14]. It is also what Pharaoh meant by his saying to Moses, as God related it: ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 19], and the verse.

In al-Qasas, He, exalted, also alluded to Moses's distress and to the means by which God delivered him from it, in His saying: ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city running. He said, "O Moses, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave; indeed I am to you one of the sincere advisers."﴾ ﴿So he left it, fearful, watchful. He said, "My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people."﴾ ﴿And when he turned toward Madyan, he said, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way."﴾ (continuing to His saying) ﴿He said, "Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people."﴾ [al-Qasas: 20–25]. As for His saying ﴿and We tested you with a testing﴾, some people of knowledge said: "futun" is a verbal noun (masdar), and the masdar of a transitive triliteral verb sometimes comes in the pattern fu'ul. Others said: it is the plural of "fitna." Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "futunan" may be a masdar on the pattern fu'ul of a transitive verb, like thubur, shukur, and kufur. It may also be the plural of "fitan" or "fitna," with the feminine ending omitted, like huju and budur for hujza and budra, meaning, "We tested you with various kinds of trials."

An explanation of the testing mentioned has come in a well-known hadith among the people of knowledge, called the hadith of "al-Futun," which al-Nasa'i transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and Ibn Kathir cited in his tafsir from al-Nasa'i with its chain. It is a long hadith which indicates that the testing encompasses all the ordeals that befell Moses from Pharaoh in his childhood and adulthood: such as the fear for him of slaughter when he was an infant, for which reason he was placed in the chest and cast into the river, and the river threw him onto the shore; and such as his fear, as an adult, that Pharaoh would kill him for the Copt he had killed. On this view, the verses in which those ordeals are mentioned clarify the testing according to Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation of the term. Ibn Kathir said, after he cited the hadith of the testing in full: "Thus did al-Nasa'i narrate it in al-Sunan al-Kubra. Abu Ja'far ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also transmitted it, all of them in their tafsirs, from the hadith of Yazid ibn Harun with it. It is mawquf, from the words of Ibn 'Abbas, and there is nothing marfu' in it except a little of it. It seems that Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, received it from what is permitted to be transmitted of the Isra'iliyyat from Ka'b al-Ahbar or others. And Allah knows best." And I heard our shaykh, the hafiz Abu al-Hajjaj al-Mizzi, say the same. End of quotation.

* *

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you stayed for years among the people of Madyan; then you came, O Moses, according to a decree.﴾

The years he spent among the people of Madyan are those mentioned in His saying: ﴿He said, "I want to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you hire yourself to me for eight years; but if you complete ten, that is from you."﴾ [al-Qasas: 27]. We have already mentioned in Surah Maryam that he completed the ten years, and we explained the evidence for that from the Sunnah. Thereby you know that the term (ajal) in His saying: ﴿So when Moses had fulfilled the term﴾ [al-Qasas: 29] is ten years, not eight. Some people of knowledge said: Moses stayed in Madyan for twenty-eight years, ten of which were the dowry of his father-in-law's daughter, and eighteen which he spent by his own choice. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

The most evident of the views concerning His saying: ﴿Then you came, O Moses, according to a decree﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40] is that you came according to the decree that I decreed and that was foreknown in My knowledge, that you would come in it, so you did not delay from it nor advance beyond it, as He, exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything in measure﴾ [al-Qamar: 49], and He said: ﴿And everything with Him is by measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 8], and He said: ﴿And the command of Allah is a decree determined﴾ [al-Ahzab: 38]. Jarir said, praising 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz:

He attained the caliphate, or it was for him a decree, as Moses came to his Lord according to a decree.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in remembering Me.﴾ ﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ "In remembering Me." "Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed."

Some scholars of knowledge (ahl al-'ilm) said: The meaning of "signs" in His saying here, ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾, is the nine signs mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra' 101], and His saying: ﴿And put your hand into your pocket; it will come out white without disease, among nine signs﴾ [al-Naml 12]. The nine signs mentioned are: the staff, the white hand... to the end of them. We have already discussed them thoroughly in the surah of "Bani Isra'il" (Surat al-Isra').

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed.﴾

The root of tughyan (transgression) is exceeding the limit, and from it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose beyond its limit, We carried you in the flowing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah 11]. Allah has explained the severity of Pharaoh's transgression and his exceeding the limit in His saying about him: ﴿So he said, "I am your lord, the most high"﴾ [al-Nazi'at 24],

• and His saying about him: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas 38],

• and His saying about him also: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 29].

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And do not slacken﴾ is the present tense of wanā, yanī, according to the rule of Ibn Malik in the Khulasa:

"Delete [the waw] from the imperative and the present of 'kawa'ada', and this is consistently applied to 'kaʿida'."

Al-wanā in the language means weakness, slackness, fatigue, and exhaustion. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays in his Mu'allaqah:

"Swift, when the galloping steeds in exhaustion raised dust at al-Kadid al-Murakkal."

And the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"Muhammad did not slacken since Allah forgave him what passed and what remained."

So His saying: ﴿and do not slacken in remembering Me﴾ means: do not weaken, and do not tire, in remembering Me. Allah has praised those who remember Him in all their states in His saying: ﴿Those who remember Allah standing, sitting, and on their sides﴾ [Al 'Imran 191], and He commanded the remembrance of Allah at the encounter with the enemy in His saying: ﴿When you meet a company, stand firm and remember Allah much﴾ [al-Anfal 45], as has been explained previously.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this noble verse: The meaning is that the two of them should not tire in remembering Allah while confronting Pharaoh, so that the remembrance of Allah may be a help to them against him, a strength for them, and a conquering authority over him, as came in the hadith: "Indeed, My servant, every servant of Mine, is the one who remembers Me while he is engaged with his opponent." End of quote from him.

Some scholars of knowledge said: ﴿and do not slacken in remembering Me﴾ means: do not cease in remembering Me. They cited for this the saying of Tarafah:

"As if the tall cooking pots before them were domes they built, never ceasing to boil."

That is, they never cease to boil. Its meaning returns to what we have mentioned. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 44:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he will be reminded or fear [Allah]﴾.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded His prophets Musa and Harun, upon them both and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, that they should say to Pharaoh, while conveying the message of Allah to him, ﴿gentle speech﴾, that is, soft, easy, tender words, containing nothing that would anger or repel him. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has explained the meaning of gentle speech in this verse by His saying: ﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed. And say, "Would you like to purify yourself? And I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear [Him]"﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 17-18]. And this, by Allah, is the utmost of gentleness, softness and tenderness of speech, as you see. What Musa and Harun were commanded in this noble verse, Allah has alluded to in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction, and argue with them in a manner that is best﴾ [An-Nahl: 125].

Issue

From this noble verse it is derived that calling to Allah must be with kindness and gentleness, not with harshness, severity and violence, as we have explained in Surah "Al-Ma'idah" in the discussion of His saying: ﴿You are responsible for yourselves﴾ [verse 105]. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this verse: Yazid al-Raqashi said, regarding His saying ﴿And speak to him with gentle speech﴾ [Ta-Ha: 44]: "O you who show affection to one who opposes him, how then would he treat one who supports and calls to him?" End of quote. And indeed he spoke truly who said:

*Even if Pharaoh, when he transgressed and spoke against Allah with falsehood and lies,*

*Had turned in repentance to Allah, seeking forgiveness, he would have found Allah none but Forgiving.*

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾, we have previously mentioned the saying of some scholars: that "la'alla" in the Qur'an carries the meaning of causation (ta'lil), except in the verse of Surah "Ash-Shu'ara'": ﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, perhaps you may abide forever﴾ [129], where it means "as if" (ka'anna). We have also previously mentioned that "la'alla" comes in Arabic to express causation. From this is his saying:

*You said to us, "Cease the wars, so that we may cease,"*
*And you gave us every firm covenant.*

*When we ceased the war, your pledges became*
*Like a mirage shimmering in the open plain.*

So his saying "la'allana nakuff" means: in order that we may cease.

And some scholars said: ﴿perhaps he will be reminded or fear﴾ means according to your hope and expectation, so the hoping and expecting indicated by "la'alla" refers to the side of the humans. Al-Qurtubi attributed this view to the senior grammarians, such as Sibawayh and others.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So go to him and say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel and do not torture them. We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. And peace is upon him who follows guidance."﴾

The dual alif in His saying "fa'tiyāhu" (فَأْتِياهُ) refers to Musa and Harun, and the pronoun (hā') refers to Fir'awn. That is: "So come to Fir'awn and say to him, 'Indeed, we are two messengers to you from your Lord, so send with us the Children of Israel,' that is, release them and let them go with us wherever they wish, and do not torture them."

The torture that Allah forbade Fir'awn to inflict on the Children of Israel is that mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿And [recall] when We saved you from the people of Fir'awn, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 49]. It is also mentioned in Surat Ibrahim in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when Musa said to his people, "Remember the favor of Allah upon you when He saved you from the people of Fir'awn, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive."﴾ [Ibrahim: 6]. In Surat al-A'raf, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [recall] when We saved you from the people of Fir'awn, who were afflicting you with the worst torment, killing your sons and keeping your women alive.﴾ [al-A'raf: 141]. In Surat al-Dukhan, in His saying: ﴿And We had already saved the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment, from Fir'awn. Indeed, he was haughty among the transgressors.﴾ [al-Dukhan: 30–31]. And in Surat al-Shu'ara', in His saying: ﴿And this is a favor you bestow upon me, that you have enslaved the Children of Israel.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 22].

What Allah commanded Musa and Harun in this verse of Ta-Ha, namely that they should say to Fir'awn that they are the messengers of his Lord to him, and that he should be commanded to send the Children of Israel and not torture them, He indicated in other than this place, such as His saying in Surat al-Shu'ara': ﴿So come to Fir'awn and say, "Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds," [saying], "Send with us the Children of Israel."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16–17].

Admonition

If it is said: what is the reason for the singular in His saying ﴿Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ in al-Shu'ara', although they are two messengers, as the word "messenger" came dual in Ta-Ha? So what is the reason for the dual in Ta-Ha and the singular in al-Shu'ara', when each of the two expressions, the dual and the singular, is intended to refer to Musa and Harun?

What appears to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the word "rasul" (messenger) is originally a verbal noun (masdar) that is used as a descriptive, and when a masdar is used as a descriptor it is mentioned and kept singular, as we have mentioned many times before. So the singular in al-Shu'ara' is in view of the original status of "rasul" as a masdar. The dual in Ta-Ha is in view of its acquired descriptive function, turning away from the original. For this reason "rasul" is pluralized in consideration of its acquired descriptive quality, and it is kept singular while meaning the plural, in view of its original status as a masdar. An example of its plural is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 253] and similar verses in the Qur'an. An example of its singular used to mean the plural is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb al-Hudhali:

*Convey to her on my behalf, and the best of messengers is the one who knows best the sides of the news.*

And from the use of "rasul" to mean the masdar in its original sense is the saying of another poet:

*Surely the slanderers have lied, for I did not speak before them with any word, nor did I send them with a messenger.*

That is, with a message.

And the saying of another:

*Ah, convey to the Banu 'Usm a messenger, that I am independent of your ... [people].*

That is, convey to them a message.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿We have come to you with a sign﴾ is intended to mean the category of sign, which applies to the staff, the hand, and others, by the evidence of other verses indicating that.

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And peace is upon him who follows guidance﴾ includes peace upon Fir'awn if he follows guidance. It is understood from the verse that whoever does not follow guidance has no peace upon him, and that is so. That is why, at the beginning of the letter that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans, it stated:

"In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), to Heraclius, the great one of the Romans: Peace be upon him who follows guidance. To proceed: I invite you with the call of Islam..." to the end of his letter (ﷺ).

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So say, "Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord"﴾, the verse.

It indicates that they are two messengers, namely Musa and Harun. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So say, "Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16] gives the impression that the messenger is one.

The answer is in two respects:

The first: the meaning of His saying ﴿Indeed, we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ is that each one of us is a messenger of the Lord of the worlds, like the saying of al-Burjumi: [Tawil meter]

*So indeed I and Qayyar in it are strangers.*

This was permissible because the intended meaning is evident from the context of the speech.

The second: the original form of "rasul" is a masdar, like "qabul" and "walu'," so it was used as a noun, and therefore its plural and dual are permissible, in view of its being used as a descriptive; and it is permissible to keep it singular while intending the dual or plural, in view of its original status as a masdar. From the use of "rasul" for other than the singular is the saying of the poet:

*Convey to her on my behalf, and the best of the messen-* ger is the one who knows best the sides of the news.

That is, "the best of the messengers." The use of "rasul" to mean the masdar is frequent, and from it is his saying:

*Surely the slanderers have lied, for I did not speak before them with any word, nor did I send them with a messenger.*

That is, with a message.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away.﴾

What Allah, exalted and most high, mentions in this noble verse about Musa and Harun is that Allah revealed to them both that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away. Something of this nature is indicated in many verses of the Book of Allah, the Exalted.

For example, His saying: ﴿But as for one who transgressed and preferred the worldly life, indeed, Hellfire will be his refuge.﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 37–39]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire flaming fiercely. None will burn therein except the most wretched, who denied and turned away.﴾ [Al-Layl: 14–16]

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed, but denied and turned away. Then he went to his family, swaggering. Woe to you, and woe! Then woe to you, and woe!﴾ [Al-Qiyamah: 31–35]

And other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said, "Then who is your Lord, O Musa?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Our Lord is the One who gave each thing its creation and then guided [it]."﴾

In this noble verse, exalted and majestic is He, He mentions that when Musa and Harun had conveyed to Pharaoh what they had been commanded to convey, he said to them: "Who is your Lord, the one you claim sent you to me?" – pretending that he did not know Him. He did not recognize any god for them other than himself, as he said: ﴿I do not know for you any god other than myself﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and he said: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 29]. Exalted is He, in another place, has made clear that his saying ﴿Then who is your Lord﴾ was the feigned ignorance of one who knows that he is a servant owned by the Lord of the worlds, and that is in His saying: ﴿[Musa] said, "You certainly know that these have not sent down [these signs] except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as evidence"﴾ [al-Isra': 102], and His saying: ﴿And when Our signs came to them as visible, they said, "This is clear magic." And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 13–14], as has previously been explained. The question of Pharaoh about the Lord of Musa, and Musa's answer to him, came clarified in Surat ash-Shu'ara' more fully than here, in His saying: ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?" [Musa] said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you are certain." He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?" He said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the earliest." He said, "Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is a madman." He said, "Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them, if you were rational." He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned." He said, "Even if I come to you with something clear?" He said, "Then bring it, if you should be of the truthful." So he threw down his staff, and at once it was a serpent, manifest. And he drew out his hand, and at once it was white for the observers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 23–33], to the end of the story.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿He said, "Our Lord is the One who gave each thing its creation and then guided [it]"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], there are for the scholars several interpretations, none of which contradicts another, all of them are true, and there is no obstacle to the verse including all of them. Among them: the meaning of ﴿gave each thing its creation and then guided﴾ is that He gave each thing a counterpart to its creation in form and shape, such as the males of the children of Adam, He gave them counterparts of their creation among the females as spouses. And as for the males of the beasts, He gave them counterparts of their creation in their form and shape among the females as spouses. So He did not give a human a creation contrary to his own, so as to marry him to female beasts, nor beasts to female humans, then He guided all of them to the path of marriage from which comes offspring and increase, how it is to be done, and He guided all of them to all their benefits of food, drink, and other things.

This view is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, through the chain of 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, and from as-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. And from Ibn 'Abbas also: ﴿then guided﴾ means He guided it to affection, association, and marriage.

Some of the people of knowledge said: ﴿gave each thing its creation and then guided﴾ means: He gave each thing its suitability, then guided it to what makes it right. This is narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Some of the people of knowledge said: ﴿gave each thing its creation and then guided﴾: that is, He gave each thing its appropriate form suited to it. So He did not place the human in the form of an animal, nor the animal in the form of a human, but He created each thing in the shape suited to it, measuring it precisely, as the poet said:

"For everything He has a form, and thus Allah does whatever He wills."

By "creation" he means "form." This view is narrated from Mujahid, Muqatil, 'Ata'iyyah, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿then guided﴾ each kind to its provision and to its mate.

Some of the people of knowledge said: ﴿gave each thing its creation﴾: that is, He gave each thing its form and shape that corresponds to the benefit attached to it, just as He gave the eye the shape that corresponds to sight, and the ear the shape that suits hearing. Likewise the nose, the foot, the tongue, and others: each one of them corresponds to the benefit attached to it, without deputizing for it. This view is narrated from ad-Dahhak. On all these mentioned views, His saying ﴿each thing﴾ is the first object of ﴿gave﴾, and ﴿its creation﴾ is the second object.

Some of the people of knowledge said: indeed ﴿its creation﴾ is the first object, and ﴿each thing﴾ is the second object. On this view the meaning is: He, exalted is He, gave the creatures everything they need, then guided them to the way of using it. It is known that the object of the two objects in the pattern of kasa (to clothe), and from it "gave" in the verse, there is no obstacle to delaying it and placing the last object first, provided the ambiguity is avoided and nothing occurs that requires following the original order, as is known in the science of grammar. The author of the Khulasah alluded to this with his saying:

"The original order is required by a compelling reason, and abandoning that original order is sometimes seen as necessary."

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, said: There is no obstacle to the noble verse including all the views mentioned. For there is no doubt that Allah gave the creatures everything they need in this world, then guided them to the way of benefiting from it. And there is no doubt that He gave each kind its suitable shape and form, and gave each male and female the shape suitable to them from their own kind for marriage, affection, and association. And He gave each organ the shape fitting the benefit attached to it. So glory be to Him, exalted is He! How great is His majesty and how perfect is His power!

In these things mentioned in the meaning of this noble verse there are decisive proofs that He, exalted is He, is the Lord of everything, and that He alone is the One worshipped, exalted is He:

﴿There is no deity except Him. Everything will perish except His Face. His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Qasas: 88].

Taqi ad-Din Abu al-'Abbas Ibn Taymiyyah, in his treatise on the sciences of the Qur'an, established that this kind of difference among the early scholars (salaf) regarding the meanings of verses is not a real contradictory difference in which one contradicts the other, but a difference of variety, which does not make one contradict the other, and the verses encompass all of it, so it is proper to take them as including all of that. He clarified that this is the approach followed by the principles of the four Imams, may Allah be pleased with them, and he attributed it to a group of the best people of the four schools. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said, "Then who is your Lord, O Musa?"﴾.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Said, "Then who is your Lord"﴾ requires that the addressees be two, and His saying ﴿O Musa﴾ requires that the addressee be one. The answer is in three aspects:

The first: that Pharaoh intended to address Musa alone, and when an addressee shares the speech with another who is not addressed, the addressee is given precedence over the other, as if you addressed a man who shares a matter with another, the second being absent, so you say to the one present of them: "What is the matter with you, did you both do such-and-such?" while the addressee is one. This is evident.

The second aspect: that he addressed both of them together, and singled out Musa with the call, because he was the principal in the message.

The third: that he addressed both of them together, and singled out Musa with the call to match the endings of the verses while the meaning is clear. A parallel to the verse is His saying: ﴿So do not let him expel you both from the Garden, so you would suffer﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117]. It may be answered that the woman is a follower of her husband; and that the hardship of toil and labor is borne by men more than women; and that the address was to Adam alone, and the woman was mentioned in what Adam was addressed with, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117]. So she was mentioned in what Adam was addressed with, while the addressee was him alone; and therefore He said "so you would suffer," because the address was not directed to her. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 53:

Allah's words: ﴿He who made the earth for you a cradle, and threaded for you therein roads, and sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants.﴾ ﴿Eat, and pasture your livestock. Indeed in that are signs for people of intellect.﴾

These readers recited this word: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and al-Kisāʾī read "mahdan" (مَهْدًا) with a fatḥah on the mīm and a sukūn on the hāʾ, without an alif. The rest of the Seven (al-sabʿah) read it with a kasrah on the mīm and a fatḥah on the hāʾ followed by an alif. (Qirāʾah: a recognized mode of Qur'anic recitation.) Al-mihād means the bedding/couch, and al-mahd has the same meaning. That its origin is a verbal noun (maṣdar) does not preclude its use as a noun for a bed.

His words in this verse, ﴿He who made the earth for you﴾, are in the position of a descriptive adjunct (naʿt) for "my Lord" (رَبِّي) in His earlier words, ﴿Said he: "The knowledge of it is with my Lord in a Book; my Lord neither errs nor forgets"﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 52]. That is: my Lord, who made the earth a cradle for you, does not err. It may also be the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, meaning: He is the One who made the earth for you. It may also be in the accusative of praise (naṣb ʿalā al-madḥ), and this is better than positing an implied verb such as "I mean" (aʿnī) as the governing agent of the accusative. Al-Shinqiti pointed to these grammatical (iʿrāb) possibilities in al-Khulāṣah with his words:

"Put it in the nominative or the accusative, if you break off, with a hidden subject (mubtadaʾ) or a hidden governing verb that will not appear."

Thus said many scholars. The verified view is that it is necessarily the predicate of an omitted subject, because it is a new, independent statement from Allah's speech. It cannot be attached to Mūsā's words, ﴿my Lord does not err﴾, because His words ﴿and We brought forth﴾ specify that it is part of Allah's speech, as Abū Ḥayyān noted in al-Baḥr. And Allah knows best.

In these two verses, may He be exalted, has shown four of His great signs which indicate that He alone is the One worthy of worship. Along with being signs of His perfect power and His right to be worshipped alone to the exclusion of others, they are also among the great blessings upon the children of Adam.

The first: His spreading out the earth in this marvelous pattern.

The second: His making in it roads through which the children of Adam pass and by which they reach from one region to another.

The third: His sending down water from the sky in this marvelous pattern.

The fourth: His bringing forth various kinds of plants from the earth.

As for the first, which is His making the earth a cradle, He mentioned the favour of it, together with using it as proof that He alone is the One worthy of worship, in many places in His Book. Such as His words: ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say: "The Mighty, the All-Knowing created them." He who made the earth for you a cradle…﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9–10], and His words: ﴿Have We not made the earth a bed, and the mountains as pegs?﴾ [al-Nabaʾ: 6–7], and His words: ﴿And the earth — We spread it out, and how excellent are the Spreaders!﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt: 48], and His words: ﴿And He it is who stretched out the earth and placed therein firm mountains and rivers﴾ [al-Raʿd: 3]. The verses of this kind are very many.

As for the second, which is His making roads in it, the favour and the proof were mentioned in many verses. Such as His words in al-Zukhruf: ﴿And if you ask them who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say: "The Mighty, the All-Knowing created them." He who made the earth for you a cradle, and made for you therein roads, that you may be guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 9], (p-22) and His words: ﴿And We made in it wide passages as roads, that they may be guided﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 31]. We have already presented the verses that indicate this in surah al-Naḥl, in the discussion of His words: ﴿and rivers and roads, that you may be guided﴾ [al-Naḥl: 15].

As for the third and fourth, which are the sending down of water from the sky and the bringing forth of plants from the earth by it, both have been repeated in the Qur'an as favours and as proofs together. Such as His words: ﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky, from it is drink, and from it are trees in which you pasture [your animals]﴾ ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby crops, olives, date palms, and grapes﴾ [al-Naḥl: 10–11]. We have already presented the verses that indicate this.

As for His words in this noble verse: ﴿and sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth﴾, it is an iltifāt (a shift in grammatical person) from the third person (ghaybah) to the first person of speech (takallum), in the form of magnification (taʿẓīm). Its parallel in the Qur'an is His words in al-Anʿām: ﴿And it is He who sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby the growth of every thing, then We brought forth from it green [shoots], from which We bring forth grain layered﴾ [al-Anʿām: 99], and His words in Fāṭir: ﴿Do you not see that Allah sent down water from the sky, and We brought forth thereby fruits of varying colours?﴾ [Fāṭir: 27], and His words in al-Naml: ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow thereby gardens of delightful beauty﴾ [al-Naml: 60].

This shift from the third person to the first person in the form of magnification in all these verses, regarding the growth of plants, shows the greatness of the matter of causing plants to grow, because if water had not descended and nothing had grown, people would have perished from hunger and thirst. It therefore indicates His greatness, may He be exalted, the intense need of creation for Him, and the obligation of their obedience to Him, may He be exalted.

His words in this verse: ﴿pairs of various plants﴾ mean kinds that differ, of various types of plants. Al-azwāj is the plural of zawj, and here it means a kind of plant, as He said in surah al-Ḥajj: ﴿And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down water upon it, it stirs and swells and grows every beautiful pair﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 5], that is, every beautiful kind of plant. And He said in surah Luqmān: ﴿He created the heavens without pillars that you see, and cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and dispersed therein every kind of creature. And We sent down water from the sky and made to grow therein every noble pair﴾ [Luqmān: 10], that is, every good type of plant. And He said in surah Yā-Sīn: (p-23) ﴿Glorified is He who created all the pairs, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 36], and other verses.

His word ﴿various﴾ (shattā) is a descriptive adjunct (naʿt) of His word ﴿pairs﴾ (azwājan) [Ṭā-Hā: 53]. The meaning of His words ﴿pairs of various plants﴾ is kinds differing in forms, quantities, benefits, colours, smells, and tastes. It has been said that shattā is a plural of "plant" (nabāt), meaning a plant that is diverse, as we have explained. The more apparent view is the first. The word shattā is the plural of shatīt, like marīḍ and marḍā. Al-shatīt means dispersed. From this is the saying of Ruʾbah describing camels that came together and then scattered, while they raised high dust:

"They came together, then they lowered their heads, scattered, while they stirred up the high dust that flies."

A thaghr shatīt means one with gaps, because its teeth are spread apart, meaning that some of them are not stuck to others.

His words in this noble verse: ﴿and threaded for you therein roads﴾ — we have already mentioned that the meaning of salaka (threading) is inserting. His word "salaka" here means that He placed within the earth, among its valleys and mountains, roads with wide passages through which creation passes. He expressed this here with His words: ﴿and threaded for you therein roads﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 53], and He expressed it in other places with the word "made" (jaʿala), such as His words in al-Anbiyāʾ: ﴿And We made in it wide passages as roads, that they may be guided﴾ [al-Anbiyāʾ: 31], and His words in al-Zukhruf: ﴿He who made the earth for you a cradle and made for you therein roads that you may be guided﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 10]. In some places He expressed it with the word "cast" (alqā), such as His words in al-Naḥl: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it shake with you, and rivers and roads, that you may be guided﴾ [Luqmān: 15 as cited], because the conjunction of "roads" with "firm mountains" is clear evidence of this.

His words in this noble verse: ﴿Eat, and pasture your livestock﴾ mean: eat, O people, from the fruits and grains which We have brought forth for you from the earth by the water which We sent down, from all that is food for you of grains, fruits, and the like; and pasture your livestock, that is, let them graze and send them out to pasture that is suitable for their eating.
