One says: the livestock grazed the herbage (raʿat al-māshiyah al-kalaʾ), and its owner pastured it (raʿāhā ṣāḥibuhā), meaning he let it graze and sent it out. The verb is both intransitive and transitive (yalzamu wa-yataʿaddā). The command in His words ﴿Eat and pasture﴾ is for permission (ibāḥah). The favour contained in it, and the proof that the Benefactor deserves worship for this alone, is not hidden.

What He mentioned in this noble verse, of favour upon the children of Adam with their provision and the provision of their livestock, has been clarified in other places:

• Such as His words in surah al-Sajdah: ﴿Then We bring forth thereby crops, of which their livestock eat, and themselves. Do they not see?﴾ [al-Sajdah: 27],

• and His words in al-Nāziʿāt: ﴿He brings forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ ﴿and the mountains He set firm﴾ ﴿as a provision for you and your livestock﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 31–33],

• and His words in ʿAbasa: ﴿Then We split the earth, splitting﴾ ﴿and caused to grow therein grain﴾ ﴿and grapes and herbage﴾ ﴿and olives and date palms﴾ ﴿and gardens dense﴾ ﴿and fruit and pasture﴾ ﴿as a provision for you and your livestock﴾ [ʿAbasa: 25–32],

• and His words in al-Naḥl: ﴿It is He who sent down water from the sky; from it is drink, and from it are trees in which you pasture [your animals]﴾ [al-Naḥl: 10],

and other verses.

His words in this noble verse ﴿for people of intellect (ūlī al-nuhā)﴾ mean: for possessors of minds. Al-nuhā is the plural of nuhyah, with a ḍammah on the nūn, and it means intellect (ʿaql), because it restrains its possessor from what is unbecoming. The Arabs say: "the man became nahū" (nahuwa al-rajul) in the pattern faʿula with a ḍammah, when his nuhyah (intellect) became complete. Its origin is nahuya with a yāʾ, but the yāʾ was changed to a wāw because it is the lām of a verb after a ḍammah, as he indicated in al-Khulāṣah with his words:

"Turn the yāʾ into a wāw after a ḍammah, whenever it is found as the final radical of a verb or before a tāʾ."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 55:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more.﴾

The pronoun in His saying "from it" (minha) and in His saying "into it" (fiha) both refer back to "the earth" (al-ard) mentioned in His saying, ﴿Who made the earth for you a cradle﴾.

Three matters are mentioned in this noble verse:

The first: that He created the children of Adam from the earth.

The second: that He will return them into it.

The third: that He will bring them forth from it once more. These three matters mentioned in this verse are explained clearly in other places.

As for His creating them from the earth, He mentioned it in several places in His Book, such as His saying, ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust﴾ [al-Hajj: 5], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾ [al-Rum: 20], and His saying in Surat al-Mu'min: ﴿He is the One who created you from dust﴾ [Ghafir: 67], along with other verses.

The verified view is that the meaning of His creating mankind from dust is that He created their father Adam from it, as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam; He created him from dust﴾ [Al 'Imran: 59]. Since He created their father from dust, and they were followers of him in creation, it is true of them that they were created from dust. As for what some of the scholars claim (p-25), that the meaning of their being created from dust is that when the sperm-drop falls into the womb, the angel appointed over the womb goes and takes dust from the place where the person will be buried, and scatters it upon the sperm-drop, and Allah creates the soul from the sperm-drop and the dust together, this is contrary to the verified view. This is because the Qur'an indicates that the stage of the sperm-drop comes after the stage of dust, with an interval. It is not simultaneous with it, as shown by the sequential ordering between them with "then" (thumma) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then indeed We created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop﴾ [al-Hajj: 5],

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He is the One who created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop﴾ [Ghafir: 67], along with the verse,

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay. Then We made him a sperm-drop in a firm place﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 12-13],

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Exalted in Might, the Merciful. Who perfected everything He created and began the creation of man from clay. Then He made his descendants from an extract of despised water﴾ [as-Sajdah: 6-8].

Likewise, what some of the exegetes claim, that the meaning of their being created from dust is that what is intended is that they were created from the foods that grow from the earth, is plainly untenable, as you see.

As for the second matter, He also mentioned it in other places, namely in His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 25-26]. His saying ﴿kifatan﴾ [al-Mursalat: 26] means their place in which they are gathered, i.e., in which they are gathered together: the living upon its surface, and the dead in its belly. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿and into it We will return you﴾.

As for the third matter, namely their being brought forth from the earth alive on the Day of Resurrection, it is explained clearly in many verses.

• Such as His saying: ﴿And He gives life to the earth after its death; and thus you will be brought forth﴾ [ar-Rum: 19], i.e., from your graves alive after death,

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We revived thereby a dead land; thus will be the emergence﴾ [Qaf: 11], i.e., from the graves by resurrection on the Day of Resurrection,

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then when He calls you with a single call from the earth, immediately you will come out﴾ [ar-Rum: 25],

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Until, when they carry heavy clouds, We drive them to a dead land and send down water therewith and bring forth from it all of the fruits; thus We will bring forth the dead, that you may remember﴾ [al-A'raf: 57],

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day they will emerge from the graves swiftly, as though they were rushing to a target﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 43],

• and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The Day they hear the Cry in truth; that is the Day of Emergence﴾ [Qaf: 42].

The verses of this kind are very numerous.

His saying in this noble verse, ﴿From it We created you﴾ and so on, is like His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said: In it you will live, and in it you will die, and from it you will be brought forth﴾ [al-A'raf: 25]. The word "tarah" in His saying ﴿once more﴾ means "time" (p-26), i.e., occasion.

And in the hadith of the Sunan: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) attended a funeral, and when they wished to bury the deceased, he took a handful of dust and threw it into the grave and said, ﴿From it We created you﴾; then he took another and said, ﴿and into it We will return you﴾; then another and said, ﴿and from it We will bring you forth once more﴾."

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 56:

God's words: ﴿And We showed him all of Our signs, but he denied them and refused.﴾

The stronger of the two views is that the possessive in His words "Our signs" (āyātinā) is understood with the sense of a known reference (ʿahd), like the definite article "al-" (the alif and lam). The "signs" meant here, referring to those known to Musa, are all of them, namely the nine mentioned in His words: ﴿And We gave Musa nine clear signs﴾ [al-Isra' 17:101], and His words: ﴿Put your hand into your garment; it will come out white without disease, among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people﴾ [al-Naml 27:12]. Some scholars said: the nine signs mentioned are the staff, the white hand, the splitting of the sea, the rock from which twelve springs gushed forth, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the lifting of the mountain above them as though it were a canopy. We have already presented the words of the scholars on the nine signs in the commentary on surah al-Isra'. Some scholars said: the generality is on its apparent meaning, and that God showed Pharaoh all the signs that Musa brought and that other prophets brought, by Musa informing him of all his miracles and the miracles of all the other prophets. The first view is the apparent one.

God, exalted is He, has made clear in other places that the signs He showed Pharaoh and his people varied, some being greater than others, as He said in surah al-Zukhruf: ﴿And We did not show them a sign except that it was greater than its companion﴾ [43:48], and His words: ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:23], and His words: ﴿So he showed him the greatest sign﴾ [al-Nazi'at 79:20]. In both places, "the greatest" (al-kubra) is the feminine form of "the greater" (al-akbar), which is a comparative form indicating that it is greater than others.

As for His words in this noble verse: ﴿but he denied and refused﴾, it means that despite the signs, the miracles which God showed him that testify to the truthfulness of His prophet Musa, he denied the messenger of his Lord, Musa, and refused to accept the truth. God, exalted is He, has also explained in other places the extent of his refusal, obstinacy and arrogance towards Musa in many passages of His Book.

- As in His words: ﴿They said, "Whatever sign you bring us to enchant us with, we will not believe in you."﴾ [al-A'raf 7:132],
- and His words: ﴿But when he brought them Our signs, at once they laughed at them﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:47],
- and His words: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:29],
- and His words: ﴿And Pharaoh called out among his people, saying, "O my people, is not mine the kingdom of Egypt, and these rivers flowing beneath me? Then will you not see? Or am I better than this one who is despicable and can hardly express himself? So why were bracelets of gold not put upon him, or why did the angels not come with him in succession?"﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:51–53],

(p-27)

His purpose in all of this is to exalt his own status and belittle the status of Musa, and that it is impossible for the superior to follow the inferior.

God, exalted is He, has made clear that Pharaoh denied and refused while knowing that what Musa brought was true, and that the signs which he denied and refused to accept were sent down by none but God. This is in His words: ﴿And they denied them while their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml 27:14], and His words: ﴿He said, "You have certainly known that these signs were not sent down except by the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights; and I truly think you, O Pharaoh, are doomed."﴾ [al-Isra' 17:102], along with other verses. The word ﴿We showed him﴾ (araynāhu) is, according to the correct view, derived from ra'á in the sense of seeing with the eye (al-ru'yah al-basriyyah).

The commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 57:

﴿He said: "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Moses?"﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentions that when He showed Pharaoh His signs through His prophet Moses, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, Pharaoh said: the signs that Moses brought are magic, and he intends by them to drive Pharaoh and his people out of their land.

As for his claim, and his people's claim, that Moses is a magician, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has mentioned it in many places in His Book.

- As in His saying: ﴿So when Our signs came to them as clear evidence, they said, "This is clear magic."﴾ [an-Naml: 13],
- and His saying: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us, they said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾ [Yunus: 76],
- and His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71],
- and His saying: ﴿And they said, "O magician, invoke for us your Lord..."﴾ (the verse) [az-Zukhruf: 49],

along with other verses besides these.

As for their claim that he intends to drive them out of their land by magic, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has also mentioned it in several places in His Book.

- As in His saying in this surah: ﴿He said, "Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Moses?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 57],
- and His saying in "al-A'raf" (the Heights): ﴿The chiefs of the people of Pharaoh said, "Indeed, this is a knowing magician. He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 109–110],
- and His saying in "ash-Shu'ara'" (the Poets): ﴿He said to the chiefs around him, "Indeed, this is a knowing magician. He wants to drive you out of your land with his magic, so what do you advise?"﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 34],
- and His saying in "Yunus" (Jonah): ﴿They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away from what we found our fathers upon, and that you two may have greatness in the land?"﴾ [Yunus: 78]. And the magicians of Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, these two are magicians who intend to drive you out of your land with their magic and do away with your ideal way of life.﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63].

(p-28) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, may He be exalted, mentions that Pharaoh, may Allah curse him, when he saw Allah's signs and His dazzling miracles, and claimed that they were magic, swore that he would surely bring Musa magic like the signs of Allah which he himself claims are magic. He has explained in another place that their bringing of magic and gathering of the magicians was by the agreement of his chiefs upon that. As in His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿The chiefs of Pharaoh's people said, "Indeed, this is a knowing magician. He wants to drive you out of your land, so what do you advise?" They said, "Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers who will bring you every knowing magician."﴾ [al-A'raf: 109-110]. And His saying in "ash-Shu'ara'": ﴿He said to the chiefs around him, "Indeed, this is a knowing magician. He wants to drive you out of your land with his magic, so what do you advise?" They said, "Delay him and his brother, and send into the cities gatherers who will bring you every knowing magician."﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 34-37]. This is because His saying ﴿so what do you advise﴾ in both places indicates that Pharaoh's saying ﴿So we will surely bring you magic like it﴾ came after consultation and the agreement of the chiefs among them upon that.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Set for us a appointment, which we will not fail, neither we nor you, at a place equidistant﴾. ﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment, and let the people be gathered in the forenoon."﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, may He be exalted, mentions that when Pharaoh promised Musa that he would bring magic like what Musa had brought, according to his claim, he said to Musa, ﴿Set for us an appointment which we will not fail, neither we nor you﴾. Al-ikhlaf means not fulfilling a promise. He decided that the place of gathering, for the contest and the overpowering in magic according to his claim, would be a place equidistant (sawa). The most correct of the sayings concerning His word ﴿sawa﴾, in the reading with kasra and damma, is that it is a middle place where the edges of the town are equal in it, because it is centrally located between them, so it is not closer to the east than the west, nor to the south than the north. This is the meaning of the exegetes' saying "a place equidistant," i.e., evenly and fairly, so that all people can attend. His word ﴿sawa﴾ derives from istiwa' (equality), because the distance from the center to the two extremes has no disparity, but is equal. The word ﴿sawa﴾ has three dialectal forms: with damma, with kasra and shortened vowel, and with fatha on the sin and lengthened vowel. The first two are read here and not the third; and an example of the third is ﴿to a word that is equal between us and you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 64]. Among the Arabs' usage of ﴿a place equidistant﴾ for a place centrally between the two parties is the verse of Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi, which Abu 'Ubayda recited as evidence for this:

"Indeed our father had settled in a town equidistant between Qays Aylan and al-Fizr."

(p-29) Al-Fizr is Sa'd ibn Zayd Manat ibn Tamim. He means: he settled in a town whose distance is level between Qays Aylan and al-Fizr. Musa, peace and blessings be upon him and our Prophet, agreed to what Pharaoh asked of him regarding the appointment, and decided that its time would be the day of adornment. The statements of the scholars concerning the day of adornment all return to it being a day known to them, on which they gather and adorn themselves, whether we say it is their festival day, or the day of 'Ashura', or the day of Nawruz, or a day on which they would set up a market and adorn themselves with various kinds of adornment.

Al-Zamakhshari said: Musa only appointed them that day so that the exaltation of Allah's word and the manifestation of His religion, and the humiliation of the disbeliever and the vanishing of falsehood, would be before the eyes of witnesses in the crowded assembly, to strengthen the desire of whoever desires to follow the truth, to weaken the resolve of the falsifiers and their partisans, and so that the matter would be spoken of much, to be known in every desert and town, and to spread among all people of tents and cities. End quote.

The verbal noun formed from "an" and its clause in His saying ﴿and let the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾ is in a genitive position, conjoined to ﴿the adornment﴾, meaning: your appointment is the day of adornment and the gathering of people; or it is in a nominative position, conjoined to His saying ﴿the day of adornment﴾, according to the majority reading with raf'. Al-hashr means gathering, and al-duha is from the beginning of the day when the sun shines. Al-duha may be masculine or feminine. Whoever makes it feminine considers it the plural of dahwa; whoever makes it masculine considers it a singular noun on the pattern fu'l with damma then fatha, like Surad and Zufar. It is diptotic when you do not mean the forenoon of a specific day, without disagreement. If you mean the forenoon of your specific day, it is said it is prohibited from tanwin like saḥar; and it is said not.

What He, may He be exalted, mentioned in this noble verse, that the contest between Musa and the magicians was set for a time on a known day on which people gather, so that they may know the victor from the vanquished, has been pointed out in another place, as His saying, may He be exalted, in "ash-Shu'ara'": ﴿So the magicians were gathered for the appointment of a known day﴾ ﴿And it was said to the people, "Will you gather?"﴾ ﴿"Perhaps we may follow the magicians if they are the victors."﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 38-40].

So His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿for the appointment of a known day﴾.

The known day is the day of adornment mentioned here, and its appointed time is the time of the forenoon mentioned in His saying ﴿and let the people be gathered in the forenoon﴾.

* *

Notice

Know that in the interpretation of this noble verse there are kinds of difficulty well known among the scholars, and we will mention, God willing, the aspects of difficulty in it, and clarify the removal of difficulty from them.

Know first that the triliteral verb, if it is a mithal (initial weak radical, like waʿada and waṣala), then the analogical form of its mimi verbal noun and of its noun of place and time is all maf'il (with fatha on the mim and kasra on the ʿayn), so long as it is not defective in the final radical. If it is defective in the final radical, the analogical form is maf'al (with fatha on the mim and the ʿayn), as is known in the science of morphology.

Having known that, know that His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿Set for us an appointment﴾ is suitable, by the morphological analogy, to be a mimi verbal noun meaning the promise, or to be a noun of time meaning the time of the promise, or to be a noun of place meaning the place of the promise. Among the usages of al-maw'id in the Qur'an as a noun of time is His saying: ﴿Indeed, their appointment is the morning﴾ [Hud: 81], i.e., the time of their promised destruction is the morning. Among its usages in the Qur'an as a noun of place is His saying: ﴿And indeed, Hell is their appointed place, all of them﴾ [al-Hijr: 43], i.e., the place of their promised punishment.

The aspect of difficulty here is that His saying ﴿we will not fail it, neither we nor you﴾ indicates that al-maw'id is a verbal noun, because what is failed is the promise, not its time or its place.

And His saying, ﴿a place equidistant﴾, indicates that al-maw'id in the verse is a noun of place.

And His saying, ﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾, indicates that al-maw'id in the verse is a noun of time. If we say that al-maw'id in the verse is a verbal noun, the mention of the place in ﴿a place equidistant﴾ and of the time in ﴿the day of adornment﴾ becomes difficult. If we say that al-maw'id is a noun of place, His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾ becomes difficult, because the place itself is not failed; only the promise is failed, and His saying ﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment"﴾ also becomes difficult. If we say that al-maw'id is a noun of time, His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾ becomes difficult, and His saying ﴿a place equidistant﴾ also becomes difficult. These are the aspects of difficulty in this noble verse. The scholars have answers to this, among them what al-Zamakhshari mentioned in al-Kashshaf. He said: The word al-maw'id in His saying ﴿Set for us an appointment between us and you﴾ cannot be other than a time, a place, or a verbal noun. If you make it a time, considering that His saying ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾ corresponds to it, two things follow for you: that you make the time something failed, and that a governing verb is missing for "place"; and if you make it a place, in accordance with His saying ﴿a place equidistant﴾, it also follows for you that you attribute the failing to the place, and it does not correspond to His saying ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment.﴾ ... He went on: So it remains that it is made a verbal noun in the sense of promise, and a governed omitted noun is assumed, i.e., the place of the promise, and the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ refers to the promise, and ﴿a place﴾ is a substitute for the omitted place.

(p-31) If you say: how does His saying ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment﴾ correspond to it, when you must make it a time, while the question is about a place, not a time?

I say: it corresponds in meaning though not in wording, because they must gather on the day of adornment at a specific place known for their gathering on that day. By mentioning the time, the place is known. End of the relevant point. And there is no hiding what is in this answer of artificiality, omission, and substitution from the omitted.

The one who restricts this (the author) - may Allah pardon and forgive him - says: The most evident answer I have to the difficulties we mentioned in this noble verse is that Pharaoh asked Musa to specify the place of the appointment, and that it be a place equidistant, i.e., a middle place between the edges of the town, as we explained. Musa agreed to that and specified the time of the promise, that it would be the day of adornment in the forenoon. For the promise must have a place and a time. Knowing this, know that what appears to me most preferable is the view of those who say that in His saying ﴿Set for us an appointment between us and you﴾, it is a noun of place, i.e., the place of the promise, and His saying "a place" is a substitute for His saying "an appointment." For when al-maw'id is a noun of place, it becomes the very place itself, so it becomes clear that "a place" is a substitute. There is no difficulty with the pronoun in "we will not fail it" on this view. The way to remove the difficulty is that the known rule in morphology is that the noun of place is derived from the verbal noun as the verb is derived from it, so the noun of place is resolved into a verbal noun and a place. So "al-manzil" is, for example, the place of descent, "al-majlis" the place of sitting, and "al-maw'id" the place of promise. When it becomes clear to you that the verbal noun is latent in the meaning of the noun of place, the pronoun in His saying ﴿we will not fail it﴾ refers to the verbal noun latent in the meaning of the noun of place, as its reference to the verbal noun latent in the meaning of the verb in His saying ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8]: the "it" refers to justice understood from "be just." Likewise His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿we will not fail it﴾, i.e., the promise latent in the meaning of the noun of place which is the appointment, because it is the place of promise. Its meaning is a construct phrase whose last part is the word "promise," and that is the referent of the pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾.

When you know the meaning of this statement which Allah reported that Pharaoh said to Musa, know that His saying about Musa, ﴿He said, "Your appointment is the day of adornment,"﴾ indicates that he implicitly agreed to Pharaoh's request, and added the specification of the time of the promise by His saying ﴿Your appointment is the day of adornment.﴾ There is no difficulty in that. This is what appears to us to be correct. The closest of the views mentioned by the scholars after this, in my opinion, is the saying of those who say that (p-32) the appointment in the verse is a verbal noun; on this view, ﴿we will not fail it﴾ refers to the verbal noun, and ﴿a place﴾ is in the accusative governed by a verb implied by the appointment, i.e., "we have made it a place equidistant." Making the place accusative as an object of the verbal noun which is "appointment," or as one of the two objects of "set," is not correct in my apparent view. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse, ﴿a place equidistant (sawan)﴾, was read by Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, and Hamzah as "sawan" with damma on the sin, and the rest with kasra. The meaning of the two readings is one, as previously stated.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 60:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew and gathered his plot, then came.﴾

Concerning His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse, ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew﴾, some scholars said: its meaning is that Pharaoh withdrew, turning away from that place, in order to prepare what he needed of what he and Musa had agreed upon. Evidence for this interpretation is His saying, exalted is He, in Surah "al-Nazi'at" concerning the same story: ﴿Then he turned his back, striving. And he gathered [his people] and proclaimed﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 22-23]. His saying ﴿and gathered﴾ means: he gathered the magicians.

Other scholars said: the meaning of His saying ﴿Then Pharaoh withdrew﴾ is that he turned away from the truth that Musa had brought. From the meaning of this interpretation is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and gathered his plot﴾, the apparent meaning is that what is meant by ﴿his plot﴾ is the magic he gathered in order to overcome Musa, in his own assumption. Accordingly, what is meant by His saying ﴿and gathered his plot﴾ is his gathering of the magicians from the regions of his kingdom. Two things indicate this. The first is that the Qur'an calls magic a "plot" (kayd), as in His saying ﴿What they have produced is only the plot of a magician﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69], and His saying, exalted is He, concerning the magicians: ﴿So gather your plot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 64], and their "plot" was their magic. The second is that what Pharaoh gathered was the magicians, as indicated by verses from the Book of Allah. Such as His saying, exalted is He, in "al-A'raf": ﴿And send to the cities gatherers﴾ ﴿who will bring you every learned magician﴾ [al-A'raf: 111-112]. His saying ﴿gatherers﴾ means: those who gather, collecting the magicians from the regions of his kingdom. And His saying in "al-Shu'ara'": ﴿And send to the cities gatherers﴾ ﴿who will bring you every learned magician﴾ ﴿So the magicians were assembled for an appointed day of a known time﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 36-38], and His saying in "Yunus": ﴿And Pharaoh said: Bring me every learned magician﴾ [Yunus: 79].

As for His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿then came﴾, meaning: Pharaoh came with his magicians to the appointed meeting, to overcome the Prophet of Allah, Musa, with his magic, in his own assumption.

(p-33) His statement, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw."﴾

In this noble verse, Exalted and Most High mentions that when Pharaoh gathered the magicians and they assembled with Moses for the contest, they said to him, showing him good manners: ﴿Either you throw first, or we will be the first to throw.﴾ He, Exalted, has explained their statement in other places, such as His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw, or we will be the ones who throw."﴾ [al-A'raf: 115]. We have already mentioned, in the introduction to this blessed book, that among the types of clarification it contains is that the object of a verb is omitted in one place and then made clear in another place, so we will clarify that here. In this verse the object of "throw" (tulqi) and the first object of "threw" (alqa) have been omitted. Exalted is He has made clear in other places that the object of Moses' throwing is his staff, as in His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿And We revealed to Moses, "Throw your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they were faking﴾ [al-A'raf: 117], and His saying in "al-Shu'ara'": ﴿So Moses threw his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were faking﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 45], and His saying here: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have made﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69]. What is in his right hand is his staff, as Exalted is He said: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?" He said, "It is my staff"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17].

Exalted is He has also made clear in another place that the object of their throwing is their ropes and their staffs, as in His saying in "al-Shu'ara'": ﴿So they threw their ropes and their staffs and said, "By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we will be the victorious."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 44]. Exalted is He has also indicated this here by His saying: ﴿He said, "Rather, you throw." And suddenly their ropes and staffs appeared to him, because of their magic, to be moving﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66], because the speech contains an ellipsis indicated by the context, and the implied meaning is: He said, "Rather, you throw," so they threw their ropes and their staffs, and suddenly their ropes and staffs appeared to him, because of their magic, to be moving.

The verbal noun formed from "an" (that) and its clause in His saying ﴿an tulqiya﴾ and in His saying ﴿an nakuna﴾ has two possibilities of i'rab (grammatical analysis). The first is that it is in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by a verb omitted and indicated by the context, the implied meaning being: "either you choose to throw," i.e., you choose your throwing first, or you choose our throwing first. The implied form of the second verbal noun is: "and either you choose that we be..." i.e., our being the first to throw. The second is that it is in a position of nominative (raf'), and accordingly it has been said that it is a subject (mubtada'), the implied meaning being: "either your throwing first, or our throwing first." It has also been said that it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, i.e., "either the matter is our throwing or your throwing."

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿قالَ بَلْ ألْقُوا﴾.

ذَكَرَ جَلَّ وعَلا في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ: أنَّ نَبِيَّهُ مُوسى عَلَيْهِ وعَلى نَبِيِّنا الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ لَمّا خَيَّرَهُ سَحَرَةُ فِرْعَوْنَ أنْ يُلْقِيَ قَبْلَهم أوْ يُلْقُوا قَبْلَهُ قالَ لَهم: ألْقُوا يَعْنِي ألْقُوا [p-٣٤] ما أنْتُمْ مُلْقُونَ كَما صَرَّحَ بِهِ في ”الشُّعَراءِ“ في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿قالَ لَهم مُوسى ألْقُوا ما أنْتُمْ مُلْقُونَ﴾ [الشعراء: ٤٣] وذَلِكَ هو المُرادُ أيْضًا بِقَوْلِهِ في ”الأعْرافِ“ ﴿قالَ ألْقُوا فَلَمّا ألْقَوْا سَحَرُوا أعْيُنَ النّاسِ﴾ [الأعراف: ١١٦].

تَنْبيهٌ

قَوْلُ مُوسى لِلسَّحَرَةِ: ألْقُوا المَذْكُورُ في ”الأعْرافِ، وطه، والشُّعَراءِ“ فِيهِ سُؤالٌ مَعْرُوفٌ، وهو أنْ يُقالَ: كَيْفَ قالَ هَذا النَّبِيُّ الكَرِيمُ لِلسَّحَرَةِ ألْقُوا. أيْ: ألْقُوا حِبالَكم وعِصِيَّكم، يَعْنِي اعْمَلُوا السِّحْرَ وعارِضُوا بِهِ مُعْجِزَةَ اللَّهِ الَّتِي أيَّدَ بِها رَسُولَهُ، وهَذا أمْرٌ بِمُنْكَرٍ ؟، والجَوابُ: هو أنَّ قَصْدَ مُوسى بِذَلِكَ قَصْدٌ حَسَنٌ يَسْتَوْجِبُهُ المَقامُ، لِأنَّ إلْقاءَهم قَبْلَهُ يَسْتَلْزِمُ إبْرازَ ما مَعَهم مِن مَكائِدِ السِّحْرِ، واسْتِنْفادِ أقْصى طُرُقِهِمْ ومَجْهُودِهِمْ. فَإذا فَعَلُوا ذَلِكَ كانَ في إلْقائِهِ عَصاهُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ وابْتِلاعِها لِجَمِيعِ ما ألْقَوْا مِن إظْهارِ الحَقِّ وإبْطالِ الباطِلِ ما لا جِدالَ بَعْدَهُ في الحَقِّ لِأدْنى عاقِلٍ. ولِأجْلِ هَذا قالَ لَهم: ألْقُوا، فَلَوَ ألْقى قَبْلَهم وألْقَوْا بَعْدَهُ لَمْ يَحْصُلْ ما ذَكَرْنا، والعِلْمُ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ تَعالى.

* *

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَإذا حِبالُهم وعِصِيُّهم يُخَيَّلُ إلَيْهِ مِن سِحْرِهِمْ أنَّها تَسْعى﴾.

قَرَأ هَذا الحَرْفَ ابْنُ ذَكْوانَ عَنِ ابْنِ عامِرٍ ”تُخَيَّلُ“ بِالتّاءِ، أيْ: تُخَيَّلُ هي أيِ: الحِبالُ، والعِصِيُّ أنَّها تَسْعى. والمَصْدَرُ في ”أنَّها تَسْعى“ بَدَلٌ مِن ضَمِيرِ الحِبالِ، والعِصِيُّ الَّذِي هو نائِبُ فاعِلٍ لِـ ”تُخَيَّلُ“ بَدَلُ اشْتِمالٍ. وقَرَأ الباقُونَ بِالياءِ التَّحْتِيَّةِ. والمَصْدَرُ في سِحْرِهِمْ أنَّها تَسْعى نائِبُ فاعِلٍ لِـ ”تُخَيَّلُ“.

وَفِي هَذِهِ الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ حَذْفٌ دَلَّ المَقامُ عَلَيْهِ، والتَّقْدِيرُ: قالَ بَلْ ألْقُوا فَألْقَوْا حِبالَهم وعِصِيَّهم، فَإذا حِبالُهم وعِصِيُّهم يُخَيَّلُ إلَيْهِ مِن سِحْرِهِمْ أنَّها تَسْعى. وبِهِ تَعْلَمُ أنَّ الفاءَ في قَوْلِهِ فَإذا حِبالُهم عاطِفَةٌ عَلى مَحْذُوفٍ كَما أشارَ لِنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ ابْنُ مالِكٍ في الخُلاصَةِ بِقَوْلِهِ:

؎وَحَذْفَ مَتْبُوعٍ بَدا هُنا اسْتَبِحْ

وَ ”إذا“ هي الفُجائِيَّةُ، وقَدْ قَدَّمْنا كَلامَ العُلَماءِ فِيها فَأغْنى ذَلِكَ عَنْ إعادَتِهِ هُنا. والحِبالُ: جَمْعُ حَبْلٍ، وهو مَعْرُوفٌ. و ”العِصِيُّ“ جَمْعُ عَصا، وألِفُ العَصا مُنْقَلِبَةٌ عَنْ واوٍ، ولِذا تُرَدُّ إلى أصْلِها في التَّثْنِيَةِ: ومِنهُ قَوْلُ غَيْلانَ ذِي الرُّمَّةِ: [p-٣٥]

؎فَجاءَتْ بِنَسْجِ العَنْكَبُوتِ كَأنَّهُ ∗∗∗ عَلى عَصَوَيْها سابِرِيٌّ مُشَبْرَقُ

وَأصْلُ العِصِيِّ عُصُوو عَلى وزْنِ فُعُولٍ جَمْعُ عَصا. فَأُعِلَّ بِإبْدالِ الواوِ الَّتِي في مَوْضِعِ الَّلامِ ياءً فَصارَ عُصُويًا، فَأُبْدِلَتِ الواوُ ياءً وأُدْغِمَتْ في الياءِ، فالياءانِ أصْلُهُما واوانِ. وإلى جَوازِ هَذا النَّوْعِ مِنَ الإعْلالِ في واوَيِ اللّامِ مِمّا جاءَ عَلى فَعَوْلٍ أشارَ في الخُلاصَةِ بِقَوْلِهِ:

؎كَذاكَ ذا وجْهَينِ جا الفُعُولُ مِن ∗∗∗ ذِي الواوِ لامُ جَمْعٍ أوْ فَرْدٍ يَعِنْ

وَضَمَّةُ الصّادِ في وعِصِيُّهم أُبْدِلَتْ كَسْرَةً لِمُجانَسَةِ الياءِ، وضَمَّةُ عَيْنِ ”عِصِيِّهِمْ“ أُبْدِلَتْ كَسْرَةً لِاتِّباعِ كَسْرَةِ الصّادِ. والتَّخَيُّلُ في قَوْلِهِ يُخَيَّلُ إلَيْهِ مِن سِحْرِهِمْ أنَّها تَسْعى هو إبْداءُ أمْرٍ لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ، ومِنهُ الخَيالُ. وهو الطَّيْفُ الطّارِقُ في النَّوْمِ. قالَ الشّاعِرُ:

؎ألا يا لِقَوْمِي لِلْخَيالِ المُشَوِّقِ ∗∗∗ ولِلدّارِ تَنْأى بِالحَبِيبِ ونَلْتَقِي

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعالى في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ الكَرِيمَةِ: ﴿يُخَيَّلُ إلَيْهِ مِن سِحْرِهِمْ أنَّها تَسْعى﴾ يَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّ السِّحْرَ الَّذِي جاءَ بِهِ سَحَرَةُ فِرْعَوْنَ تَخْيِيلٌ لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ في نَفْسِ الأمْرِ. وهَذا الَّذِي دَلَّتْ عَلَيْهِ آيَةُ ”طه“ هَذِهِ دَلَّتْ عَلَيْهِ آيَةُ ”الأعْرافِ“ وهي قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَلَمّا ألْقَوْا سَحَرُوا أعْيُنَ النّاسِ﴾ [الأعراف: ١١٦]، لِأنَّ قَوْلَهُ: ﴿سَحَرُوا أعْيُنَ النّاسِ﴾ يَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّهم خَيَّلُوا لِأعْيُنِ النّاظِرِينَ أمْرًا لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ. وبِهاتَيْنِ الآيَتَيْنِ احْتَجَّ المُعْتَزِلَةُ (Mu'tazila) ومَن قالَ بِقَوْلِهِمْ عَلى أنَّ السِّحْرَ خَيالٌ لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ.

والتَّحْقِيقُ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ جَماهِيرُ العُلَماءِ مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ: أنَّ السِّحْرَ مِنهُ ما هو أمْرٌ لَهُ حَقِيقَةٌ لا مُطْلَقَ تَخْيِيلٍ لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ، ومِمّا يَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّ مِنهُ ما لَهُ حَقِيقَةٌ قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿فَيَتَعَلَّمُونَ مِنهُما ما يُفَرِّقُونَ بِهِ بَيْنَ المَرْءِ وزَوْجِهِ﴾ [البقرة: ١٠٢] فَهَذِهِ الآيَةُ تَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّهُ شَيْءٌ مَوْجُودٌ لَهُ حَقِيقَةٌ تَكُونُ سَبَبًا لِلتَّفْرِيقِ بَيْنَ الرَّجُلِ وامْرَأتِهِ وقَدْ عَبَّرَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ بِما المَوْصُولَةِ وهي تَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّهُ شَيْءٌ لَهُ وُجُودٌ حَقِيقِيٌّ. ومِمّا يَدُلُّ عَلى ذَلِكَ أيْضًا قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَمِن شَرِّ النَّفّاثاتِ في العُقَدِ﴾ [الفلق: ٤] يَعْنِي السَّواحِرَ اللّاتِي يَعْقِدْنَ في سِحْرِهِنَّ ويَنْفُثْنَ في عُقَدِهِنَّ. فَلَوْلا أنَّ السِّحْرَ حَقِيقَةٌ لَمْ يَأْمُرِ اللَّهُ بِالِاسْتِعاذَةِ مِنهُ. وسَيَأْتِي إنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ أنَّ السِّحْرَ أنْواعٌ: مِنها ما هو أمْرٌ لَهُ حَقِيقَةٌ، ومِنها ما هو تَخْيِيلٌ لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ. وبِذَلِكَ يَتَّضِحُ عَدَمُ التَّعارُضِ بَيْنَ الآياتِ الدّالَّةِ عَلى أنَّ لَهُ حَقِيقَةً، والآياتُ الدّالَّةُ عَلى أنَّهُ خَيالٌ.

[p-٣٦] فَإنْ قِيلَ: قَوْلُهُ في ”طه“: ﴿يُخَيَّلُ إلَيْهِ مِن سِحْرِهِمْ﴾ [طه: ٦٦]، وقَوْلُهُ في ”الأعْرافِ“: ﴿سَحَرُوا أعْيُنَ النّاسِ﴾ [الأعراف: ١١٦] الدّالّانِ عَلى أنَّ سِحْرَ سَحَرَةِ فِرْعَوْنَ خَيالٌ لا حَقِيقَةَ لَهُ، يُعارِضُهُما قَوْلُهُ في ”الأعْرافِ“: ﴿وَجاءُوا بِسِحْرٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ [الأعراف: ١١٦] لِأنَّ وصْفَ سِحْرِهِمْ بِالعِظَمِ يَدُلُّ عَلى أنَّهُ غَيْرُ خَيالٍ. فالَّذِي يَظْهَرُ في الجَوابِ، واللَّهُ أعْلَمُ أنَّهم أخَذُوا كَثِيرًا مِنَ الحِبالِ، والعِصِيِّ، وخَيَّلُوا بِسِحْرِهِمْ لِأعْيُنِ النّاسِ أنَّ الحِبالَ، والعِصِيَّ تَسْعى وهي كَثِيرَةٌ. فَظَنَّ النّاظِرُونَ أنَّ الأرْضَ مُلِئَتْ حَيّاتٍ تَسْعى، لِكَثْرَةِ ما ألْقَوْا مِنَ الحِبالِ، والعِصِيِّ فَخافُوا مِن كَثْرَتِها، وبِتَخْيِيلِ سَعْيِ ذَلِكَ العَدَدِ الكَثِيرِ وصَفَ سِحْرَهم بِالعِظَمِ. وهَذا ظاهِرٌ لا إشْكالَ فِيهِ. وقَدْ قالَ غَيْرُ واحِدٍ: إنَّهم جَعَلُوا الزِّئْبَقَ عَلى الحِبالِ، والعِصِيِّ، فَلَمّا أصابَها حُرُّ الشَّمْسِ تَحَرَّكَ الزِّئْبَقُ فَحَرَّكَ الحِبالَ، والعِصِيَّ، فَخُيِّلَ لِلنّاظِرِينَ أنَّها تَسْعى. وعَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ: أنَّهم كانُوا اثْنَيْنِ وسَبْعِينَ ساحِرًا، مَعَ كُلِّ ساحِرٍ مِنهم حِبالٌ وعِصِيٌّ. وقِيلَ: كانُوا أرْبَعَمِائَةٍ. وقِيلَ كانُوا اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ ألْفًا. وقِيلَ أرْبَعَةَ عَشَرَ ألْفًا. وقالَ ابْنُ المُنْكَدِرِ: كانُوا ثَمانِينَ ألْفًا. وقِيلَ: كانُوا مُجْمِعِينَ عَلى رَئِيسٍ يُقالُ لَهُ شَمْعُونُ. وقِيلَ: كانَ اسْمُهُ يُوحَنّا مَعَهُ اثْنا عَشَرَ نَقِيبًا، مَعَ كُلِّ نَقِيبٍ عِشْرُونَ عَرِيفًا، مَعَ كُلِّ عَرِيفٍ ألْفُ ساحِرٍ. وقِيلَ: كانُوا ثَلاثَمِائَةِ ألْفِ ساحِرٍ مِنَ الفَيُّومِ، وثَلاثَمِائَةِ ألْفِ ساحِرٍ مِنَ الصَّعِيدِ وثَلاثَمِائَةِ ألْفِ ساحِرٍ مِنَ الرِّيفِ فَصارُوا تِسْعَمِائَةِ ألْفٍ، وكانَ رَئِيسُهم أعْمى ا ه. وهَذِهِ الأقْوالُ مِنَ الإسْرائِيلِيّاتِ (Isra'iliyyat)، ونَحْنُ نَتَجَنَّبُها دائِمًا، ونُقَلِّلُ مِن ذِكْرِها، ورُبَّما ذَكَرْنا قَلِيلًا مِنها مُنَبِّهِينَ عَلَيْهِ.

The Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on Surah 20, Verse 69 (Part 1 of 7)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow what they have crafted. What they have crafted is only a magician's ruse﴾.

Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Qunbul from Ibn Kathir, Hisham from Ibn 'Amir, and Shu'bah from 'Asim recited this letter with a open *ta'* (تَ), lightened (*mukhaffafah*), followed by an open *lam* (لَ), then an open *qaf* (قَ) that is doubled (*mushaddadah*), followed by a sukun *fa'* (فْ). It is the present tense (*mudari'*) of *talqaf* (تَلْقَفُ), and its original form is *tatalaqqaf* (تَتَلَقَّفُ) with two *ta's*, one of which was dropped for lightness, as indicated in the *Khulasa* (the Alfiyyah of Ibn Malik) by his saying:

*"What begins with two ta's may be shortened to one ta', as in 'kataba yyana al-'ibar' (the ta' of the verb is retained alone)."*

The present verb is in the jussive mood (*majzum*), because it is the response (*jaza'*) to the imperative *wa-alqi* (وَأَلْقِ) in His saying. Most scholars of Arabic grammar hold that the jussive in such cases is due to an implied condition indicated by the form of the imperative. Its implied form here is: "If you throw what is in your right hand, it will swallow what they have crafted."

Al-Bazzi, from Ibn Kathir, recited it like the recitation we mentioned, except that he doubles the *ta'* of *talqaf* when connected (*wasl*). The rationale for doubling the *ta'* is the assimilation (*idghambu*) of one of the two *ta's* into the other. This is permissible in every verb that begins with two *ta's*, as it is here. The *Khulasa* indicates this with his saying:

*"Unfasten the hamzah-related verbs and assimilate, without fear, as in 'tatajalla' and 'tastatir'."*

The point of evidence in it is its first part, such as *tatajalla* (تَتَجَلَّى). An example of it in the past tense is the saying of the poet:

*"She turns away the clamor when it [the lip] clings to her, a sweet taste, when the kisses follow one another."*

Its original form is *tatabi'a* (تَتابَعَ). Ibn Dhakwan from Ibn 'Amir recited it like the recitation attributed to the majority, except that he pronounces the *fa'* with a *damma*. So the present tense, according to his recitation, is in the nominative (*marfu'*). The reason for its nominative is that the verbal clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "Throw what is in your right hand while it is swallowing what they have crafted." Or it is a new (*mustanifah*) clause, in which case it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "It [the staff] is swallowing what they have crafted."

Hafs from 'Asim recited *talqaf* with an open *ta'*, a sukun *lam*, and an open *qaf* that is lightened, with the jussive. It is the present tense of *laqifahu* (لَقِفَهُ), with a kasra in the past and a fatha in the present, *yalqafuhu* (يَلْقَفُهُ). The meanings of the two recitations are one, because the meaning of *talaqqafahu* and *laqifahu* is to take hold of it quickly. What is meant by His saying *talqaf ma sana'u* (تَلْقَفْ مَا صَنَعُوا) in all the recitations is that it swallows everything they have fabricated and invented of ropes and staffs, which they made the people imagine were moving. Their crafting in His saying, *ma sana'u* (مَا صَنَعُوا), is in reality an action of their deception: by their sorcery they caused people to imagine that the ropes and staffs were moving, not that the ropes and staffs themselves were the crafting, since they are the creation of Allah, may He be exalted. It is known that everything, whatever it may be, occurs by His exalted will, the cosmic and predestined will.

This meaning, which He, may He be exalted and high, mentioned here in this noble verse, is that He commanded His Prophet Musa, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, to throw what was in his right hand, that is, his right hand, which was his staff. So behold, it swallowed what they were fabricating of ropes and staffs, which they had made him imagine were moving. He clarified this elsewhere, such as His saying in *al-A'raf*:

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Throw your staff," and behold, it swallowed what they were faking.﴾ ﴿So the truth was established, and what they had been doing was nullified.﴾ ﴿So they were overcome there and returned humiliated.﴾ [al-A'raf: 117–119]

And His saying in *ash-Shu'ara'*:

﴿So Musa threw his staff, and behold, it swallowed what they were faking.﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 45]

The mention of the staff in *al-A'raf* and *ash-Shu'ara'* makes clear that what is meant by *ma fi yaminik* (مَا فِي يَمِينِكَ) in *Ta Ha* is his staff, as is not hidden.

His saying in this noble verse, *ma ya'fikun* (مَا يَأْفِكُونَ), means: what they invent and fabricate of falsehood. This is their claim that the ropes and staffs were truly moving. Its root comes from their saying: *afakahu 'an shay'in ya'fikuhu 'anhu* (أَفَكَهُ عَنْ شَيْءٍ يَأْفِكُهُ عَنْهُ) (of the pattern *daraba*): when he turned him away from it and reversed him. The root meaning of *al-afk* (الأفك), with a fatha, is reversal and turning away from something. From it comes the name given to the towns of the people of Lut, and the *mu'tafikat* (المُؤْتَفِكَات), because Allah overturned them, that is, reversed them, as He said:

﴿So We made its highest part its lowest, and rained upon it stones﴾ [al-Hijr: 74].

From it is His saying: ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾ [adh-Dhariyat: 9], that is, whoever is turned away from it is diverted. And His saying: ﴿They said, "Have you come to us to turn us away from our gods?"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 22], that is, to divert us from worshipping them. And the saying of 'Amr ibn Udhaynah:

*"If you are turned away from the most excellent manliness, then among others [too] they have been turned away."*

The most common use of this root is for falsehood, because it is a turning and reversal of a matter from its reality through lying and fabrication, as He said:

﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 7], and He said: ﴿That is their falsehood and what they used to fabricate﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 28], and other verses.

His saying in this noble verse, *innama sana'u kayda sahir* (إِنَّمَا صَنَعُوا كَيْدُ سَاحِرٍ), *ma* (مَا) is a relative pronoun (*mawsulah*) and is the subject of *inna* (إِنَّ), and *kayd* (كَيْدُ) is its predicate. The returning pronoun to the relative pronoun is omitted, in the manner of the statement in the *Khulasa*:

". . . . . . . . . . . ."
*"Omission is common among them, clearly, in a connected returning pronoun, if it is in the accusative after a verb or a participle, like 'man narjuhu yahab' (whom we hope, he will give)."*

The estimated sense is: "Indeed, what they crafted is the ruse of a magician." As for the recitation of the one who recited *kayda sahirin* (كَيْدَ سَاحِرٍ) with the accusative, then *ma* is a *kafffah* (كَافَّة, a particle that prevents the government of *inna*), and *kayd* is the direct object of *sana'u*. This recitation is not one of the canonical seven (*sab'iyyah*). As for the recitation of Hamzah and al-Kisa'i, *kayda sihr* (كَيْدُ سِحْرٍ), with a kasra on the *sin* and a sukun on the *ha'*, the apparent reading is that the construction is explicative (*bayaniyyah*), because the *kayd* that is attributed to *sihr* is what is meant by *sihr*. We have expanded the discussion of such matters in other places. *Kayd* means scheming.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the magician does not prosper wherever he comes﴾.

We have previously mentioned in *Surah Bani Isra'il* that a verb in the context of negation is among the forms of generality (*sigha 'umum*), because according to some scholars it resolves into a verbal noun (*masdar*) and a time, and according to others into a verbal noun, a time, and an attribution. The verbal noun is implicit in its meaning by consensus (*ijma'*), and this implicit verbal noun has the status of an indefinite noun, so it returns to an indefinite noun in the context of negation, which the majority hold to be a form of generality. It is therefore clear that a verb in the context of negation is among the forms of generality, and likewise a verb in the context of a conditional, because an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional is also a form of generality. Most scholars hold to what we have mentioned, that a verb in the context of negation or condition is a form of generality, though some disagree when the verb is not emphasized by a verbal noun. If it is emphasized by one, then it is a form of generality without dispute, as indicated in *Maraqi as-Su'ud* by his saying, coordinating with the forms of generality:

*"Like 'lam ashrab' (I did not drink) or 'in shariba' (if he drinks), they agreed that a verbal noun brings it, if it is a verbal noun."*

The verification of this question is that it is not restricted to a transitive verb to the exclusion of an intransitive one, contrary to those who claim that, and that there is no difference between emphasizing with a verbal noun and not doing so. This is because grammarians agree that mentioning the verbal noun after the verb is an emphasis of the verb, and emphasis does not produce a ruling; rather it is merely a strengthening of something established before it, as is well known. The disagreement among scholars about whether the generality of the verb mentioned is by direct indication (*dalalat al-mutabaqah*) or by implication (*dalalat al-iltizam*) is also well known. Once you know this, be aware that His saying in this noble verse, *wa-la yufliḥu as-sahiru* (وَلا يُفْلِحُ السَّاحِرُ), and the rest of the verse, includes the negation of all kinds of success (*falah*) from the magician. He emphasized this by generalizing in places with His saying *haythu ata* (حَيْثُ أتى), and that is evidence of his disbelief. This is because success (*falah*) is not negated absolutely and generally except from the one in whom there is no good, and he is the disbeliever. Two matters indicate what we have mentioned:

The first is what came in the verses that indicate that the magician is a disbeliever, such as His saying:

﴿And Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

His saying, *wa-ma kafara Sulayman* (وَمَا كَفَرَ سُلَيْمَانُ), indicates that if he had been a magician, and far be it from him, he would have been a disbeliever. His saying, *wa-lakinna ash-shayatin kafaru yu'allimuna an-nasa as-sihr* (وَلَكِنَّ الشَّيَاطِينَ كَفَرُوا يُعَلِّمُونَ النَّاسَ السِّحْرَ), is explicit about the disbelief of the one who teaches magic. And His saying, may He be exalted, about Harut and Marut, confirming this:

﴿And they did not teach anyone until they said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]

And His saying:

﴿And they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. And they had certainly known that whoever purchased it would have no share (*khalaq*) in the Hereafter.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]

*Khalaq* (خَلاق) means a share. The total negation of a share in the Hereafter applies only to the disbeliever, we seek refuge in Allah, may He be exalted. These verses are clear proofs that among magic is that which is outright disbelief, and there is no doubt about that.

The second matter is that it is known from surveying the Qur'an that the majority of its usage of the expression *la yufliḥu* (لا يُفْلِحُ) refers to the disbeliever,

• like His saying in *Surah Yunus*:

﴿They said, "Allah has taken a son." Glory be to Him! He is the Self-Sufficient. To Him belongs what is in the heavens and what is on the earth. You have no authority for this. Do you say about Allah that which you do not know?﴾ ﴿Say, "Indeed, those who invent falsehood against Allah will not succeed."﴾ ﴿[For them is] enjoyment in this world; then to Us is their return; then We will make them taste the severe punishment because they used to disbelieve.﴾ [Yunus: 68–70],

• and His saying in *Yunus* also:

﴿So who is more unjust than one who invents against Allah a lie or denies His verses? Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.﴾ [Yunus: 17],

• and His saying in *al-An'am*:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents against Allah a lie or denies His verses? Indeed, the wrongdoers will not succeed.﴾ [al-An'am: 21].

And other verses besides these.

From the implication of the contrary of the mentioned verses it is understood that, on the other side of those attributes which required the negation of success from the magicians and other disbelievers, success is attained. This is indeed the case, as He, may He be exalted and high, clarified in many verses, such as His saying:

﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5],

and His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿The believers have certainly succeeded.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1].

The verses of this kind are numerous.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse, *wa-la yufliḥu as-sahir* (وَلا يُفْلِحُ السَّاحِرُ), is the present tense of *aflaḥa* (أفْلَحَ), meaning to attain success (*falah*). *Falah* in Arabic is used for winning what is sought. From it is the saying of Labid:

*"So be sensible, if you are not yet sensible; and indeed whoever has intellect has succeeded."*

His saying, *wa-laqad aflaḥa man kana 'aqal* (وَلَقَدْ أفْلَحَ مَن كانَ عَقَلَ), means that whoever Allah has granted intellect has won the greatest object of pursuit. *Falah* is also used for remaining and enduring in bliss. From it is the saying of Labid:

*"If a living being could attain falah, the wrestler with spears would have attained it."*

His saying, *mudrik al-falah* (مُدْرِكُ الفَلاحِ), means remaining. And the saying of al-Adbat ibn Quray' as-Sa'di, and it was said to be Ka'b ibn Zuhayr:

*"For every worry among worries there is a relief, and the evening and the morning have no falah with them."*

He means that with the alternation of night and day there is no remaining. Some scholars interpreted *hayya 'ala al-falah* (حَيَّ عَلَى الفَلاحِ) in the adhan and the iqamah according to each of these two meanings.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse, *haythu ata* (حَيْثُ أتى), *haythu* (حَيْثُ) is a word that indicates place, just as it indicates time at times, and it has sometimes been given the meaning of a conditional. So His saying, *wa-la yufliḥu as-sahiru haythu ata* (وَلا يُفْلِحُ السَّاحِرُ حَيْثُ أتى), means: wherever he heads and travels. This is a well-known Arabic idiom used to express generality, as in the saying: "So-and-so is characterized by such-and-such wherever he goes, whichever path he takes, and wherever he is." Of this type is the saying of Zuhayr:

*"The companions have departed and did not return for those they left behind, and they provisioned you with longing, whichever path they took."*

Al-Qurtubi said in his explanation of this verse, *wa-la yufliḥu as-sahiru haythu ata*: that is, he does not win or escape wherever he comes on earth. It was said: wherever he schemes. The meaning in the verse is what we have clarified, and Allah knows best.

* *

Issues related to this noble verse

The first issue: know that in language, *sihr* (السِّحْر) is applied to everything whose cause is hidden, subtle, and fine. Therefore the Arabs say of a thing that is extremely hidden: "More hidden than magic." From it is the saying of Muslim ibn al-Walid al-Ansari:

*"You made the signs of affection between us snares of glances, which are more hidden than magic."*

*"So I recognize from them the union in the softness of their gaze, and I recognize from them the estrangement in the sidelong glance."*

For this reason the beauty of the two eyes is called *sihr*, because they strike hearts with their arrows in secret. From it is the saying of the woman who ardently praised Nasr ibn Hajjaj al-Sulami:

*"And look at the magic flowing in his glances, and look at the blackness of the eye in his drooping gaze."*

**Second issue:** Regarding the definition of magic (sihr) in the technical sense, it is not possible to define it with a definition that is both comprehensive and exclusive, because of the great number of different types that fall under it. No common quality can be established among them that would include all of them and exclude everything else. For this reason, the scholars' definitions of it differ considerably.

* *

**Third issue:** Know that al-Fakhr al-Razi, in his commentary, divided magic into eight types.

**The first type:** the magic of the Kaldaniyyin and the Kasdaniyyin (Chaldeans), who in ancient times worshipped the stars and claimed that they were the governors of this world, and that good and evil, happiness and misfortune, proceed from them. They were the people whom God Most High sent Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to refute and to oppose in their claims. He (al-Razi) spoke at length about this type of magic.

The author of these notes, may God pardon and forgive him, says: It is well known that this type of magic is disbelief (kufr) without any dispute, because in it they drew near to the stars as Muslims draw near to God, and they hoped for good from the stars and feared evil from them, just as Muslims hope in their Lord and fear Him. They are disbelievers who, in their magic, draw near to the stars through manifest disbelief (al-kufr al-bawah).

**The second type of magic:** the magic of people of imaginations and strong souls. He then argued for the influence of imagination (wahm) by saying that a person can walk on a plank laid on the surface of the earth, but cannot walk on it if it is stretched over a river or the like. He said: "This is only because the imagining of falling, when it becomes strong, brings it about." He also said: "The physicians have agreed to forbid the one suffering from jaundice (al-marur) from looking at red things, and the one suffering from epilepsy (al-masru') from looking at things that are strongly glittering and revolving. This is only because souls were created obedient to imaginations."

He said: The author of al-Shifa' related from Aristotle, in his work on the natures of animals, that when a hen greatly resembles roosters in voice and in behaviour with roosters, there grows on her leg something like what grows on the leg of a rooster. He said: Then the author of al-Shifa' said: "This indicates that bodily states follow psychic states." He said: The nations have agreed that verbal supplication devoid of inner desire is weak in effect and has no influence. This indicates that aspirations and souls have effects... up to the end of his words on this type of magic, and he spoke at length about it.

It is well known that evil souls have effects by the permission of God Most High. Among the clearest legal proofs for this is his saying (ﷺ): "The evil eye is real; if anything could outstrip the decree, the evil eye would outstrip it." This sound hadith indicates that the aspiration of the one who casts the evil eye and the strength of his soul in evil, God has made a cause for influence on the one afflicted by the evil eye.

Al-Razi said, regarding this type of magic: "When you know this, we say: souls that perform these acts may be very strong, so they dispense in these acts with the use of instruments and tools, and they may be weak, so they need the use of these instruments. Its verification is that when the soul is elevated above the body and strongly drawn toward the world of the heavens, it becomes as though it were one of the heavenly spirits, and so it is strong in influencing the substances of this world. But if it is weak and strongly attached to this bodily self, then it has no action at all except upon this body." Up to the end of his words. What is in it is not hidden from one who examines it.

The Hafiz Ibn Kathir said in his commentary on Surat al-Baqarah, after quoting the words of al-Razi that we mentioned just now, the following text: "Then he (al-Razi) pointed to the treatment of this disease by reducing food and withdrawing from people." I say: What he points to is the use of states (al-tasarruf bi'l-hal), and it is of two kinds. Sometimes it is a sound, legal state, by which a person acts in what God and His Messenger (ﷺ) have commanded and refrains from what God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ) have forbidden. These states are gifts from God Most High and marvels (karamat) for the righteous of this community, and this is not called magic in the Shari'ah. Sometimes the state is corrupt, and its possessor does not comply with what God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ) have commanded, and does not act through it in that matter. These are the states of the wretched who oppose the Shari'ah, and God's giving them these states does not indicate His love for them. Just as the Dajjal has among the extraordinary things of custom what numerous hadiths indicate, even though he is blameworthy in the Shari'ah, may God curse him. Likewise whoever resembles him among those who oppose the Muhammadan Shari'ah, upon its bearer be the best of prayers and peace. The words of Ibn Kathir, may God Most High have mercy on him, end here.

**The third type of the mentioned kinds of magic:** seeking help from earthly spirits, meaning subjugating the jinn and making them serve. He said:

Know that the affirmation of the jinn is among what some later philosophers and the Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) have denied. As for the great philosophers, they did not deny the affirmation of them, except that they named them "earthly spirits." The jinn mentioned are of two kinds: believers and disbelievers, and the disbelievers are the devils (shayatin).

Al-Razi said in his discussion of this type of magic: "The connection of rational souls with them is easier than their connection with the heavenly spirits, because of the affinity and nearness between them. Then the practitioners of the craft (ashab al-sana'a) and the people of experience (ashab al-tajriba) have witnessed that connection with these earthly spirits is achieved through easy acts such as incantations (ruqa), fumigation (dakhn), and abstraction (tajrid). This type is called 'the amulets' (al-'aza'im) and the work of subjugating the jinn." Al-Razi also spoke at length about this type of magic.

**The fourth type of magic:** imaginings and deception of the eyes (al-takhayyulat wa'l-akhdh bi'l-'uyun). The basis of this type is that the sight may see a thing contrary to what it is in reality, due to accidental causes. For this reason the errors of vision are many. Do you not see that a passenger on a ship, when he looks at the shore, sees the ship standing still and the shore moving, and that indicates that the stationary is seen as moving and the moving as stationary? And a falling drop is seen as a straight line. Up to the end of al-Razi's words. He also spoke at length about this type.

Ibn Kathir said in his commentary on Surat al-Baqarah, briefly summarizing the mentioned words of al-Razi: "Its basis is that sight may err and occupy itself with a specific thing and not others. Do you not see that the skilled conjurer (sha'badhi) displays the performing of something that bewilders the minds of those who look at it, and draws their eyes to it, until, when they are completely absorbed in that thing by staring and the like, he quickly performs another act with great speed, and then something appears to them other than what they had expected, so they marvel greatly at it. Had he been silent and not spoken in a way that turns the thoughts to the opposite of what he intends to do, and had the souls and imaginations not been moved to other than what he intends to produce, the observers would have noticed everything he does. He said: The more the conditions weaken the sense of sight in some kind of defect, the better the act is. Such as when the conjurer sits in a place that is very bright or very dark, so the seeing faculty does not hold firm to its conditions in that state." From him, end of quote.

It is not hidden that the magic of the magicians of Pharaoh was of this type. It was imagining and deception of the eyes, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then their ropes and their staffs appeared to him, by their magic, as though they were moving﴾ [Ta-Ha: 66]. So the application of "imagining" in the verse to their magic is a clear text on this. This is also indicated by His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿When they cast, they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116]. For the casting of magic upon the eyes of the people in the verse indicates that their eyes imagined something other than the actual reality. And God knows best.

**The fifth type of magic:** the wondrous acts that appear from the composition of machines arranged according to geometric proportions, such as a horseman on a horse holding a trumpet, which, every time an hour of the day passes, sounds the trumpet without anyone touching it. Among them are the statues that the Romans and the Indians make, so that the viewer cannot distinguish them from a human being, to the extent that they make them laughing and weeping, so that in them one can distinguish between the laughter of joy, the laughter of shame, and the laughter of one who gloats.

These aspects are among the subtle matters of wondrous appearances (makhayil). Al-Razi said: "The magic of the magicians of Pharaoh was of this kind." From this category also is the construction of clocks. And there falls under this category the science of moving heavy weights, which is to move a great weight with a light and easy instrument. In reality this should not be counted as magic, because for it there are known and precious causes, and whoever is acquainted with them is able to do it. But since acquaintance with them is difficult, the people of the outward (ahl al-zahir) count this as magic, because its source is hidden. End of quote.

I have known that al-Razi holds that the magic of the magicians of Pharaoh was of this last type, because the magicians placed mercury on the ropes and staffs, and the heat of the sun moved it, so the ropes and staffs moved, and they thought that it was a true natural movement. What appears to us is that it is of the type that preceded it, as we have mentioned, and there is no obstacle to two types being combined in one thing, so that it falls under both. And God Most High knows best.

Ibn Kathir said, after mentioning the words of al-Razi that we cited on this type of magic: "I say: Of this kind are the tricks of the Christians upon their common people, by the lights they show them, such as the matter of the lamp of the Church of the Resurrection (Qumama) which they have in Bayt al-Maqdis, and what they devise of bringing fire secretly into the church and lighting that lamp by a subtle craft, which is passed off on the rabble among them. As for their elite, they acknowledge this, but they interpret it as a means of gathering their companions upon their religion, and so they consider it permissible for themselves. Among them there is a resemblance to the ignorant and foolish among the devotees of the Karramiyya (a sect) who consider it permissible to fabricate hadiths concerning encouragement and warning, and so they enter among those about whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever deliberately lies about me, let him take his seat in the Fire,' and his saying: 'Narrate from me, but do not lie about me, for whoever lies about me will enter the Fire.'

Then he (al-Razi) mentioned here, that is al-Razi, as a report from some monks, that he heard the voice of a bird with a sorrowful voice and weak movement, and when the birds hear it they feel pity for it and bring it from the fruit of the olive tree in its nest so that it may sustain itself with it. This monk undertook to make a bird in its form and succeeded in making it hollow, so that when the wind entered it, a sound was heard from it like the sound of that bird. He retired into a hermitage (sawma'a) that he built and claimed that it was over the grave of one of their righteous men, and he hung that bird in one of its places. When the olive season came, he opened a door from its side, so the wind entered the interior of this figure and every bird heard its sound too, in its form, so the birds came and carried away a great amount of olives. The Christians saw nothing but that olive in this hermitage, and they did not know its cause. Thus he deceived them and made them imagine that this was one of the marvels (karamat) of the owner of that grave. Upon them be the continuous curses of God until the Day of Resurrection." End of the words of Ibn Kathir.

Al-Razi mentioned in this question, which Ibn Kathir reported from him, that the bird mentioned is called al-Baraṣil, that the one who made its image is called Arjʻiyanus al-Musiqar, that he placed it on the ancient Temple of Jerusalem (Urshalim) when he renewed it, and that the one who first undertook the building of that Temple was Ustarkhus the ascetic.

Al-Shinqiti, the author of this commentary, said, may Allah pardon him and forgive him:

This fifth type, which al-Razi counted among the kinds of magic, is the amazing works that appear from assembling machines arranged according to geometric ratios... etc. It should not today be counted among the kinds of magic, because its causes have become clear and familiar to people due to the advancement of material science. What is clear and has become ordinary does not fall within the definition of magic. Many matters whose causes were once hidden have today become very apparent. And Allah knows best.

The sixth type of magic: seeking help from the special properties of medicines, such as putting into someone's food some drugs that dull and remove the intellect, and smoking intoxicating substances, like the brain of a donkey; if a person consumes it, his intellect becomes dull and his shrewdness decreases. This was said by al-Razi. Then he said: "Know that there is no way to deny special properties, for the effect of the magnet is observed. However, people have exaggerated about it and mixed truth with falsehood and true with false." End of al-Razi's words.

Ibn Kathir said, after mentioning this type of magic citing al-Razi: "I say: Among this category are many who claim poverty and deceive ignorant people with these special properties, claiming that these are states they have acquired from contact with fires, handling snakes, and other such tricks." End of Ibn Kathir's words.

The seventh type of magic mentioned: binding the heart (ta'liq al-qalb), which is that the magician claims he knows the Greatest Name, and that the jinn obey him and submit to him in most circumstances. When it happens that the listener to this is weak-minded and of little discernment, he believes it is true, and his heart becomes attached to it. A kind of terror and fear arises in him, and when fear arises the sensing faculties weaken; then the magician is able to do whatever he wishes. Al-Razi said: Whoever has experienced affairs and known the conditions of people of knowledge knows that attachment of the heart has a great effect in carrying out actions and concealing secrets.

Ibn Kathir said, after quoting this type of magic from al-Razi: "This pattern is called al-tanbala, and it is only promoted upon weak-minded human beings. In the science of physiognomy (firasa) there is what guides one to recognize the complete intellect from the deficient one. If the noble one is skilled in the science of firasa, he recognizes who among other people will submit to him."

The eighth type of magic: striving through tale-bearing (al-namima) and sowing discord (al-tadrib) in subtle, hidden ways, and this is widespread among people. End of quote. Tadrib among people means inciting some of them against others.

Ibn Kathir said, after quoting this last type from al-Razi: "I say: Tale-bearing is of two kinds. Sometimes it is done in order to stir up strife among people and to divide the hearts of the believers; this is unanimously agreed to be forbidden. But if it is done for the purpose of reconciliation between people and uniting the word of the Muslims, as came in the hadith, 'The liar is not one who conveys good (between people)', or if it is done for the purpose of undermining and dividing the gatherings of disbelievers, then this is a matter that is desired, as came in the hadith, 'War is deception', and as Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud did in dividing the ranks of the confederates from Quraydah: he went to these and conveyed news about those to them, and carried some other report from these to those, then he sowed enmity between them, so souls became estranged and separated. Only one with far-reaching insight takes such cunning. And to Allah is the help sought."

Then al-Razi said: "This is the sum of what is said concerning the divisions of magic and the explanation of its types and categories."

I say: The reason I included many of these mentioned types under the art of magic is the subtlety of their means. For magic linguistically is an expression for what is subtle and whose cause is hidden. For this reason, it came in the hadith, "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence," and suhur (the pre-dawn meal) was named suhur because it occurs hidden at the end of the night. And siḥr (the lungs) is the organ of nourishment, and it was named so because of its concealment and the subtlety of its channels to the parts and folds of the body, as Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr to 'Utba: "Has his sihr swelled?" meaning: has his lung swelled from fear?

A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ died between my sahr and my nahr." And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They bewitched the eyes of the people﴾ [al-A'raf: 116], meaning they concealed their action from them. End of Ibn Kathir's words, may Allah have mercy on him.

This is the summary of the eight divisions which al-Razi mentioned in his tafsir in Surat al-Baqara as the divisions of magic. Scholars have various classifications of it, most of which return to these divisions. The Shaykh, my master Abdullah ibn al-Hajj Ibrahim al-Alawi al-Shinqiti, author of many beneficial works, divided it in his poem called (Rushd al-Ghafil) and its commentary on it, in which he explained the kinds of the sciences of evil so that they may be avoided, into several categories:

(Among them) a category called (al-Haymiya) (hay-mi-yah), with a kasra on the ha', followed by a yā' with two dots below, then a mim, then a yā', followed by the feminine long alif, on the pattern of kibriya'. He said: It is what is composed of celestial properties attributed to the states of the spheres; some of its known effects appear on the one upon whom something of it is performed, known to magicians, and perception may remain for him, or it may be completely taken from him, so his states become like those of a sleeper without distinction, until he imagines the passing of many years in a short time, the birth of children, the ending of lifetimes, and other things in an hour or similar short time. Whoever has not had this done to him finds nothing of what is mentioned. This is imagination with no reality. End.

(Among them) a type called (al-Simiya') with a kasra on the unpointed sin, and its remaining letters like those of the previous. He said: It is an expression for what is composed of earthly properties, such as a special oil or special liquids, with which perception remains, and it may be completely taken away, to the end of what was mentioned under al-Haymiya.

(Among them): a type which is harmful incantations. He said: like the incantations of the Jahiliyya and the people of India, and they may be disbelief. He said: For this reason Malik forbade incantations in non-Arabic languages. Ibn Zakariyya said in his commentary on (al-Nasiha): what causes harm is not called ruqya; rather that is called sihr.

(Among them): a category called the properties of certain realities which have influence over souls, such as the comb, the (mushaqqa), and the dried pollen of the male date palm, and the story of the Jew who bewitched the Prophet ﷺ and the payment for his sorcery is well known. Its explanation will come, Allah willing.

Among the examples of this category according to its practitioners: that some kinds of dogs, when stoned with a rock, bite it; if they are stoned with seven stones and bite each one, and those stones are thrown into water, whoever drinks from it, the magicians claim that specific known effects appear in him. May Allah curse them.

(Among them): a type called (al-Tilasim), which is an expression for inscribing special names connected to the spheres and stars, according to their claim, on a body of metals or other things, from which a special property arises, bound in the customary course of things. Along with that there must be a righteous soul for these works, for the special property does not operate through the hand of some souls.

(Among them): a type called (al-Azaim), and they claim that every kind of angel has names they were commanded to glorify, and whenever they are adjured by them, they obey, respond, and do what is asked of them. End of quote. The corruption of this claim is not hidden.

(Among them): a type they call the (Istikhdam) for the stars and the jinn. The practitioners of istikhdam claim that the stars have spiritual perceptions. When the stars are confronted with a special incense and a special garment worn by the one who handles the incense, the spiritual nature of the star sphere becomes obedient to him, and whenever he wants something, it does it for him, according to their claim. May Allah curse them. This type is from the magic of the Chaldeans mentioned earlier. Likewise, the kings of the jinn, they claim that if they do special things for each of their kings, they obey and do what they wish. He said: The conditions of these matters are fully recorded in their books. He mentioned many other kinds of the sciences of evil: such as geomancy (khatt), figures (ashkal), birth charts (mawalid), lots (qur'a), omens (fa'l), the science of the shoulder-blade (ilm al-katif), music (al-musiqa), thunder-lore (al-ra'diyy), soothsaying (kihana), and other things.

Geomancy (al-khatt al-ramli) is well known. Ashkal is the plural of shakl, and its science is called the science of tables and the science of talismanic squares (awfaq), which are well known and are from falsehood.

Mawalid is the plural of mawlid, and it is that one claims, from knowledge of the star that was rising at the birth of a person, that he will be a sultan or a scholar, or rich or poor, or long-lived or short-lived, and the like.

The qur'a is what they call the lot of the prophets, and its substance is a table drawn in whose houses are names of prophets and names of birds. After the table there are translations; for each name there is a specific translation, and in it are mentioned matters of benefits and harms. The person is told: close your eyes and place your finger on the table. When he places it on a name, its translation is read to him so that he believes that what is mentioned in it will happen to him. He said: The scholars have counted this among the seeking of decisions by arrows.

By omens (fa'l) he means acquired omens, such as when a person wants to marry or travel, for example, so he goes out to hear what is understood from it as advancing or refraining, and this includes looking into the Qur'an for that purpose. It is not hidden that this is a kind of seeking decisions by arrows. As for what presents itself without acquisition, such as when one hears someone say, "Unsuccessful," it is not of this category, as the authentic hadiths have stated.

The science of the shoulder-blade: a science which people of evil and misguidance claim that whoever knows it, when he looks at the shoulder-blades of sheep, becomes aware of matters of the unseen, and perhaps the practitioner claims that the sultan will die on such-and-such date, or that cheapness or high prices will occur, or the death of notables such as scholars and righteous people; and he may mention the matter of treasures or buried hoards, and the like. Music is well known, and all of it is from falsehood, as is not hidden from one who has knowledge of the noble Shari'a.
