Al-ra'diyyat (thunder-lore): a science whose practitioners claim that if thunder occurs at such-and-such time of the year and month, it is a sign of unseen matters: of drought and fertility, of abundance and scarcity of trade in the markets, of many deaths and the destruction of livestock, of the end of a dynasty, and the like. The difference between 'iyafa (geomancy/reading traces) and kihana, although both share the claim of knowing the unseen, is that 'iyafa is specific to past matters, while kihana is specific to future matters. End of his words.

The sciences of evil are many. Our purpose in mentioning what we have mentioned of them is to alert to their baseness and ugliness in the Shari'a, and that some of them are outright disbelief, and some lead to disbelief, and the least of their ranks is strict prohibition. Some hadiths and reports indicate that 'iyafa, tarq and tiyara are from magic. We have already presented the meaning of that in (al-An'am). And from the Prophet ﷺ, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Whoever acquires a branch of the stars has acquired a branch of magic, increasing as it increases." Narrated by Abu Dawud with a sound chain. And for al-Nasa'i, from the hadith of Abu Hurayra: "Whoever ties a knot and then blows into it has practiced magic, and whoever practices magic has committed shirk, and whoever hangs anything upon himself is left to it."

* *

Fourth issue

The scholars differed concerning magic: is it a reality, or is it mere imagination with no reality? The verified position is that some of it is a reality, as we have presented, and some of it is imagination, as its explanation has preceded. This is understood from the divisions of magic previously mentioned in the words of al-Razi and others.

* *

Fifth issue

The scholars differed concerning the one who learns sorcery and practises it. Some of them said: he becomes a disbeliever (kafir) by that act. This is the view of the majority of scholars, including Malik, Abu Hanifah, the companions of Ahmad, and others. There is a report from Ahmad that implies he does not become a disbeliever. There is also a report from al-Shafi'i that when someone has learned sorcery, it is said to him: "Describe your sorcery to us." If he describes what necessitates disbelief, such as the sorcery of the people of Babylon, which involves drawing near to the stars and believing that they do what is asked of them, then he is a disbeliever. If what he describes does not necessitate disbelief, then if he believes it to be permissible, he is a disbeliever, and otherwise he is not. The statements of the people of knowledge on this matter are many and well known.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The correct position on this issue is to make a distinction. If the sorcery involves venerating other than Allah, such as the stars, the jinn, and other things that lead to disbelief, then it is disbelief without any dispute. Of this type is the sorcery of Harut and Marut mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah, for it is disbelief without dispute, as shown by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], and His words: ﴿And they do not teach anyone until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], and His words: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102], and His words, the Exalted: ﴿And the sorcerer does not prosper wherever he goes﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69], as has been explained earlier. If the sorcery does not necessitate disbelief, such as seeking help through the special properties of certain things, such as ointments and other things, then it is forbidden with a severe prohibition, but it does not bring its practitioner to disbelief. This is the correct position, if Allah, the Exalted, wills, on this issue on which the scholars differed.

* *

The Sixth Issue

Know that the scholars differed regarding whether the sorcerer is put to death merely by performing sorcery and practising it, or not. Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir: Ibn Hubayrah said: Is he killed merely for performing sorcery and practising it? Malik and Ahmad said: Yes. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah said: No. As for if he kills a person by his sorcery, then he is put to death according to Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad. Abu Hanifah said: He is not put to death unless this is repeated from him, or he confesses to it regarding a specific person. When he is killed, they say he is put to death as a prescribed punishment (hadd), except al-Shafi'i, who said that he is put to death in that case as retaliation (qisas).

Is the sorcerer's repentance accepted if he repents? Malik, Abu Hanifah, and Ahmad, according to the well-known view from them, said: It is not accepted. Al-Shafi'i and Ahmad in another narration said: The repentance is accepted.

As for the sorcerer from the People of the Book, according to Abu Hanifah he is killed just as a Muslim sorcerer is killed. Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ahmad said: He is not killed, referring to the story of Labid ibn al-A'sam.

They also differed concerning a Muslim woman sorcerer. According to Abu Hanifah, she is not killed, but is imprisoned. The three (Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad) said: Her ruling is the same as that of a man. Abu Bakr al-Khallal said: Abu Bakr al-Marwazi informed us, saying: Umar ibn Harun read to Abu Abd Allah, meaning Ahmad ibn Hanbal, reporting: Yunus informed us from al-Zuhri, who said: The sorcerer of the Muslims is put to death, and the sorcerer of the polytheists is not put to death, because "a woman from the Jews bewitched the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he did not kill her." Al-Qurtubi transmitted from Malik that he said regarding a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection): He is put to death if he kills by his sorcery. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad transmitted from Malik two narrations regarding a dhimmi who practises sorcery: one is that he is asked to repent, and if he embraces Islam, well and good, otherwise he is put to death; the second is that he is put to death even if he embraces Islam.

As for the Muslim sorcerer: if his sorcery includes disbelief, he is declared a disbeliever according to the four Imams and others, due to the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And they do not teach anyone until they say, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. However, Malik said: If he is discovered, his repentance is not accepted, because he is like a zindiq (heretic). If he repents before being discovered and comes repentant, we accept him. If his sorcery kills someone, he is put to death. Al-Shafi'i said: If he says, "I did not intend to kill," then he is mistaken and must pay the blood money (diyah). End of the words of Ibn Kathir, may Allah, the Exalted, have mercy on him.

An-Nawawi said in his commentary on Muslim: As for learning and teaching it, it is forbidden. If it includes what necessitates disbelief, he is declared a disbeliever, and otherwise not. If it does not include what necessitates disbelief, he is disciplined (ta'zir) and asked to repent from it, and he is not put to death according to us. If he repents, his repentance is accepted. Malik said: The sorcerer is a disbeliever who is put to death for sorcery, is not asked to repent, and his repentance is not accepted, but rather his killing is obligatory. The issue is based on the disagreement over the acceptance of the repentance of the zindiq, for the sorcerer in his view is a disbeliever as we have mentioned, while in our view he is not a disbeliever. In our view the repentance of the hypocrite and the zindiq is accepted. Qadi Iyad said: The view of Malik is also the view of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and it is reported from a group of the Companions and the Successors. Our companions said: If the sorcerer kills a person by his sorcery and confesses that he died by his sorcery, and that it usually kills, then retaliation (qisas) becomes obligatory for him. If he says that it caused death but that it may or may not kill, then there is no retaliation, and the blood money is due from his own property (not from his paternal kin ('aqilah)), because the 'aqilah does not bear what is established by the confession of the offender. Our companions said: Killing by sorcery cannot be established by evidence (bayyinah), but only by the sorcerer's confession, and Allah knows best. End of the words of an-Nawawi.

Ibn Hajar said in Fath al-Bari, in discussing al-Bukhari's chapter heading "The Chapter on Sorcery" and the words of Allah: ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]: This verse has been used as evidence that sorcery is disbelief and that its learner is a disbeliever. This is clear in some of its types which I mentioned earlier, namely worshipping the devils or the stars. As for the other type, which belongs to trickery and deception (sha'wadhah), the one who learns it does not become a disbeliever at all. An-Nawawi said: The practice of sorcery is forbidden and is among the major sins by consensus. The Prophet ﷺ counted it among the seven destructive sins. Some of it is disbelief, and some of it is not disbelief but a major sin. If it contains a statement or action that necessitates disbelief, then it is disbelief, and otherwise not. As for learning and teaching it, it is forbidden, to the end of the words of an-Nawawi which we quoted earlier. Then Ibn Hajjah, when he quoted him, said: There is great disagreement on the issue and many details, and this is not the place to expound them.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The correct position on this issue, if Allah, the Exalted, wills, is that sorcery is of two types, as previously mentioned. Some of it is disbelief, and some of it does not bring its practitioner to disbelief. If the sorcerer uses sorcery that is disbelief, there is no doubt that he is put to death as a disbeliever, due to the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him."

In my view, the stronger of the two opinions regarding his being asked to repent is that he is asked to repent, and if he repents, his repentance is accepted. I have explained in my book (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab), in Surah Al 'Imran, that the stronger of the two views with evidence is that the repentance of the zindiq is accepted, because Allah did not command His Prophet nor his ummah ﷺ to probe the hearts of people, but rather to be content with the outward. What they conceal in their inner selves is left to Allah, the Exalted. This is contrary to Imam Malik and his companions, who say that the sorcerer has the ruling of the zindiq, because he persists in disbelief, and the zindiq's repentance is not accepted in his view unless he comes repentant before being discovered. In my view, the stronger of the two opinions is that the female sorcerer has the same ruling as the male sorcerer, and that if she disbelieves by her sorcery, she is put to death just as a man is put to death, because the word "man" (man) in His words: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him," includes females according to the stronger and more correct of the two opinions, if Allah, the Exalted, wills. Among the evidences for this are His words, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female﴾ [an-Nisa: 124], which includes females under the word "whoever" (man), and His words: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear immorality﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30], and His words: ﴿And whoever of you is devoutly obedient to Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 31], and other verses besides these. Regarding this issue, namely the inclusion of the word "man" of females in the Qur'an and the Sunnah, the author indicated in Maraqi as-Su'ud with his words:

"Is the inclusion of 'man' of females a deviation? Among those who are Muslims they have differed."

As for the case where the sorcerer performs sorcery that does not bring its practitioner to disbelief, this is the point of disagreement among the scholars. Those who said that he is put to death even if he did not become a disbeliever by his sorcery, most of them said: He is put to death as a prescribed punishment (hadd), even if he killed a person by his sorcery. Al-Shafi'i alone, in this case, held that he is put to death as retaliation (qisas), not as a prescribed punishment.

These are the arguments of the two groups and their discussion:

As for those who said absolutely that if he practises his sorcery, even if he has killed no one by it, they relied on reports from the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and on a hadith that came with this meaning, but it is not authentic. Among the reports indicating this is what al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih, in the Book of Jihad, in the chapter on the jizyah: Ali ibn Abd Allah narrated to us, Sufyan narrated to us, who said: I heard Amr say: I was sitting with Jabir ibn Zayd and Amr ibn Aws, and Bajalah narrated to them in the year seventy, the year Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr performed Hajj with the people of Basrah, at the steps of Zamzam, saying: I was a scribe for Juz' ibn Mu'awiyah, the uncle of al-Ahnaf. Then the letter of Umar ibn al-Khattab came to us a year before his death: "Kill every sorcerer, and separate every person who is within the forbidden degree from among the Magians." He said: So we killed three sorcerers in one day, and we separated those within the forbidden degrees among them. It was also narrated by Ahmad and Abu Dawud. Know that the phrase "Kill every sorcerer," etc., in this report is omitted in some of al-Bukhari's narrations and present in some of them, and it is present in the narrations of Musaddad and Abu Ya'la. Said in Fath (al-Bari).

Among the reports indicating this also is what Malik narrated in the Muwatta from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'd ibn Zurarah, that it reached him that Hafsah, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, killed a slave girl of hers who had bewitched her, and she had made her a mudabbarah (one freed upon her owner's death), so she ordered her and she was killed. Malik said: The sorcerer who practises sorcery and no one else has practised it for him, is like the one whom Allah, Blessed and Exalted, mentioned in His Book: ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. So I see that such a person should be killed if he practises it on his own initiative. End of quotation from the Muwatta.

Similar to this was narrated by Abd al-Razzaq. Among the reports indicating this is what al-Bukhari narrated in his Tarikh al-Kabir: Ishaq narrated to us. Khalid al-Wasiti narrated to us, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abu Uthman: There was a man with al-Walid who was playing, and he slaughtered a person and severed his head. Then Jundub al-Azdi came and killed him. Amr ibn Muhammad narrated to me, Hushaym narrated to us, from Khalid, from Abu Uthman, from Jundub al-Bajali: that he killed him. Musa narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahid narrated to us, from Asim, from Abu Uthman: Jundub ibn Ka'b killed him.

In (Fath al-Majid Sharh Kitab at-Tawhid) by the scholar Shaykh Abd al-Rahman ibn Hasan, may Allah, the Exalted, have mercy on him, after he referred to the words of al-Bukhari in the aforementioned history, and it was narrated by al-Bayhaqi in ad-Dala'il at length, and in it: Al-Walid then ordered him imprisoned. He mentioned the story in full, and it has many chains of transmission. End of quotation from it.

The following are reports from three of the Companions concerning the killing of the sorcerer: ʿUmar, his daughter the Mother of the Believers Ḥafṣah, and Jundub, may Allah be pleased with them all. No opposing view from the Companions is known. This is reinforced by what al-Tirmidhi and al-Dāraqutnī narrated from Jundub, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The legal punishment for the sorcerer is striking him with the sword." Al-Tirmidhi declared the chain of this hadith weak and said: "The correct version from Jundub is that it is mawqūf (halting at a Companion)." Its weakness is due to the presence in its chain of Ismāʿīl ibn Muslim al-Makkī, who is weak in ḥadīth. In Fatḥ al-Majīd he also said, in discussing the aforementioned hadith of Jundub: Ibn al-Sakan narrated from the hadith of Buraydah that the Prophet ﷺ said: "He is struck with one blow, and he becomes a community unto himself." End of quotation from him.

Ibn Kathīr said in his Tafsir, after mentioning its weakening by the aforementioned Ismāʿīl: "I say: al-Ṭabarānī has narrated it through another route, from al-Ḥasan, from Jundub, as a marfūʿ (attributed to the Prophet ﷺ) report." End of quotation. This strengthens it, as you see.

These reports, against which no Companion is known to have objected to those who acted upon them, together with the attested marfūʿ hadith mentioned, constitute the evidence of those who say he is to be killed absolutely. The reports and the hadith in them indicate that he is killed even if his sorcery did not reach the level of disbelief, because the sorcerer whom Jundub, may Allah be pleased with him, killed practised sorcery of the kind of charlatanry and the seizing of eyes, to the extent that people imagined he had severed a man's head, while the reality was otherwise. ʿUmar's saying "Kill every sorcerer" indicates this by the form of generality. Among those who acted in accordance with these reports and this hadith are Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfah, Aḥmad in the more sound of his two narrations, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, Ibn ʿUmar, Ḥafṣah, Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allāh, Jundub ibn Kaʿb, Qays ibn Saʿd, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and others, as Ibn Qudāmah transmitted from them in al-Mughnī, in contrast to al-Shāfiʿī, Ibn al-Mundhir, and those who agreed with them.

Those who argued that, if his sorcery did not reach the level of disbelief, he is not killed, cited the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd agreed upon: "The blood of a Muslim person is not lawful except in one of three cases..." and we have mentioned it repeatedly. The sorcery whose practitioner does not disbelieve is not among the three mentioned. al-Qurṭubī, championing this view, said: "This is correct; the blood of the Muslims is inviolable and is not made lawful except with certainty, and there is no certainty in the presence of disagreement. And Allah knows best."

They also argued that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, sold a mudabbarah (a slave-woman granted freedom upon her owner's death) of hers who had practised sorcery on her; and had it been obligatory to kill her, her sale would not have been permissible. This was stated by Ibn al-Mundhir and others. As for what some have attempted, namely reconciling the aforementioned evidences by taking the sorcery in the sense that entails disbelief according to the view of those who say he is killed, and taking it in the sense that does not entail disbelief according to the view of those who say he is not killed, this does not hold. This is because the reports concerning his killing came regarding the killing of a sorcerer whose sorcery was of the kind of charlatanry, like the sorcerer of Jundub whom he killed; and that is not of the kind that entails disbelief which removes one from the religion of Islam, as has already been clarified. Thus reconciliation is not possible. Accordingly, preference must be applied: some prefer not killing, on the basis that the blood of Muslims is forbidden except with certainty; and some prefer killing, on the basis that its evidences are specific, and a general text does not conflict with a specific one, since the specific governs the general according to the majority of the scholars of legal theory, as is established in its proper place.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The more evident view to me is that the sorcerer whose sorcery does not reach the level of disbelief and by which he has not killed anyone is not to be killed. This is due to the definitive texts and the consensus on the sanctity of the blood of Muslims generally, except by clear evidence. The killing of a sorcerer whose sorcery does not make him a disbeliever has nothing established from the Prophet ﷺ concerning it, and daring to shed the blood of a Muslim without a sound proof from the Book or an attested marfūʿ Sunnah is not apparent to me. Knowledge rests with Allah the Exalted; however, the view that he is killed absolutely is very strong, due to the Companions' action in this regard without any objection.

* *

The Seventh Issue

Know that people differ concerning learning sorcery without practising it: is it permissible or not? The verified position, which is that of the majority, is that it is not permissible. Among the clearest evidences for this is Allah's explicit statement that it harms and does not benefit, in His saying: ﴿and they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. Since Allah affirmed that sorcery is harmful and negated that it is beneficial, how could it be permissible to learn that which is pure harm with no benefit in it?!

Al-Fakhr al-Rāzī, in his Tafsir at Surat al-Baqarah, asserted that it is permissible, rather obligatory. He said, in its text:

(The Fifth Issue) Regarding the claim that knowledge of sorcery is neither ugly nor forbidden: the verifiers agree upon this, because knowledge in itself is noble; and also because of the generality of His saying: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9]; and because if sorcery were not known, it would not be possible to distinguish it from a miracle, and knowing that the miracle is a miracle is obligatory, and what the obligatory depends upon is itself obligatory. Thus this requires that acquiring knowledge of sorcery be obligatory, and what is obligatory cannot be forbidden or ugly. End of quotation in his words.

The weakness and invalidity of this speech is not hidden. Ibn Kathīr critiqued it in his Tafsir after quoting it verbatim as we mentioned, saying:

This statement is open to objection in several respects. First, his saying "knowledge of sorcery is not ugly": if he means it is not ugly by reason, then his opponents among the Muʿtazilah deny this; and if he means it is not ugly by the Law, then in this noble verse, His saying ﴿and they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them﴾ is a condemnation of the knowledge of sorcery. In the Sunan there is: "Whoever comes to a fortune-teller or soothsayer has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad," and in the Sunan: "Whoever ties a knot and blows into it has practised sorcery." And his saying "nor is it forbidden; the verifiers agree upon this": how is it not forbidden with what we have mentioned of the verse and the hadith? And the agreement of the verifiers would require that the leading scholars or most of them had explicitly stated this issue. Where are their explicit statements on this?!

Then his inclusion of the knowledge of sorcery within the generality of His saying ﴿Say: are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ [al-Zumar: 9] is open to objection, because this verse only praises those who know the Legal knowledge. And when you say this is included in it! Then your elevating it to the obligation of learning it, on the grounds that knowledge of the miracle is not attained except through it, is weak, nay corrupt. This is because the greatest miracle of our Prophet, upon whom be prayers and peace, is the Mighty Qur'an, "falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it; a revelation from the All-Wise, the Praiseworthy."

Furthermore, knowledge that it is a miracle does not depend at all upon knowing sorcery. Moreover, it is known necessarily that the Companions, the Followers, the leaders of the Muslims and their common folk knew the miracle and distinguished it from others, and they did not know sorcery, nor learn it, nor teach it. And Allah knows best. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that this statement of Ibn Kathīr is correct, that his refutation of al-Rāzī hits its mark, and that learning sorcery should not be a matter of dispute regarding its prohibition, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they learned what harmed them and did not benefit them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102]. As for Ibn Kathīr's statement in the aforementioned speech: "In the Ṣaḥīḥ: 'Whoever comes to a fortune-teller or soothsayer...' etc.", if he means that the hadith is authentic in this respect, there is no objection; but if he means it is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs or one of them, that is not so.

From all of this you know that the words of Ibn Ḥajar in Fatḥ al-Bārī: "Some scholars have permitted learning sorcery for two reasons: either to distinguish what in it is disbelief from other things, or to remove it from one who has fallen into it.

As for the first: there is no prohibition in it except from the standpoint of belief; so when belief is sound, knowing a thing merely in itself does not entail prohibition, like one who knows the manner of the worship of idolaters toward idols, because the manner of what the sorcerer teaches is only the narration of a saying or an action, unlike practising it and acting upon it.

As for the second: if it cannot be accomplished, as some claim, except by some kind of disbelief or sin, then it is not permissible at all; otherwise it is permissible for the aforementioned purpose." End of quotation, is contrary to the verified position, since no one may permit what Allah has explicitly declared harmful and not beneficial; moreover, learning it may be a means to practising it, and a means to the forbidden must be blocked, as we have previously stated. He said in al-Marāqī:

"Blocking the means to the forbidden is an absolute obligation, just as opening them to what is obligatory."

This is the apparent position to us. And knowledge rests with Allah the Exalted.

* *

The Eighth Issue

Know that the scholars differ concerning untying sorcery from the one bewitched. Some permitted it, and some forbade it. Among those who permitted it was Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, may Allah have mercy on him. al-Bukhārī said in his Ṣaḥīḥ (Chapter: Is sorcery extracted?): Qatādah said: I said to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib: a man has an affliction (ṭibb), or is held back from his wife, may it be untied from him, or may it be unbound? He said: There is no harm in it; they only intend reform by it. As for what benefits, he did not forbid it. End of quotation from him. Al-Muzanī inclined to this view. al-Shāfiʿī said: There is no harm in the nushrah (untying). Reported by al-Qurṭubī. He also said: Ibn Baṭṭāl said: In the book of Wahb ibn Munabbih: he takes seven leaves of green lote-tree, pounds them between two stones, then sprinkles them with water and recites over it the Verse of the Throne, then sips from it three sips and bathes. It will remove from him everything that is in him, if Allah wills, and it is good for a man who has been prevented from his spouse. End of quotation from him.

Among those who permitted the nushrah, which is the untying of sorcery from the bewitched, were Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī, ʿĀmir al-Shaʿbī, and others. Among those who disliked it was al-Ḥasan. In the Ṣaḥīḥ, from ʿĀʾishah, that when Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam bewitched the Prophet ﷺ she said to him: "Why did you not seek untying?" He said: "As for Allah, He has healed me, and I disliked to stir up evil against the people."

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The verified position in this issue, from which one should not deviate, is that extracting sorcery, if it is done by the Qur'an, such as the two Refuges (al-Muʿawwidhatayn), the Verse of the Throne, and the like of what may be used for ruqyah, then there is no objection to it. If it is done by sorcery, or by non-Arabic words, or by what its meaning is not understood, or by any other kind not permitted, then it is prohibited. This is clear and it is the correct position, God willing, as you see.

Ibn Ḥajar said in Fatḥ al-Bārī the following: (Supplement) Ibn al-Qayyim said: Among the most beneficial remedies, and the strongest found of untying, is the resisting of sorcery, which is from the influences of evil spirits, by the divine remedies: remembrance, supplication, and recitation. When the heart is filled with Allah, populated with His remembrance, and has a regular portion of remembrance, supplication, and turning to Him, which it does not neglect, that is among the greatest causes preventing sorcery from striking it. He said: The authority of sorcery's influence is over weak hearts. For this reason, what it most affects is women, children, and the ignorant, because evil spirits only act upon spirits they find prepared for what suits them. End of abridged quotation. The hadith of this chapter, and the permissibility of sorcery being worked upon the Prophet ﷺ despite his great station, his sincere turning to Allah, and his constancy in his litany, stand in tension with this; but the matter may be resolved by saying that what he mentioned applies to the general case, and that it happened to the Prophet ﷺ only to show that such a thing is possible. And Allah knows best. End of quotation from Fatḥ al-Bārī.

* *

The Ninth Issue

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 69 (part 6 of 7):**

Know that the scholars differed over determining the extent to which the effect of magic (sihr) can reach the one who is bewitched (maswur). Know also that this question has an intermediate position and two extremes.

The first extreme is that about which there is no disagreement: that the effect of magic can reach such things as separating a man from his wife, and the sickness that afflicts the bewitched person through magic, and the like. The evidence for this is the Qur'an and the authentic Sunnah. As for the Qur'an, it is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And they learn from the two [angels] that by which they cause separation between a man and his wife﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:102]. In this noble verse, the Majestic and Exalted One explicitly states that among the effects of magic is causing separation between a man and his wife.

As for the Sunnah, there is what is established in the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) and others, from the hadith of ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), in several closely similar wordings, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was bewitched until he began to imagine that he was going to his wives, while he was not going to them. Then he said: "O ʿĀʾishah, do you know that Allah has given me a ruling on what I asked Him about? Two men came to me; one of them sat at my head and the other at my feet. The one at my head said to the other: 'What is the matter with the man?' The other said: 'He is bewitched (matbub).' He said: 'Who bewitched him?' He said: 'Labid ibn al-Aʿsam, a man from Banu Zuraiq, an ally of the Jews, who was a hypocrite.' He said: 'With what?' He said: 'With a comb and combings (mushatah).' He said: 'Where?' He said: 'In the sheath of a male date-palm spathe, under a stone (rāʿūfah) in the well of Dharwan.'" She said: "So the Prophet (ﷺ) went to the well until he extracted it, and said: 'This is the well that was shown to me. Its water is like an infusion of henna, and its palm trees are like the heads of devils.' Then it was extracted." She said: "I said: 'Why did you not let it out (tanashsharta)?'" He said: "As for Allah, He has cured me, and I dislike to stir up evil against any of the people." This is the wording of al-Bukhari in some of his narrations of this hadith. The story is well known and authentic.

In this authentic hadith, the effect of magic upon him (ﷺ) caused him illness, as evidenced by his saying: "As for Allah, He has cured me." In some of the established narrations in Sahih al-Bukhari and others, the wording is: one of them said to his companion: "What is the man's ailment?" He said: "He is matbub," that is, "bewitched (maswur)." This is an explicit statement that magic caused him pain.

As for the claim of some people who deny this story, arguing that it is impermissible with regard to him (ﷺ), based on the saying of Allah about the disbelievers, rejecting their claim: ﴿You follow none but a man bewitched﴾ [al-Isra' 17:47], it is baseless, because authentic, established narrations cannot be rejected by such claims. You will see at the end of the discussion of this question, if Allah wills, an explanation of the reason for this.

The second extreme, about which there is no disagreement, is that the effect of magic cannot reach the level of reviving the dead, splitting the sea, and the like.

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir: "The Muslims have agreed (ajmaʿa) that there is no magic by which Allah would bring about the sending down of locusts, lice, and frogs, the splitting of the sea, the transformation of the staff, the reviving of the dead, the making of a dumb animal speak, and the like of the great signs of the Messengers, upon them be blessings and peace. So this and similar things must be firmly held to be impossible, such that Allah would not do them at the will of a magician." Al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib said: "We have prevented this only by consensus (ijmaʿ); were it not for that, we would have permitted it." End of al-Qurtubi's words.

As for the intermediate position, it is the subject of disagreement among the scholars. It concerns whether it is permissible for magic to transform a man into a donkey, for example, or a donkey into a man; whether a magician may fly in the air, or make himself so thin that he enters through a narrow window, or stand atop a reed, or walk on a thin thread, or walk on water, or ride a dog, and the like. Some people permit this. Al-Fakhr al-Razi affirmed its permissibility in his tafsir, and so did the author of Rushd al-Ghafil, and others. Others forbid such things.

The author of these notes (may Allah pardon him and forgive him) says: As for the matter of Allah's being able to do all of that, and that He causes whatever effects He wills upon whatever causes He wills, even if there is no rational connection explaining the link between cause and effect, as we have set forth in full in surah Maryam, then there is no barrier to that. Allah, the Majestic and Exalted, says: ﴿But they could not harm anyone thereby except by the permission of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:102]. As for the establishment in fact that such things have actually occurred, no convincing evidence has been established for it. This is because most of what its proponents cite as evidence are accounts that were not transmitted from trustworthy (ʿudul) reporters, and what did occur of them may well be of the kind of trickery (shaʿwadhah) and the sleight of the eyes, not a transformation of one reality into another reality. This is what appears most correct to me, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

(p-60) **Note (tanbih):**

Know that the effect of magic that occurred upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) does not entail any deficiency, nor any impossibility in the law (shariʿah), such that the authentic narrations would have to be rejected because of it. This is because it belongs to the category of human accidents (aʿrad bashariyyah), like illnesses that affect bodies, and it never affected in any way what pertains to the conveying of the message (tabligh). The argument of whoever prohibits this, claiming it to be impossible in his case (ﷺ), based on the verse ﴿When the wrongdoers say: "You follow none but a man bewitched"﴾ [al-Isra' 17:47], is rejected, as we will clarify, Allah willing, at the end of this discussion.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: Al-Mazari said: Some of the innovators (mubtadiʿah) denied this hadith, claiming that it diminishes the station of prophethood and casts doubt upon it. They said: Anything that leads to that is false. They claimed that permitting this removes confidence in the laws they have established, since it would follow that he could imagine seeing Gabriel when it was not him, and that revelation was coming to him when nothing had been revealed to him. Al-Mazari said: All of this is rejected. This is because the evidence has been established for the truthfulness of the Prophet (ﷺ) in what he conveys from Allah the Exalted, and for his infallibility (ʿismah) in conveying it. And the miracles bear witness to his confirmation. So permitting what the evidence has established to be contrary is false. As for what concerns some matters of worldly life, for which he was not sent and for which the mission was not given, he is subject in that to what afflicts human beings, like illnesses. It is not far-fetched that Allah should make something in a worldly matter appear that has no reality, while he remains protected from such a thing in matters of religion. He said: Some people have said that the meaning of the hadith is that he (ﷺ) imagined that he had intercourse with his wives when he had not had intercourse with them, and this often happens to a person in dreams, so it is not far-fetched that it could be imagined to him while awake.

I say: This has been stated explicitly in the narration of Ibn ʿUyaynah in the chapter that follows this one, and its wording is: "until he began to imagine that he was going to his wives while he was not going to them." And in the narration of al-Humaydi: "that he was going to his family and was not going to them." Al-Dawudi said: "Yura" with a *damma* on its first letter, meaning "it is thought (yuzann)." Ibn al-Tin said: "Yara" is vocalized with a *fatha* on its first letter. I say: It is from opinion (ra'y), not from seeing (ru'yah), so it returns to the meaning of supposition (zann). In the unconnected narration (mursal) of Yahya ibn Yaʿmar in ʿAbd al-Razzaq: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was bewitched," from ʿĀʾishah, "until he denied his sight (anker basarahu)." And in his (ʿAbd al-Razzaq's) mursal narration from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab: "until he almost denied his sight." ʿIyad said: It becomes clear from this that the magic only took hold of his body and the outward parts of his limbs, not of his discernment or his belief. I say: And in the unconnected narration of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Kaʿb in Ibn Saʿd, the sister of Labid ibn al-Aʿsam said: "If he is our prophet, he will be informed; otherwise, this magic will bewilder him until his mind is gone." I say: So the first part occurred, as in this authentic hadith. And (p-61) some scholars said: It does not necessarily follow from his thinking that he had done something when he had not done it that he should be certain of doing it; rather, that is only the kind of passing thought that comes to mind and does not become established. Thus no argument remains for the heretic based on this.

ʿIyad also said: It is possible that what is meant by the aforementioned imagining is that there appeared to him, from his vigor, what he was accustomed to from his former habit of being able to have intercourse; then when he approached the woman he lost that strength, as is the state of one who is bound by magic (maʿqud). His saying in the other narration, "until he almost denied his sight," means that he became like one who has denied his sight, such that when he saw a thing, it seemed to him to be other than its true form; but when he looked at it carefully, he recognized its reality. What supports all that has preceded is that it has not been reported from him (ﷺ) in any report that he said a statement and it turned out contrary to what he had said. Al-Muhallab said: The protection of the Prophet (ﷺ) from the devils does not prevent them from attempting their scheming against him. It has passed in the Sahih that a devil wanted to spoil his prayer, but Allah enabled him to overcome it. Likewise, magic did not reach him with harm that would introduce a deficiency into what pertains to conveying the message; rather, it is of the same kind as the harm that he suffered from other illnesses: weakness in speech, or inability to perform some action, or the occurrence of an imagining that does not persist but passes away. And Allah nullifies the schemes of the devils.

Ibn al-Qassar argued that what afflicted him was of the nature of an illness, based on his saying at the end of the hadith: "As for me, Allah has cured me." But the use of this as proof is open to scrutiny. Nevertheless, what supports his claim is that in the narration of ʿAmrah from ʿĀʾishah, in al-Bayhaqi's Dala'il: "He would turn around and not know what his ailment was." And in the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas in Ibn Saʿd: "The Prophet (ﷺ) fell ill, and he was prevented from women, and food, and drink. Then two angels descended upon him." The hadith [continues]. End of what is taken from (Fath al-Bari).

In any case, he (ﷺ) is infallible by consensus from everything that would cause a defect in the conveying of the message and in the legislation. As for human accidents, such as kinds of illnesses, pains, and the like, the Prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, are subject to what human beings are subject to, because they are human, as Allah the Exalted said about them: ﴿We are only human beings like you, but Allah bestows His favor upon whom He wills of His servants﴾ [Ibrahim 14:11], and similar verses.

As for the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the wrongdoers say: "You follow none but a man bewitched"﴾ [al-Isra' 17:47], its meaning is that they claim he (ﷺ) is bewitched or drugged (matbub), that magic has disordered him so that his mind has become confused and his affair has become obscure to him. They say this in order to repel people from him. Mujahid said: "Maswur" means "deceived (makhdu'),” like the saying ﴿Then how are you deluded?﴾ [al-Muminun 23:89], meaning, "From where are you being deceived?" The meaning of this returns to what came before it, because one who is deceived is overpowered in his mind. Abu ʿUbaydah said: "Maswur" means that he has a *sihr*, that is, a windpipe (ri'ah), so he cannot do without food and drink; thus he is like you and is not an angel. This is like their saying: ﴿What is this messenger that he eats food and walks in the markets?﴾ [al-Furqan 25:7], and the saying of Allah about the disbelievers: ﴿This is none but a human being like you; he eats of what you eat and drinks of what you drink﴾, and ﴿If you obey a human being like yourselves, indeed, you would then be losers﴾ [al-Muminun 23:33–34], and similar verses. It is said of everyone who eats or drinks, whether a human or other, that he is "maswur" and "musahhar." From this is the saying of Labid:

> So if you ask us what we are, we are but sparrows among these food-fed (musahhar) people.

And the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

> We see ourselves in two states, by a matter unseen, and we are fed (nusʿar) with food and drink.

That is, we are nourished and sustained.

Since you know that the scholars' statements on His saying "maswur" return to their claim that his mind was disordered by magic or by deception, or that he is a human being, you know that there is no evidence in the verse to prevent some incidental effects that have no connection to the conveying of the message and the legislation, as you see. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

As I indicated earlier, regarding the ruling on a sorcerer from among the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimma), and the scholars' disagreement over his execution, and the argument of those who said he is not to be executed based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) not executing Labid ibn al-A'sam, who had bewitched him: the view that he (ﷺ) executed him is weak, and it has not been established that he executed him. The most apparent of the opinions in our view is that he is not to be held in greater sanctity than a Muslim sorcerer; rather, he is to be executed just as a Muslim sorcerer is executed. As for the Prophet's (ﷺ) not executing Ibn al-A'sam, the authentic narrations have made clear that he left off killing him to avoid stirring up strife (fitna), which indicates that were it not for that, he would have executed him. He (ﷺ) also left off the hypocrites lest people say: "Muhammad kills his own companions." This would produce repulsion from the religion of Islam, along with the scholars' consensus on executing the zindiq, who is a term for the hypocrite. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

God, exalted is He, mentions in this noble verse that when the magicians of Pharaoh saw Moses' staff swallow all their ropes and staffs, they fell down in prostration to Allah, Exalted is He, saying: "We believe in Allah, who is the Lord of Harun and Musa." Allah guided them through that divine proof to this great guidance. Allah, Exalted is He, has clarified this meaning in other places, such as His words in al-A'raf: ﴿And We revealed to Musa, "Throw down your staff," and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsified.﴾ ﴿So the truth took place, and what they had been doing was proved false.﴾ ﴿So they were overcome there and became humiliated.﴾ ﴿And the magicians were thrown down prostrate.﴾ ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ [al-A'raf: 117-122], (p-63) and His words in ash-Shu'ara': ﴿So Musa threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they had falsified.﴾ ﴿And the magicians were thrown down prostrate.﴾ ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds,﴾ ﴿the Lord of Musa and Harun."﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 45-48]. His words "fa-ulqiya" (so they were thrown down) indicate the strength of the proof they witnessed, as if someone had seized them and cast them down in prostration by force, because of the greatness of the miracle they witnessed. It is also mentioned in their story that they saw their places in Paradise while prostrating. The apparent meaning is that this is among the narrations from Israelite sources (isra'iliyyat). He called them "magicians" while they were prostrating to Allah as believers, looking to their former state, like His words: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾ [an-Nisa': 2], where He called them "orphans" after they had reached maturity, looking to their former state, as is well known in its proper place.

The apparent reason that Harun is mentioned before Musa in this verse is to observe the endings of the verses (fawasil, the rhyme-endings of the verses).

Know that the knowledge of magic, despite its baseness, and despite Allah's declaration that it neither harms nor benefits, was a cause of the faith of Pharaoh's magicians. For because of their knowledge of magic, they recognized that the miracle of the staff was beyond the realm of magic, and that it was a divine matter, so no doubt entered them about it. Thus this became the cause of their firm faith, which neither threat nor intimidation could shake. Had they not been thoroughly knowledgeable about magic, it would have been possible for them to suppose that the matter of the staff was of the same kind as sorcery and trickery. And knowledge is with Allah, Exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 71:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Said [Pharaoh], "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your leader who taught you magic. So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees. And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting."﴾

In this noble verse, exalted and majestic is He, He mentions that when the magicians of Pharaoh believed in the Lord of Harun and Musa, Pharaoh said to them, rejecting their action: "Have you believed in him?" That is, you have affirmed him in that he is a prophet sent by Allah. "And have you believed in Allah before I give you permission?" He means that they did not refrain from believing until he gave them leave, because he claimed that it was not right for them to do anything without his permission. He also said to them: "Indeed, Musa is your leader," that is, the chief of the magicians and their teacher, "who taught you magic." Then he threatened them, swearing that he would cut off their hands and feet on opposite sides, meaning, for example, the right hand and the left foot. This is because it is more severe for a person than cutting them from one side, since if their cutting were from one side, one complete sound side would remain to him, unlike cutting them on opposite sides. The right side weakens with the cutting of the hand, and the left side weakens with the cutting of the foot, as is well known. And that he would crucify them on the trunks of palm trees; the trunk of the palm tree is the roughest of tree trunks, and crucifixion upon it is more severe than crucifixion upon other trunks, as is well known.

What Allah, exalted is He, mentions here about him I also clarify in another place. As in His saying in Surat ash-Shu'ara': ﴿Said [Pharaoh], "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your leader who taught you magic. But you are going to know. I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all."﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 49]. He mentioned this also in Surat al-A'raf and added in it the explicit statement of the agent. He said: Pharaoh's claim that Musa and the magicians colluded to show that he had defeated them by trickery, so that they might cooperate to expel Pharaoh and his people from Egypt. This is in His saying: ﴿Said Pharaoh, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, this is a plot you have plotted in the city to expel its people from it. But you are going to know."﴾ ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides; then I will surely crucify you all.﴾ [al-A'raf: 123-124]. His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿And I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾ shows that crucifixion on the trunks of palm trees is what He intends by His saying in al-A'raf and ash-Shu'ara': ﴿and I will surely crucify you all﴾ [al-A'raf: 124; ash-Shu'ara': 49]. That is, on the trunks of palm trees. The use of "fi" (in) with "salaba" (to crucify) is a well-known Arabic usage, and from it is the saying of Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil:

"They crucified the Abdi in the trunk of a palm tree, so let Shayban never sneeze except with a severed nose."

It is known among the scholars of rhetoric that in such a verse there is a metaphor of a dependent kind in the meaning of the particle, as will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, the clarification of their words on that and the like in Surat al-Qasas. We have clarified in our book entitled (Man' Jawaz al-Majaz fi al-Munazzal li al-Ta'abbud wa al-I'jaz) that what the rhetoricians call types of metaphor, all of them, are Arabic expressions which the Arabs uttered in their language. We have also explained the reason why metaphor is not permissible in the Qur'an and what follows from that of prohibition.

As for His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more lasting﴾, some of the people of knowledge said: "Which of us" means: me, or the Lord of Musa, is more severe in punishment and more lasting. Al-Qurtubi limited himself to this. According to this, Pharaoh claims that his punishment is more severe and more lasting than the punishment of Allah. This is like His saying: ﴿I am your lord, the most high﴾ [an-Nazi'at: 24], and His saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38], and His saying: ﴿If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 29]. Some said: "Which of us" means: me, or Musa, is more severe in punishment and more lasting. According to this, it is like mockery of Musa, for belittling him, and that he is not able to punish one who does not obey him. This is like His saying: ﴿Or am I better than this one who is despised?﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 52].

And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

Know that the scholars differed: did Pharaoh do to them what he threatened them with, or did he not do it to them? Some people said: he killed them and crucified them. Others denied that, and the more apparent of the two in my view is that he did not kill them, and that Allah protected them from him because of their firm faith in Allah, exalted is He, for Allah says to Musa and Harun: ﴿You two and whoever follows you are the victors﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. And knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us, nor over Him who created us. So decree whatever you will decree. You can only decree concerning this worldly life."﴾

His saying: "We will never prefer you" means: we will never choose to follow you, or to be of your party, or to be safe from your punishment, over "the clear proofs that have come to us," such as the miracle of the staff, which came to us and whose authenticity we are certain of. The waw in His saying "and Him who created us" is a conjunctive waw (wāw al-ʿaṭf) connecting to "mā" in His saying "over what has come to us." The meaning is: we will not choose you over the clear proofs that have come to us, nor over "Him who created us," that is, who brought us into being and brought us out from nothingness into existence. It has also been said that the waw is the waw of oath (wāw al-qasam), and the object of the oath is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. That is: "By Him who created us, we will not prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us. So decree whatever you will decree," that is, do what you are going to do. "So we will not turn back from what we are upon." "You can only decree concerning this worldly life" means: your command only takes effect in it. Here "this" (hādhihi) is in the accusative as an adverb of place (ẓarf), according to the most correct view. That is: there is nothing in it that matters, because of its swift passing and ending.

What He, exalted and majestic, related about them in this place, namely their steadfastness in faith and their indifference to the threats and warnings of Pharaoh out of desire for what is with Allah, He has mentioned in other places, such as His saying about them in Ash-Shu'ara', in the same story: ﴿They said, "No harm! Indeed, we are to our Lord returning."﴾ [Ash-Shu'ara' 26:50], and His saying in Al-A'raf: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are to our Lord returning." ... "And you do not resent us except that we believed in the signs of our Lord when they came to us. Our Lord, pour upon us patience and cause us to die as Muslims."﴾ [Al-A'raf 7:125–126].

As for His saying ﴿So decree whatever you are decreeing﴾, the returning pronoun of the relative clause (ʿāʾid al-ṣila) is omitted, meaning "whatever you are decreeing it," because it is in the genitive by the attributive adjective (al-waṣf), as he indicated in the Khulasa (Ibn Malik's Alfiyya) with his saying:

*"Thus is the omission of what is governed by an adjective in the genitive, as in 'you are a decider' after the imperative of 'qaḍā' (to decree)."*

A parallel to this in Arabic speech is the saying of Saʿd ibn Nashib al-Mazini:

*"And it seems small in the eyes of my possessions when my right hand is bent, [reaching] what I was seeking."*

That is: "seeking it" (ṭālibahu), with the pronoun omitted. (p. 66)

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 73:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic to which you compelled us. And Allah is better and more enduring.﴾

In this noble verse, Exalted and Majestic is He mentions that when Pharaoh, may Allah curse him, said to the magicians what he said when they believed, they said to him: ﴿Indeed we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins﴾ [Taha: 73], meaning their past sins, such as disbelief and other disobediences. ﴿And what you compelled us to of magic﴾, that is: and that He may forgive us what you compelled us to of magic. What He mentioned here about them has been indicated elsewhere, like His saying, exalted is He, about them in ash-Shu'ara': ﴿Indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾ ﴿Indeed, we aspire that our Lord will forgive us our sins because we were the first of the believers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 50-51], and His saying about them in al-A'raf: ﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience and cause us to die as Muslims﴾ [al-A'raf: 126].

Regarding Taha, there is a well-known question, which is: their saying ﴿and what you compelled us to of magic﴾ [Taha: 73] indicates that he compelled them to it, although other verses indicate that they did it willingly, not under compulsion, like His saying in Taha: ﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves and conferred secretly﴾ ﴿They said, "Indeed, these two are magicians who want to expel you from your land with their magic and do away with your ideal way of life."﴾ ﴿So assemble your plot, then come in unison; and he has succeeded today who prevails.﴾ [Taha: 62-63]. Their saying: ﴿So assemble your plot, then come in unison﴾ [Taha: 64] is explicit that they were not compelled. Likewise His saying about them in ash-Shu'ara': ﴿They said to Pharaoh, "Will there be a reward for us if we are the victors?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 41], and His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿They said, "Indeed there will be for us a reward if we are the victors."﴾ ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."﴾ [al-A'raf: 113-114]. Those verses indicate that they were not compelled.

For the scholars there are well-known answers to this question:

(Among them): that he compelled them to set out from their places in order to oppose Moses with their magic. When they were compelled to come and were commanded to perform magic, they came willingly. So their compulsion relates to the beginning of the matter, and their willingness relates to the end of the matter; the aspect is separated, and by this the contradiction is removed. What supports this is His saying: ﴿And send into the cities gatherers﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 36] and His saying: ﴿And send into the cities gatherers﴾ [al-A'raf: 111].

(Among them): that he used to compel them to teach their children magic while they were young, and that this is what they meant by their being compelled to magic. This does not conflict with the fact that they did what they did of magic after they had learned it and grown up, willingly.

(p-67) (Among them): that they said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses while he is asleep." He did so, and they found him beside his staff. They said: "This is not the magic of a magician!", because when a magician sleeps his magic becomes void. But he refused except that they should oppose him, and he obligated them to that. When they found no escape from it, they did it willingly. The most apparent of these in my view is the first, and Allah knows best.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿khataya﴾ is the plural of khati'ah, which is a great sin, such as disbelief and the like. The pattern fa'ilah is pluralized as fa'a'il, and the hamzah in fa'a'il is substituted for the ya' in fa'ilah; similar to it are the alif and the waw, as he indicated in the Khulasah with his saying:

"The extension was added as a third in the singular, a hamzah appearing in the like of kala'id."

So the original of khataya was "khata'iy" with a kasrah on the ya', which is the ya' of khati'ah, and a hamzah after it, which is the final radical of the word. Then the ya' was replaced by a hamzah in the manner of substitution in sahaif, so it became khata'i'; with two hamzahs. Then the second was replaced by a ya' because of the obligation to replace a final hamzah after a kasrah-ed hamzah with a ya', so it became khata'iy. Then the first hamzah was given a fathah for lightness, so it became khata'aiy. Then the ya' was replaced by an alif because it was vowelled and what preceded it was open, so it became khata'a'a with two alifs between which is a hamzah, and the hamzah resembles the alif, so there gathered the semblance of three alifs; the hamzah was then replaced by a ya', so it became khataya after five operations. To what we have mentioned he indicated in the Khulasah with his saying:

"Open and restore the hamzah in what has been made defective as a lam, and in the like of hirawah make it a waw... etc."

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring﴾. Its apparent and immediately understood meaning is: that the meaning is better than Pharaoh and more enduring than him, because He is everlasting, His dominion does not cease, He is not humbled, He does not die, and He is not deposed. As we have clarified this meaning in Surat an-Nahl in discussing His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to Him belongs religion perpetually﴾ [an-Nahl: 52]. That is, unlike Pharaoh and other kings of this world, who do not endure, but die, or are deposed, or are humbled after honor. Most exegetes hold that the meaning is: that His reward is better than what Pharaoh promised them in his saying: ﴿They said to Pharaoh, "Will there be a reward for us if we are the victors?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Yes, and indeed you will be among those brought near."﴾ [al-A'raf: 113-114]. And "more enduring" means more lasting, because what Pharaoh promised them is transient, while Allah's reward is lasting, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿What is with you will end, and what is with Allah is lasting﴾ [an-Nahl: 96], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring﴾ [al-A'la: 16]. Some scholars said: "And more enduring" means: more enduring in punishment than your punishment, and more lasting than it. Accordingly, it is a rebuttal of Pharaoh's saying: ﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more enduring﴾ (p-68) The meaning of "more enduring" is: more lasting in duration.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, majestic and exalted, mentions that indeed (i.e., the matter and the affair) whoever comes to his Lord on the Day of Resurrection in the state of being a criminal (i.e., one who committed the crime in the world until he died upon that, like the disbeliever, we seek refuge in Allah, exalted), for him with Allah is Hell, in which he will be punished. So he does not die, so that he may find rest, nor does he live a life in which there is comfort.

I will clarify what he mentioned here in other places:

• Like His saying: ﴿As for those who disbelieve, for them is the fire of Hell. It will not be decreed for them so that they die, nor will its punishment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one.﴾ [Ar-Rum: 36]

• And His saying, exalted: ﴿And they sought victory, and every obstinate tyrant was disappointed. Ahead of him is Hell, and he will be given to drink of pus, which he will gulp down but will hardly swallow. Death will come to him from every place, but he will not die, and ahead of him is a harsh punishment.﴾ [Ibrahim: 15–17]

• And His saying, exalted: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We replace them with other skins so they may taste the punishment.﴾ [An-Nisa: 56]

• And His saying, exalted: ﴿And the most wretched will avoid it, the one who will burn in the greatest fire, then he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ [Al-A'la: 11–13]

• And His saying, exalted: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us!" He will say, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 77]

Besides these, there are other verses. A parallel to this in the speech of the Arabs is the saying of Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah ibn Utbah ibn Mas'ud, one of the seven jurists of Medina:

"Ala man li-nafsin la tamutu fa-yanqadi shaqaha, wa la tahya hayatan laha ta'mu"

(Is there anyone for a soul that does not die, so that its misery may end, and does not live a life that has any sweetness?)

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds, for them are the high ranks﴾.

In this noble verse, Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, mentions that whoever comes to Him on the Day of Resurrection in the state of being ﴿a believer who has done righteous deeds﴾, meaning in the world, and dies upon that, ﴿for them﴾ with Allah ﴿are the high ranks﴾. Al-'Ula (the high) is the plural of 'ulya, which is the feminine of al-a'la (the highest). He has alluded to this meaning in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And the Hereafter is greater in ranks and greater in preference﴾ [al-Isra: 21], and His saying: ﴿And for all there are ranks according to what they have done﴾ [al-An'am: 132], and similar verses.

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وَلَقَدْ أوْحَيْنا إلى مُوسى أنْ أسْرِ بِعِبادِي فاضْرِبْ لَهم طَرِيقًا في البَحْرِ يَبَسًا لا تَخافُ دَرَكًا ولا تَخْشى﴾.

Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this noble verse that He revealed to His Prophet Musa, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace [p-69]: that he should travel by night with His servants, who are the Children of Israel, and bring them out from the grip of Fir'awn, and that he should strike for them a path in the sea, dry (yabasan), meaning dry, with no water in it and no moisture, and that he would not fear being overtaken (darakan) by Fir'awn behind him, that he might harm him, and would not fear the sea before him that his people would drown. This story has been explained in another place, such as His saying in Surat ash-Shu'ara': ﴿And We revealed to Musa: Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued.﴾ ﴿Then Fir'awn sent heralds into the cities.﴾ ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band.﴾ ﴿And indeed they have enraged us.﴾ ﴿And indeed we are a wary multitude.﴾ ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs,﴾ ﴿and treasures and a noble station.﴾ ﴿Thus, and We made the Children of Israel inherit them.﴾ ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise.﴾ ﴿And when the two hosts saw each other, the companions of Musa said: Indeed we are overtaken.﴾ ﴿He said: No! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me.﴾ ﴿Then We revealed to Musa: Strike the sea with your staff, and it split, and each part was like a huge mountain.﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 52–63].

His saying in ash-Shu'ara', ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 63], meaning: so he struck it and it split, clarifies the meaning of His saying: ﴿Strike for them a dry path in the sea﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77]. And His saying: ﴿The companions of Musa said: Indeed we are overtaken. He said: No! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 61–62] clarifies the meaning of His saying: ﴿You shall not fear being overtaken, nor shall you dread﴾. Allah, exalted is He, has pointed to this in His saying in ad-Dukhan: ﴿So he called upon his Lord: These are a criminal people.﴾ ﴿So travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued.﴾ ﴿And leave the sea parted; indeed they are a drowned host.﴾ [ad-Dukhan: 22–24], and in other verses besides these.

We have already presented a portion of this in Surat al-Baqarah, and the story is well known and clear from the Great Qur'an.

Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read ﴿an isri﴾ with a hamzat al-wasl and a kasrah on the nun of "an", because of the meeting of two quiescent letters (iltiqa' as-sakinayn). The rest read ﴿an asri﴾ with an open hamzat al-qat' and the nun of "an" quiescent. We have already mentioned in Surat Hud that asra and sara are two dialectal forms, and we demonstrated Arabic evidence for this.

Hamzah read ﴿la takhaf﴾ with the fa' quiescent, without an alif between the kha' and the fa', and it is in the jussive mood (majzum) because it is the response (jaza') to the imperative, meaning: strike for them a dry path in the sea; you will not fear. We have already noted that this kind of jussive is governed by an omitted condition indicated by the form of the imperative, meaning: if you strike for them a dry path in the sea, you will not fear.

According to the reading of the majority, ﴿la takhafu﴾ with a damma, there is no difficulty in His saying ﴿wa la takhsha﴾, because it is a present-tense verb in the nominative, marked by a presumed damma on the alif, coordinated with the present-tense verb in the nominative which is His saying: ﴿la takhafu﴾.

As for Hamzah's reading ﴿la takhaf﴾ in the jussive, there is a well-known difficulty in His saying ﴿wa la takhsha﴾, namely that it is coordinated with a jussive present-tense verb, which requires that it also be jussive; and if it were jussive, the alif would be dropped from takhsha, according to the rule in His poem in al-Khulasah:

"And drop the alif in the three (verbs) under the jussive, and you will have decreed a binding rule."

The alif was not dropped, so the difficulty arose because of this.

It has been answered in three ways:

The first: that ﴿wa la takhsha﴾ is a new sentence (musta'naf), the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "and you do not fear", meaning: and it is part of your nature that you are secure, you do not fear.

The second: that the verb is jussive, and the alif is not the alif that is in the position of the root letter of the word, but it was added for the sake of vowel extension (litlaq) because of the verse-ending (fasilah), as in His saying: ﴿So they led us astray from the way﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67], and His saying: ﴿And you assume about Allah assumptions﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10].

The third: that lengthening a vowel by a letter of prolongation matching it is a well-known style of the Arabic language, as in the words of Abd Yaghuth ibn Waqqas al-Harithi:

"And a sheikhah of the Abshams laughs at me, as though she had never seen a Yemeni captive before me."

And the words of the rajaz poet:

"When the old woman grows angry, divorce her, and do not appease her or flatter her."

And the words of another:

"I said, when she had fallen upon her chest: O my she-camel, how much you have wandered of wide places!"

And the words of Antarah in his mu'allaqah:

"Sweat flows from the nape of a furious, swift, lofty she-camel, proud like a stallion with its teeth bared."

So the original in the first line is "kaan lam tara", but the fathah was lengthened. The original in the second is "wa la tarda-ha", but the fathah was lengthened. The original in the third is "ala al-kalkal", meaning the chest, but the fathah was lengthened. The original in the fourth is "yanba'u", meaning that sweat flows from the bone of the nape of his she-camel in actuality, but the fathah was lengthened. The lengthening of the fathah with an alif in these verses and similar ones, which we have not mentioned, is not due to poetic necessity, since the scholars of Arabic have explicitly stated that it is a well-known Arabic style. This is supported by the fact that it is also heard in prose, as in their saying in prose: kalkal, khatam, and danaq, meaning kalkalan, khataman, and daniqan.

We have clarified this issue and given many Arabic examples of it in our book "Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab", in Surat al-Balad, in the discussion of His saying: ﴿I do not swear by this city﴾ [al-Balad: 1], alongside His saying: ﴿And this secure city﴾ [at-Tin: 3].

Az-Zamakhshari said in explaining this verse, ﴿So strike for them a path﴾: "Make for them a path, from the saying: he struck for him a share in his property, and he struck the brick, meaning he made it." End of quote.

The verification is that yabasan is an adjective of the quality type (sifah mushabbahah) that came on the pattern fa'al with two fathahs, like batal and hasan. Az-Zamakhshari also said: "Yubs (dryness) is a verbal noun that was described by it. One says: yabisa yabasan and yubsan, and similar to them are 'adam and 'udm; and for this reason the feminine was described by it, so it is said: our sheep is yubs, and our she-camel is yubs, when her milk has dried up."

His saying: ﴿la takhafu darakan﴾. Darak is a verbal noun (ism al-masdar) with the meaning of "overtaking" (idrak), meaning: Fir'awn and his hosts will not overtake you, nor reach you from behind you, and you will not fear from the sea before you. According to the reading of the majority, ﴿la takhafu﴾, the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in His saying "fadrib" (strike), meaning: strike for them a path while you are not fearing being overtaken, nor fearing. It has been established in the science of grammar that when a negated present-tense verb with "la" is in a circumstantial clause, it is obligatory to link it with a pronoun and it is impermissible to link it with a waw.

- As in His saying here: ﴿Strike for them a path﴾, meaning: while you are not fearing being overtaken;
- and His saying: ﴿What is it with me that I do not see the hoopoe?﴾ [an-Naml: 20];
- and His saying: ﴿And what is it with us that we do not believe in Allah?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 84].

A parallel to this in Arabic speech is the words of the poet:

"Even if a people, for the elevation of a tribe, entered the heaven, I would enter it, not hidden."

Meaning: I would enter it while I am not concealed. By this you know that His statement in al-Khulasah:

"And a clause beginning with a present-tense verb, which contains a pronoun and is free of the waw"

has, by implication, a distinction, as is known in the science of grammar.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his hosts, and there covered them of the sea that which covered them.﴾

The verified position is that atba'a (أتبع) and ittaba'a (اتّبع) have one meaning. So His saying "fa-atba'ahum" means "ittaba'ahum" (followed them). A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So a piercing meteor followed him﴾ [al-Saffat: 10], and His saying: ﴿So Satan followed him﴾ [al-A'raf: 175], and the verse continues. The meaning is that when Musa journeyed by night with the Children of Israel, Pharaoh and his hosts followed them, ﴿and there covered them of the sea﴾ [Taha: 78], i.e., of the sea (al-bahr), "that which covered them," i.e., Allah drowned Pharaoh and his hosts in the sea, and they perished to the last one of them.

As for what He, majestic and exalted, mentioned in this noble verse, that Pharaoh and his hosts followed the Children of Israel, and that Allah drowned them in the sea, I will clarify it in other than this place (p-72). He, may He be exalted, has explained that they followed them at the beginning of the day, at the rising of the sun. Among the verses indicating that he followed them is His saying, may He be exalted, in "al-Shu'ara'" (The Poets): ﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 52], meaning: Pharaoh and his hosts will follow you. Then He explained the manner of their following, saying: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers. "Indeed, these are but a small band. And indeed, they have enraged us. And indeed, we are a cautious multitude."﴾ ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs, and treasures and a noble station. Thus it was, and We bequeathed them to the Children of Israel.﴾ ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise.﴾ So when ﴿the two companies sighted each other, the companions of Musa said, "Indeed, we are overtaken."﴾ ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53–62].

His saying in this verse: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾ means: at the beginning of the day, at the rising of the sun. Among the verses indicating this also is His saying, may He be exalted, in "Yunus": ﴿And We took the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his hosts followed them in insolence and enmity﴾ [Yunus: 90], and His saying in "al-Dukhan": ﴿So travel by night with My servants, for you will be pursued﴾ [al-Dukhan: 23], and other verses indicating his pursuit of them.

As for his drowning, he and all his people, which is alluded to by His saying here: ﴿and there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾, He has clarified it in several places in His Mighty Book:

• Such as His saying in "al-Shu'ara'": ﴿So We revealed to Musa: "Strike the sea with your staff," and it parted, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ ﴿And We brought near there the others﴾ ﴿And We saved Musa and those with him, all of them﴾ ﴿Then We drowned the others﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign, but most of them were not believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63–67].

• And His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿So We took retribution upon them and drowned them in the sea﴾ [7: 136].

• And His saying in "al-Zukhruf": ﴿So when they angered Us, We took retribution upon them and drowned them all﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 55].

• And His saying in "al-Baqarah": ﴿And when We divided the sea for you and saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on﴾ [al-Baqarah: 50].

• And His saying in "Yunus": ﴿Until, when drowning overtook him, he said, "I believe that there is no deity except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims"﴾ [Yunus: 90].

• And His saying in "al-Dukhan": ﴿And leave the sea at rest; indeed, they are a drowned army﴾ [al-Dukhan: 24], and other verses.

The expression by the ambiguous noun, which is the relative pronoun, in His saying ﴿and there covered them of the sea that which covered them﴾ [Taha: 78] indicates the magnification of the matter and the exaltation of its significance. A parallel to it in the Qur'an is His saying: ﴿when there covers the lote tree that which covers﴾ [al-Najm: 16], and His saying: ﴿And the overturned cities He hurled down; then covered them that which covered﴾ [al-Najm: 53–54], and His saying: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾ [al-Najm: 10].

And al-yamm (اليَمّ) means the sea. The meaning: there struck them from the sea that which struck them, namely drowning and complete destruction.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 79:

(p-73) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray, and did not guide them.﴾

It means that Pharaoh led his people astray from the path of truth, and did not guide them to it. In this noble verse, Allah makes clear the lie of Pharaoh in his saying: ﴿Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see, and I guide you only to the path of right conduct."﴾ [Ghafir: 29] Among the verses that clarify this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We sent Moses with Our signs and a clear authority, to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and the command of Pharaoh was not right-guiding.﴾ ﴿He will go before his people on the Day of Resurrection and lead them into the Fire, and wretched is the watering place to which they are brought.﴾ [Hud: 96–98] The rhetorical point in omitting the object in His saying "and did not guide," rather than saying "and did not guide them," is the observance of the verse endings (fawasil al-ayat). A parallel to this in the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He become displeased.﴾ [Ad-Duha: 3]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, We had delivered you from your enemy, and We made a covenant with you at the right side of the Mount, and We sent down upon you manna and quails.﴾ ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you.﴾

In this noble verse, the Mighty and Majestic mentions His favour upon the Children of Israel: that He delivered them from their enemy, Pharaoh; that He made a covenant with them at the right side of the Mount; that He sent down upon them manna and quails; and that He said to them: "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you. And do not transgress, lest My Lord become angry with you." What He mentions here, I shall clarify in other places.
