As in His saying about His favour upon them in delivering them from their enemy, Pharaoh, in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And [recall] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who subjected you to a terrible torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 49]; and His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿And [recall] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, killing your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 141]; and His saying in al-Dukhan: ﴿And We had certainly delivered the Children of Israel from the humiliating torment, from Pharaoh. Indeed, he was haughty and among the transgressors.﴾ [Al-Dukhan: 30-31]; and His saying in Surat Ibrahim: ﴿And [recall] when Moses said to his people, "Remember the favour of Allah upon you when He saved you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and keeping your women alive. And in that was a great trial from your Lord."﴾ [Ibrahim: 6]; and His saying in al-Shu'ara': ﴿Thus, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit it.﴾ [Al-Shu'ara': 59]; and His saying in al-Dukhan: ﴿Thus, and We caused another people to inherit it.﴾ [Al-Dukhan: 28]; and His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿And We caused the people who had been oppressed to inherit the eastern parts of the land and the western parts of it.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 137]; and His saying in al-Qasas: ﴿And We wished to confer favour upon those who were oppressed in the land and make them leaders and make them inheritors,﴾ up to His saying ﴿they feared.﴾ [Al-Qasas: 5-6], and other verses besides these.

(p-74) As for His saying here: ﴿And We made a covenant with you at the right side of the Mount﴾ [Ta-Ha: 80], the more apparent view is that this promise is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten﴾ [Al-A'raf: 142], the verse, and His saying: ﴿And [recall] when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 51], the verse, and His saying: ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 86], and it is the promise of the sending down of the Torah. It has been said regarding it other than this.

As for His saying here: ﴿And We sent down upon you manna and quails﴾, He has already made clear His favour upon them by this in other places, as in His saying in al-Baqarah: ﴿And We shaded you with clouds and sent down upon you manna and quails﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 57], and His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quails﴾ [Al-A'raf: 160]. Most scholars hold that the manna is terangbin (a sweet exudation, like honey-dew), which descends from the sky like dew and then solidifies, and it resembles white honey. The quails: a bird resembling the quail (sumana). It has also been said that it is the quail itself. This is the view of the majority regarding the manna and the quails. It has been said: the quails are honey. Some have rejected applying "salwa" to honey. The verified position is that "salwa" is linguistically applied to honey. From this is the saying of Khalid ibn Zuhayr al-Hudhali:

"And he swore by Allah with full effort, that you are sweeter than salwa when we extract its honey."

He means: sweeter than honey when we extract it, because al-nushur is the extraction of honey. Mu'arrij ibn 'Amr al-Sadusi said: applying salwa to honey is the dialect of Kinanah. It was named so because it consoles (yusalli). This is what al-Qurtubi said. However, most scholars hold that this is not what is meant in the verse. They differed regarding salwa: is it a plural or a singular? Some said: it is a plural, its singular being salwah, and al-Khalil recited for this the poet's verse:

"And indeed, at the remembrance of you, a tremor seizes me, as the salwah shakes off the moisture of the rain."

This line is also narrated as:

"As the sparrow shakes off, when the rain has wetted it."

According to this version there is no evidence in the line. Al-Kisa'i said: salwa is singular and its plural is salawa. Al-Akhfash said: it is a plural with no singular from its own form, like al-khayr and al-sharr, though it resembles that its singular might be salwa, like its collective, just as they said: difla, sumana and shukaa, in the singular and plural. Al-Diflaa, like dhikra: a green bitter tree of pleasant appearance, growing in valleys. Al-Shukaa, like hubaarah, and it may be pronounced with a fatha: a type of fine small green plant, with thin stalks, used as a remedy. Al-Sumana: a well-known bird.

(p-75) Its author – may Allah pardon him – said: The more apparent view to me regarding the manna is that it is a comprehensive term for what Allah bestows upon His servant without toil or fatigue; it includes the terangbin that Allah bestowed upon the Children of Israel in the wilderness, and it covers other things similar to it. This is supported by the Prophet's saying ﷺ, authentic in the two Sahihs: "Mushrooms are of the manna, and its water is a cure for the eye."

The more apparent view to me regarding salwa is that it is a bird, whether we say it is the quail or a bird resembling it, because the majority of scholars, from the early and later generations, agree upon this, although salwa is linguistically applied to honey, as we have explained.

As for His saying in this verse of Ta-Ha: ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 81], that is: of the manna and the salwa, and the imperative here is for permission and favour.

This has also been mentioned in other places, as in His saying in al-Baqarah: ﴿And We sent down upon you manna and quails: Eat of the good things with which We have provided you; and they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 57], and His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿And We shaded them with clouds and sent down upon them manna and quails: Eat of the good things with which We have provided you; and they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ [Al-A'raf: 160]. His saying "Eat" in these verses is the object of an omitted verb of saying, meaning: and We said to them, "Eat." The pronoun in His saying ﴿and do not transgress therein﴾ refers to the relative pronoun "ma" (what), meaning: Eat of the good things of what We have provided you; ﴿and do not transgress therein﴾, meaning: in what We have provided you. He forbade them from transgression in what He provided them, which is that they exceed the limits of Allah concerning it by denying His blessing through it, by being occupied by pleasure and luxury from performing the thanks due for His favours, by spending His provision which He bestowed upon them in disobedience, or by seeking help with it in sin, or by withholding the rights obligatory upon them in it, and the like.

He explained that this causes them to incur His anger, Mighty and Majestic, because the fa' in His saying "fa-yahilla" is causative, and the verb is in the subjunctive by a hidden "an" after it, since it follows a prohibition, which is a pure demand, as he indicated in the Khulasa with his saying:

"And after fa', the answer to a negation or a pure demand, 'an' is hidden and the subjunctive is obligatory."

Al-Kisa'i read this letter as "fa-yahulla" with a damma on the ha' (and "wa-man yahlul" with a damma on the lam). The rest read "yahilla" with a kasra on the ha' and "yahlil" with a kasra on the lam. According to al-Kisa'i's reading "fa-yahulla," with damma, the meaning is: My wrath will descend upon you. According to the reading of the majority, it is from halla yahillu with kasra, meaning: (p-76) when it becomes due, as in "halla daynuhu" when its payment becomes due. From it is His saying: ﴿then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾ [Al-Hajj: 33]. His saying: "fa-qad hawa" means: he perished and went down into the abyss. Its origin is that one falls from a mountain or the like and plunges to the earth and perishes. From it is the poet's saying:

"He fell from the top of a watchtower, and it crushed his liver beneath it."

And they say: "hawat ummuhu," meaning: he fell such a fall that there is no rising after it. From it is the saying of Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi:

"May his mother fall, what the morning brings as it comes, and what the night wishes when it returns."

Something of this kind is one of the interpretations of His saying: ﴿And his refuge is the Abyss﴾ [Al-Qari'ah: 9]. It is narrated from Shafi ibn Matih al-Asbahi that he said: Indeed, in Hell there is a mountain called Su'ud, up which the disbeliever climbs for forty autumns before he reaches it. Allah says: ﴿I will overwhelm him with a arduous ascent﴾ [Al-Muddaththir: 17]. And indeed, in Hell there is a palace called Hawa, from whose top the disbeliever is thrown, and he falls for forty autumns before he reaches its base. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And whoever has My wrath descend upon him has indeed fallen.﴾ Al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir said, and Allah knows best.

Know that anger is an attribute by which Allah has described Himself when His sacred limits are violated, and its effects appear upon those who incur it. We seek refuge in Allah from His wrath, Mighty and Majestic. We Muslims pass it as it has come, affirming our Lord in everything with which He has described Himself, and denying none of it, while fully declaring Him far above resemblance to the created, Glorified is He and exalted far above that. As we have clarified this in complete detail in Surat al-A'raf.

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read in this verse "qad 'anjaytukum min 'aduwwikum wa-wa'adtukum" with the first-person singular ta' in both. The rest read "wa-wa'adnakum wa-anjaynakum" with the nun of majesty, so the plural form in the majority reading is for glorification. Abu 'Amr read "wa-'adnakum" without an alif after the second waw, in the simple verbal form, from al-wa'd (promise) and not from al-mu'adah (mutual promising), with the nun of majesty.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 82:

﴿And indeed I am most forgiving to whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided.﴾

Allah, exalted and majestic is He, mentions in this noble verse that He is Ghaffar, meaning abundantly forgiving, to whoever repents to Him from his disobediences and his disbelief, believes in Him, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided. This meaning has been clarified in several places in His Book, such as His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they desist, what has already passed will be forgiven them﴾ [al-Anfal: 38], and His saying concerning those who said that Allah is the third of three: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 74] (p-٧٧) and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful. And turn back in repentance to your Lord and submit to Him﴾ [al-Zumar: 53-54], along with other verses. We have already mentioned the meaning of tawbah (repentance) and 'amal salih (righteous deeds).

His saying in this noble verse, "then remains guided," means that he stays upright and steadfast upon what was mentioned: repentance, faith, and righteous deeds, and does not break them. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30]. In the hadith: "Say: I believe in Allah, then be steadfast." And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So remain steadfast as you have been commanded﴾ [Hud: 112].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 83:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said, "They are right behind me, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased."﴾

In this noble verse, exalted and most high is He, He points to the account of His appointing Musa forty nights and his going to the appointed meeting-place, and his hastening to it ahead of his people. That is because when his Lord made the appointment with him and set the aforementioned appointed time, and he charged his brother Harun to succeed him among his people, he hurried to the appointed place, and his Lord said to him, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people?﴾

...the verse. This account, which He summarized here, He alluded to in other places, such as His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was complete at forty nights. And Musa said to his brother Harun, "Take my place among my people, act righteously, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾ ﴿And when Musa came at Our appointed time and his Lord spoke to him, he said, "My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 142–143].

In this verse there is a well-known question: that Musa's answer does not correspond to the question his Lord asked him, because the question was about the reason that hastened him away from his people, while the answer did not come in correspondence with that. For he answered with his saying: ﴿They are right behind me, and I hastened to You.﴾

Several answers have been given to this:

(Among them): that His saying, ﴿They are right behind me,﴾ means they are near, and I preceded them only by a small amount, the like of which is excused. So it is as if I had not gone ahead of them, nor hastened away from them, because of the closeness between me and them.

(Among them): that when Allah, exalted is He, addressed him with His saying, ﴿And what hastened you away from your people?﴾, there entered into him, out of awe, reverence, and magnification of Allah, exalted is He, what made him forget the corresponding answer. And Allah knows best.

(p-78) His saying, ﴿Hum ulā'i﴾, the prolonged vowel in it is the dialect of the Hijazis. Ibn Malik preferred it in al-Khulasa with his saying:

"And the prolonged form is preferable."

The dialect of the Tamimis is "ulā" with a short vowel, and it is permissible to attach the particle "lām" (of distance) to the Tamimi dialect, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"Ulālika qawmī lam yakūnū ushābah, wa-hal ya'iẓu ḍ-ḍillīla illā ulālika"

As for the Hijazi dialect with the prolonged vowel, it is not permissible to attach the lām to it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Indeed, We have tested your people after you, and the Samiri has led them astray."﴾

The apparent meaning is that the trial mentioned is their worship of the calf, so it is a trial of misguidance, like His saying: ﴿It is not but Your trial; You send astray thereby whom You will and guide whom You will﴾ [Al-A'raf: 155]. This trial of worshipping the calf is made clear in several verses, such as His saying: ﴿And when We appointed for Musa forty nights, then you took the calf [as deity] after him while you were wrongdoers﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 51], and similar verses.

His saying here, ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾, clarifies the manner of his misguiding them, which is explained in other places, such as His saying: ﴿And the people of Musa made, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾ up to His saying ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [Al-A'raf: 148]; that is, they took it as a god, and the Samiri had fashioned it for them from the ornaments of the Copts, and so he misguided them by [their] worship of it. His saying here, ﴿So the Samiri cast [it]﴾ and ﴿Then he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he [Musa] forgot"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88].

As for al-Samiri, it is said that his name was Harun, and it is said that his name was Musa ibn Zafar. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he was from a people who used to worship cows. It is also said that he was a man from the Copts, a neighbour of Musa, who believed in him and went out with him. And it is said that he was a great man among the Children of Israel, from a tribe known as the Samirah, who are well known in al-Sham. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he was from the people of Kirman.

The word fitnah (trial), in its linguistic origin, means placing gold in fire to show whether it is pure or counterfeit. The Qur'an has used it in several senses:

(First): placing in fire, like His saying: ﴿The Day they will be burned over the Fire﴾ [Adh-Dhariyat: 13], that is, they will be burned by it; and His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾ [Al-Buruj: 10], that is, they burned them in the fire of the trench.

(Second): testing, which is the most common use of fitnah. Like His saying: ﴿Your wealth and your children are only a trial﴾ [At-Taghabun: 15], and His saying: ﴿And [if] they had remained on the way, We would have given them abundant water, that We might test them therein﴾ [Al-Jinn: 16-17].

(Third): the outcome of a test when it is bad. From here, fitnah was applied to shirk, like His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ [Al-Anfal: 39], and His saying here: ﴿Indeed, We have tested your people﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85].

(Fourth): proof (argument), like His saying: ﴿Then their argument was only that they said, "By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists"﴾ [Al-An'am: 23], that is, their argument was not.

His saying, exalted is He, in this verse: ﴿and the Samiri has led them astray﴾ attributes their misguidance to him, because he was the one who caused it by fashioning the calf for them from the ornaments of the Copts, and by casting upon it the dust that had been touched by the hoof of the horse on which Jibril had come. So Allah, because of that, made it a calf, a body with a lowing sound, as Allah, exalted is He, said in this noble surah: ﴿So the Samiri cast [it], then he brought forth for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾, and He said in "Al-A'raf": ﴿And the people of Musa made, after him, from their ornaments a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾ [Al-A'raf: 148]. Al-khuwar is the sound of cows. Some scholars said: Allah, by His power, made that fashioned ornament into a body of flesh and blood, and this is the apparent meaning of His saying ﴿a calf, a body﴾.

Other scholars said: that form was not flesh, nor blood, but when the wind entered it, it made a sound like the lowing of a calf. The first view is closer to the apparent meaning of the verse, and Allah, exalted is He, is able to make inert matter into flesh and blood, just as He made Adam flesh and blood when he had been clay.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 86:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾.

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that Moses returned to his people after his coming to the appointed time (al-mīqāt), while in that return he was angry and grieved (asif) over his people because of their worship of the calf.

His saying "asifan" means: intensely angry. So asaf here means intense anger, and on this basis His saying ﴿angry and grieved﴾ means: angry, intensely angry. From the use of asaf for anger in the Qur'an is His saying, in "az-Zukhruf": ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them and drowned them all﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 55], meaning: when they angered Us by their persistence in disbelief despite the successive signs upon them, We took vengeance upon them. Some scholars said: asaf here means sorrow and distress. That is: Moses returned, being angry (p-80) and sorrowful and distressed because of his people's disbelief in worshipping the calf. It was also said: asifan means: enraged (mughtaz). The one who says this claims that the difference between ghadab (anger) and ghayz (rage) is that Allah described Himself with ghadab but it is not permissible to describe Him with ghayz. This is related by al-Fakhr al-Razi. It is not unnoticed that this does not fit the interpretation of this verse, because it returns to the first view, and there is no need for the stated distinction in that.

His saying ﴿angry and grieved﴾ are two circumstantial clauses (ḥāl). We have already mentioned earlier that the verified position is the permissibility of multiple circumstantial clauses from one referent while the governing element is one, as he indicated in the Khulasa (Alfiyya of Ibn Malik) with his saying:

"And the ḥāl may come multiple for a single noun, know this, and for a non-single noun."

What He, majestic and exalted, mentions in this verse of Ta-Ha, that Moses returned to his people ﴿angry and grieved﴾, He mentions in other than this place, and He mentions things from the effects of his aforementioned anger, such as His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me."﴾ [al-A'raf: 150]. Allah has clarified that among the effects of Moses' anger was his throwing down the tablets in which was the Torah, and his seizing his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself, as He said in "al-A'raf": ﴿And he threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself﴾ [al-A'raf: 150], and He said in "Ta-Ha," alluding to his seizing his brother by the head: ﴿He said: "O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head"﴾ [verse 94]. These verses show that reported knowledge is not like direct witnessing, because when Allah informed Moses of his people's disbelief in worshipping the calf, as He explained in His saying: ﴿We have tested your people after you, and the Samiri has misled them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 85], and this is information from Allah with certainty, without doubt, he did not throw down the tablets. But when he saw his people around the calf worshipping it, witnessing that affected him with an effect that the certain report had not produced in him, so he threw down the tablets until they broke, and seized his brother by the head dragging him toward himself, because of the intense anger that befell him at the violation of the sanctities of Allah, exalted is He.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir on surah "al-A'raf": Ibn Abi Hatim said: Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn as-Sabbah narrated to us, 'Affan narrated to us, Abu 'Awana narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "May Allah have mercy on Moses. The one who sees is not like the one who is told. His Lord, mighty and majestic, informed him that his people had been tested after him, so he did not throw down the tablets; but when he saw them and witnessed them, he threw down the tablets."

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Did the period seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so you broke your appointment with me?"﴾ ﴿They said: "We did not break our appointment with you by our own power."﴾

(p-81) In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that Moses, upon him and upon our Prophet be prayers and peace, when he returned to his people and found them having worshipped the calf after him, said to them: ﴿O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾

The most apparent of the sayings to me regarding the intended meaning of this good promise is that He promised them that He would send down to their prophet a Book containing everything they need of the good of this world and the Hereafter. This good promise mentioned here is the one mentioned in His saying: ﴿And We made an appointment with you at the right side of the Mount﴾ (verse 80), and there are other sayings besides this.

His saying: ﴿Did the period seem long to you?﴾ The interrogation here is for denial, meaning the period had not been long, as is said in the proverb: "And there is no antiquity to the covenant." Because length of time is the cause of forgetfulness, and the covenant is recent and has not been long, so how did you forget?

His saying: ﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you﴾. Some scholars said: "am" here is the disjunctive (munqati'a), and the meaning is: rather, did you wish that wrath from your Lord descend upon you? The meaning of their wishing the descent of wrath is that they did what necessitates their Lord's anger by their own will. Thus it is as if they wished the anger when they wished its cause, which is disbelief through worshipping the calf.

His saying: ﴿so you broke your appointment with me﴾. They had promised him that they would follow him when he went ahead to the appointed time, and that they would remain steadfast in obedience to Allah, exalted is He. But they worshipped the calf, devoted themselves to it, and did not follow Moses. So they broke his appointment by disbelief and by not going in his footsteps. ﴿They said: "We did not break our appointment with you by our own power."﴾ Naf' and 'Asim read "bi-malkina" with a fatha on the mim. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "bi-mulkina" with a damma on the mim. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read "bi-milkina" with a kasra on the mim. The meaning in all the readings is: we did not break your appointment by having power over our affair; had we had power over our affair we would not have broken your appointment. This is an excuse from them that they did not break the appointment by their choice, but they were overpowered in their affair by the Samiri and his scheming. This is a cold, invalid excuse, as you see! And he spoke truly who said:

"When the face of the excuse is not clear, then abandoning the excuse is better than the excuse."

As for the view of the one who said: those who said to Moses, "We did not break our appointment with you by our own power," are those who did not worship the calf, because they had promised him to follow him, and when what happened of the worship of most of them of the calf occurred, they held back from following Moses because of that, and did not dare to separate from them out of fear of division. So the excuse has a certain validity in general, as His saying in the story in this noble surah indicates: ﴿He said: "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me? Did you then disobey my order?" He said: "O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head. Indeed I feared that you would say, 'You caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92–94].

The verbal noun in His saying "bi-malkina" is idafa to its agent, and its object is omitted, meaning: by our power over our affair. Al-Qurtubi said: it is as if he said: by our power over the right course, but we erred. So it is an admission from them of error. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Did the period seem long to you?" — "al-zaman" (time), meaning the duration of his separation from them.

* *

Note (tanbih)

Every present-tense verb in the Qur'an is jussive with "lam" when preceded by the interrogative hamza, as in His saying here: ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise?﴾. There are two well-known views among the scholars:

The first: its present form is converted to past meaning and its negation converts to affirmation. Thus His saying "a-lam yi'dukum" means "wa'adakum" (He promised you), and "a-lam nashrah" means "sharahna" (We expanded), and His saying "a-lam naj'al lahu 'aynayn" means "ja'alna lahu 'aynayn" (We made for him two eyes). And so on. The reason for the conversion of the present to past is clear, because "lam" is a particle that converts the present from the sense of futurity to the sense of past, as is well known. The reason for the conversion of negation to affirmation is that the hamza is denunciatory (inkariyya), so it implies the sense of negation, and so the negation latent in it governs the explicit negation in "lam," negating it, and the negation of negation is affirmation, so it reverts to the sense of affirmation.

The second view: the interrogation in such usage is for confirmation (taqrir), which is making the addressee acknowledge so that he says "bala" (yes). Accordingly, what is meant by His saying "a-lam yi'dukum rabbukum wa'dan hasana" is to lead them to acknowledge this, so that they say "bala." A parallel to this in Arabic speech is the verse of Jarir:

"Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of all people in pouring wine?"

Now, when you know that His saying here, ﴿So Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved﴾, up to His saying "bi-malkina," Allah has made clear in it that when Moses returned to them in intense anger at what they had done, he rebuked them, and in that rebuke he said to them: ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Did the period seem long to you?﴾ (verse 86), know that some of his rebuke to them has not been explained here, and likewise some of his action, but he explained it in other than this place, as in His saying in "al-A'raf" in the same story: ﴿And when Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved, he said: "Evil is what you have done in my absence after me. Did you hasten the command of your Lord?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 150], (p-83) and he clarified some of what he did in His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿And he threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself﴾ [al-A'raf: 150]. He has indicated this here in "Ta-Ha" in His saying: ﴿He said: "O son of my mother, do not seize my beard or my head."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But we were burdened with loads of the ornaments of the people, so we threw them, and thus did as-Samiri cast.﴾ ﴿Then he brought out for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they said, "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾

Abu 'Amr, Shu'bah on the authority of 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read this word as ḥamalnā, with a fathah on the ḥā' and a light (unshaddated) mīm, in the active voice, unaugmented. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read it as ḥummilnā, with a ḍammah on the ḥā' and a kasrah on the shaddated mīm, in the passive voice. The "nā" in the first reading is the subject (fā'il) of ḥamala, and in the second it is the deputy subject (nā'ib al-fā'il) of ḥummila, with the doubling (taḍ'īf) of the verb.

Regarding awzāran (loads) in his saying "awzāran," some scholars said its meaning is "burdens" (al-athqāl), and some scholars said its meaning is "sins" (al-āthām). The rationale of the first opinion is that they were loads of the jewelry of the Copts which they had borrowed from them. The rationale of the second is that they were sins and consequences, because they were with them in the legal position of those granted safe conduct (musta'minīn) in the abode of war, and it is not permitted for one granted safe conduct to take the property of a combatant of the enemy, and because spoils of war were not lawful for them. The latter reason is stronger.

As for his saying, ﴿from the ornaments of the people﴾, what is meant by ornament (zīnah) is jewelry (ḥullī), as His saying, exalted is He, clarifies: ﴿And the people of Musa after him took from their jewelry a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾ [al-A'raf: 148]. That is, we cast them and threw them into the fire which as-Samiri had kindled in the pit, and he ordered us to throw the jewelry into it. The most apparent of the opinions in my view is that they put all the jewelry into the fire so that it would melt and become one piece, because that is easier to safeguard, until Allah's prophet Musa would see his opinion regarding it. As-Samiri intended to devise a scheme that they had not become aware of. That is because when Jibril came to take Musa to the appointed time, and he was on a horse, as-Samiri took a handful of dust that the hoof of that horse had touched. They claim in the narration that he observed the place of its track where plants were growing, so he surmised that Allah had placed in it the property of life. He took that handful of dust and kept it. When they wanted to throw the jewelry into the fire to make it one piece, or for other reasons, and put it in, as-Samiri cast that aforementioned handful of dust upon it and said to it: "Be a calf, a body with a lowing sound." So Allah made it a calf, a body with a lowing sound. Then he said to them: "This calf is your god and the god of Musa," as His saying, exalted is He, about Musa indicates: ﴿He said, "What is your matter, O Samiri?" He said, "I saw what they did not see, so I took a handful from the track of the Messenger and threw it, and thus did my soul entice me."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 95-96].

(p-84) His saying in this verse: ﴿But we were burdened with loads of the ornaments of the people﴾ is part of their corrupt and feeble excuse, and it indicates that this excuse came from those who worshipped the calf and not from others, and with it there is no remote possibility that it came from others, because there is nothing in it that specifies the excuse as coming from them in a manner that admits no other possibility. It is well known that this excuse is one that has no basis in any case.

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿but he forgot﴾, meaning: Musa forgot his god here and went to seek him in another place. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas in the narration of al-Futun, and it is the view of Mujahid. Also from Ibn 'Abbas, through the route of 'Ikrimah, ﴿but he forgot﴾ means: he forgot to remind you of Him. Also from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿but he forgot﴾, meaning: as-Samiri forgot what he had been upon of Islam, and became a disbeliever by claiming the divinity of the calf and worshipping it.

God Most High says: ﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them any word, and that it possesses for them neither harm nor benefit?﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, Majestic and Exalted, shows the foolishness of the minds of those who worshipped the calf, and how they worshipped something that cannot return an answer to one who asks it, cannot bring benefit to one who worships it, and cannot bring harm to one who disobeys it. This indicates that the object of worship cannot be incapable of benefit, harm, or returning an answer. This meaning is expressed in other places, such as His words in "al-A'raf" about the same story: ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them and does not guide them to a way? They took it, and they were wrongdoers.﴾ [al-A'raf: 148]. There is no doubt that whoever takes as a god one who does not speak to him and does not guide him to a way is among the greatest of wrongdoers. A parallel to this is His words about Ibrahim: ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which does not hear and does not see and does not avail you at all?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. He also says of him: ﴿He said, "Do they hear you when you call? Or do they benefit you or harm you?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 72-73]. And His words: ﴿Do they have feet with which they walk? Or do they have hands with which they strike? Or do they have eyes with which they see? Or do they have ears with which they hear?﴾ [al-A'raf: 195]. And His words: ﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, and who are unaware of their supplication? And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship.﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 5-6]. And His words: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord; to Him belongs dominion. And those you call upon besides Him do not possess even a date-pit's membrane. If you call them, they do not hear your call, and if they heard, they would not respond to you. And on the Day of Resurrection they will deny your association. And none can inform you like one who is All-Aware.﴾ [Fatir: 13-14].

We have already discussed at length (p-85) the interrogative hamzah followed by a conjunction particle such as the fa' or the waw, as in His words here, "Afala yarawna" (Do they not see), so there is no need to repeat it here. The majority of reciters read this letter "alla yarji'u" (that it does not return) with the raf' (nominative vowel on the verb), because "an" here is a lightened form of the heavy "anna."

The evidence that it is a lightened form of the heavy "anna" is that God explicitly states the heavy form in His words about the same matter in "al-A'raf": ﴿Did they not see that it does not speak to them and does not guide them?﴾ etc. [al-A'raf: 148]. The "ra'a" in the verse of "Ta-Ha" and "al-A'raf" is of the ma'rifah (knowledge) type, in the verified sense, because they knew with certainty that this calf, made of jewelry, does not benefit, does not harm, and does not speak.

Know that what is established in the science of grammar (ʿilm al-nahw) is that "an" has three states. The first is that it is definitely a lightened form of the heavy "anna," and it cannot be the verbal "an" that governs the imperfect verb in the subjunctive. Its rule is that it comes after a verb of knowledge and what takes its place of verbs indicating certainty, as in His words: ﴿He knows that there will be among you sick people﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and His words: ﴿That He may know that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord﴾ [al-Jinn: 28], and similar verses, and the words of the poet:

"Know, for a man's knowledge benefits him: that everything decreed will surely come."

And the words of another:

"Among youths like swords of India, who know that every one who goes barefoot and shod will perish."

When this lightened "an" is followed by an imperfect verb, that verb is put in the nominative and not the subjunctive, as in the words:

"They knew that they would be asked, so they gave generously before they were asked for the greatest of requests."

The name of this lightened "an" is usually a pronoun of concealment (mustatir), and most often it is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n). It is said that it can only be the pronoun of the matter, and its predicate is the sentence that follows it, as indicated in the "Khulasa" (the summary of Ibn Malik's grammar) with his words:

"If 'anna' is lightened, its name is concealed, and make the predicate a sentence after it."

What is heard in Arabic poetry of its name appearing explicitly and not as the pronoun of the matter is a poetic necessity, as in the words of Janub, sister of 'Amr dhu al-Kalb:

"The guest and the needy surely know, when the horizon becomes dusty and the north wind blows,
that you are a spring and a copious rain, and that you there will be the refuge."

And the words of another:

"If you, on a day of ease, had asked me for your divorce, I would not have withheld it, though you are a friend."

(p-86) The second state is that it may be either the verbal "an" that governs the imperfect in the subjunctive, or it may be the lightened form of the heavy "anna."

If an imperfect verb follows it, it may be put in the subjunctive according to the first possibility, or in the nominative according to the second possibility. On this are based the two canonical readings (of seven) in His words: ﴿And they thought there would be no fitnah (trial)﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71], with the verb "takūna" in the subjunctive and in the nominative. The rule for this "an" is that it comes after a verb that implies supposition (ẓann) or similar verbs of probability. When no separator comes between it and the verb, the subjunctive is preferred, and for this reason the reciters agreed on the subjunctive in His words: ﴿Do people think that they will be left alone?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. It is said that the "an" that comes after doubt has only the subjunctive. This was transmitted by al-Sabban in his commentary from Abu Hayyan through al-Suyuti.

The third state: "an" is not after what implies certainty, nor after supposition, nor what takes their place. Then it is definitely the verbal "an" that governs the imperfect verb in the subjunctive. To these three states he alluded in the "Khulasa" with his words:

"And with 'lan,' 'kay,' and 'an' put the verb in the subjunctive, not after knowledge, and what comes after supposition."

"So put it in the subjunctive, and keep the nominative; know that its lightening is from 'anna,' and this is regular."

* *

Note

Al-Fakhr al-Razi said in his commentary on this noble verse: "The intent here is not that if the calf could speak to them, it would be a god, because a thing may be conditioned on many conditions, so the absence of one of them requires the absence of the conditioned thing, but the presence of one of them does not require the presence of the conditioned thing." End of his words.

What he mentioned is established in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh). Everything that depends on two or more conditions is not realized except by the realization of all the conditions. So if you say to your servant, "If Zayd fasts, prays, and makes the pilgrimage, then give him a dinar," it is not permissible for him to give it except when all three conditions are met. This applies when the conditions are not attached as alternatives; in that case, one suffices. So if you say to your servant, "If Zayd fasts or prays, then give him a dirham," then giving the dirham is required by either one of the two. To this matter he alluded in "Maraqi al-Su'ud," in the section on connected specifiers, with his words:

"If something depends on two conditions, it occurs only when both conditions are met.
And what is attached as an alternative, it is established by the realization of one."

Ibn Kathir (may Allah have mercy on him) said in his commentary on this verse: "It has already been mentioned in the hadith of the Fitan from al-Hasan al-Basri (p-87) that the name of this calf was Yahmut. The summary of what these ignorant people offered as an excuse is that they scrupled about the jewelry of the Copts, so they threw it away from them and worshipped the calf. Thus they scrupled about the trivial and committed the grave matter, as in the authentic hadith from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, that a man of the people of Iraq asked him about the blood of a gnat if it fell on a garment, meaning whether one may pray in it or not. Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: 'Look at the people of Iraq! They killed the son of the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) (meaning al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him), and they ask about the blood of a gnat!'" End of his words.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 90:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And Harun had already said to them before: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command." They said, "We will not cease being devoted to it until Musa returns to us."﴾

In these two noble verses, the Most High explains that when the Samiri led the Children of Israel into trial and misguided them with the worship of the calf, the Prophet of Allah, Harun, peace be upon him and upon our Prophet, advised them, and made clear to them that their worship of the calf was a trial (fitnah) by which they had been tested, meaning disbelief and misguidance that they had committed by it. He made clear to them that their Lord is the Most Merciful, the Creator of everything, the Most High, and that a fashioned calf made of ornaments is not worshipped except by one who is tested, astray and a disbeliever. He commanded them to follow him in the affirmation of the oneness of Allah, the Most High, and in fulfilling the appointment with Musa, peace be upon them both and upon our Prophet, and to obey him in that. They openly defied him with rebellion, disobedience, and persistence in disbelief until Musa returns. This indicates that he exerted to them the utmost of his effort and capacity, and that they weakened him, rebelled against him, and did not obey him.

This meaning has been explained in another place, such as His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿[Harun] said, "O son of my mother, indeed the people oppressed me and nearly killed me, so do not let the enemies rejoice over me, and do not place me with the wrongdoing people."﴾ [al-A'raf: 150]. So their saying to him, ﴿We will not cease being devoted to it﴾, indicates their weakening of him and their rebellion against him, which is explicitly stated in "al-A'raf" as we have shown.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Qurtubi, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his tafsir of these noble verses, the following text: Imam Abu Bakr al-Tartushi was asked: "What does our master the jurist say concerning the way of the Sufis? And know, may Allah protect his life: a group of men gather and they frequently mention Allah the Most High and the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ), then they strike with a stick upon a piece of leather, and one of them stands dancing and ecstatic until he falls unconscious, and they bring something to eat. Is attending with them permissible or not? Give us a fatwa, may you be rewarded." And this saying which they recite:

"O shaykh, refrain from sins before separation and slipping,
and work for your soul righteously while the work still benefits you.
As for youth, it has passed away, and the greying of your head has come down."

Concerning this kind of thing and its like, the answer, may Allah have mercy on you: the way of the Sufis is idleness, ignorance and misguidance, and Islam is nothing but the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). As for dancing and ecstasy: the first to introduce it were the companions of the Samiri when he made for them a calf, a body with a lowing sound, and they stood dancing around it and in ecstasy, so it is the religion of the disbelievers and the worship of the calf. As for the stick: the first to adopt it were the heretics (zanadiqah), to occupy the Muslims with it away from the Book of Allah the Most High. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to sit with his companions as if birds were upon their heads out of gravity. It is therefore incumbent upon the ruler and his deputies to prevent them from attending mosques and other places. It is not lawful for anyone who believes in Allah and the Last Day to attend with them, nor to help them in their falsehood. This is the position of Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and others among the imams of the Muslims. And success is from Allah. End of his quotation in his own words.

The compiler of this work, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: We have previously mentioned in the surah of "Maryam" what indicates that some Sufis are upon the truth. There is no doubt that among them are those who are on the straight path of acting by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ), and by that they treated the diseases of their hearts, guarded them, observed them, and knew their states, and they spoke about the states of the hearts in a detailed manner, as is well known, such as 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Atiyah, or Ibn Ahmad ibn 'Atiyah, or Ibn 'Askar, I mean Abu Sulayman al-Darani, and 'Awn ibn 'Abdullah, who was called "the judge of the Ummah", and their like, and Sahl ibn 'Abdullah al-Tustari, Abu Talib al-Makki, Abu 'Uthman al-Naysaburi, Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi, al-Junayd ibn Muhammad, and whoever follows their path, because they treated the diseases of their souls by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ), and they do not deviate from acting by the Book and the Sunnah, outwardly and inwardly, and nothing contrary to the Shari'ah appeared from them. Therefore, passing a verdict of misguidance upon all Sufis is not appropriate, and it is not valid in its absolute form, and the criterion distinguishing truth from falsehood in this matter is the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (ﷺ). Whoever among them follows the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his sayings and actions, his guidance and his conduct, like those we have mentioned and their like, they are among the scholars who act, and it is not permissible to judge them as misguided. As for whoever is contrary to that, he is the misguided one.

Yes, what has become well known in recent times, and in many eras before them by inductive observation, is that the majority of those who claim Sufism in the regions of the world, except those whom Allah wills, are charlatans who display religion in order to mislead the common people, the ignorant, and weak-minded students of knowledge, so that they may take through that followers, servants, wealth and status, while they are far removed from the true Sufi path, not acting by the Book of Allah nor by the Sunnah of His Prophet. Their domination over the thoughts of weak-minded people is more severe than the domination of all colonizing peoples. Therefore it is obligatory to keep far from them and to protect oneself from their misguidance by the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet, even if some extraordinary things appear at their hands. Indeed, he spoke truly who said:

"When you see a man flying, and walking upon the surface of the sea,
and he does not stop at the limits of the Shari'ah, then he is one being led astray or an innovator."

The decisive word in this matter is His saying, the Most High: ﴿Not by your wishful thinking, nor the wishful thinking of the People of the Book: whoever does evil will be recompensed for it, and he will not find for himself besides Allah any protector or helper. And whoever does righteous deeds, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, and they will not be wronged even the speck on a date-seed. And who is better in religion than one who submits his face to Allah while being a doer of good and follows the religion of Ibrahim, a hanif?﴾ [al-Nisa': 123]. So whoever's deeds oppose the Shari'ah, like the Sufis of the last era, then he is the misguided one. And whoever's deeds conform to what our Prophet, peace be upon him, brought, then he is the guided one. We ask Allah the Most High to guide us and our believing brothers, and not to make us deviate or go astray from acting by His Book and the Sunnah of His Prophet (ﷺ), which is a clear path, its night like its day, from which none turns aside except one who is destroyed.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 92:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, ﴿from following me?﴾"﴾

Some scholars said: "lā" in His words ﴿from following me﴾ is extra (ziyadah), for emphasis (li-l-tawkid). Those who said this cited His words, may He be exalted, in al-A'raf: ﴿He said, "What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?"﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. They said: the meaning is "what prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you," as evidence by His words in the same story in Surah Sad: ﴿He said, "O Iblis, what prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands?"﴾ [38] and so on. So He omitted the word "lā" in Sad while it is present in al-A'raf, and the meaning is one. This indicates that it is extra for emphasis.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: It is known in the Arabic language that the addition of the word "lā" in a statement that carries the sense of negation (al-jahd), for emphasis, is regular (muttarid).

Such as His words here: ﴿What prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?﴾ meaning: "what prevented you from following me"; and His words "what prevented you from prostrating," as evidenced by His words in Sad: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating to what I created with My hands?﴾ and so on;

and His words, may He be exalted: ﴿So that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over anything of Allah's bounty﴾ and so on [al-Hadid: 29]. Meaning: "so that the People of the Book may know";

and His words ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not believe﴾ [al-Nisa': 65], meaning "by your Lord, they will not believe";

and His words: ﴿Nor are the good deed and the evil deed equal﴾ [41], (p-90) meaning: "nor the evil deed";

and His words: ﴿And it is forbidden for a town which We have destroyed that they will not return﴾ [al-Anbiya': 95], according to one of the two opinions;

and His words: ﴿And what will make you realize that when it comes they will not believe?﴾ [al-An'am: 109], according to one of the two opinions; and His words: ﴿Say, "Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you: that you not associate anything with Him"﴾ and so on [al-An'am: 151], according to one of the opinions concerning it.

A parallel to this in the speech of the Arabs is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"So no, by your father, daughter of al-Amiri, the people do not claim that I flee"

meaning "so by your father." And the verse of Abu al-Najm:

"I do not blame the white women for not mocking, when they saw the grey-haired old man with the bald head"

meaning "that they mock." And the verse of another:

"The Messenger of Allah was not pleased with their religion, nor were the two best men, Abu Bakr and Umar"

meaning "and Umar." And the verse of another:

"You blame me in play that I do not love it, and for play there is a constant, unforgetful caller"

meaning "that I love it." And "lā" is extra in all these verses for emphasizing the negation in them. Al-Farra' said: it is not added except in statements that carry the sense of negation, like the examples mentioned above. By negation (al-jahd) is meant denial (al-nafy) and what resembles it, such as prevention (al-man') in His words ﴿What prevented you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 89] and the like.

What appears to us, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the addition of the word "lā" for emphasizing and strengthening the statement is one of the stylistic methods of the Arabic language, and it is more prevalent in statements that carry the sense of negation, though this is attested in other contexts too. Al-Asma'i cited for the addition of "lā" the verse of Sa'idah al-Hudhali:

"Is it from you, no lightning whose flash is like a thicket whose crest is ignited by a piercing flame?"

It is narrated as "afa-min-ka" instead of "afa-anka" and "tashayyamahu" instead of "tasannamahu," meaning "is it from you lightning," with "lā" extra for emphasis, and the statement has no sense of negation. A similar example is the verse of another:

"I remembered Layla, so passion seized me, and the core of my heart almost does not break"

meaning "almost breaks." Al-Jawhari cited for the addition of "lā" the verse of al-Ajjaj:

"In a well of lā ḥūr he travelled and was unaware of its falsehood until he saw the morning dawn"

and al-ḥūr is destruction. Meaning: in a well of destruction, and "lā" is extra for emphasis. This was said by Abu Ubaydah and others. (p-91) The statement has no sense of negation. We have clarified this issue in our book (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab) in the commentary on Surah al-Balad.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you then disobeyed my command?﴾.

The apparent meaning is that the command mentioned in this verse is the one mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Moses said to his brother Aaron, "Take my place among my people, do right, and do not follow the way of the corrupters."﴾ [al-A'raf: 142].

This noble verse indicates that a command implies obligation (iqtida' al-amr lil-wujub), because He applied the name of disobedience (ma'siyah) to not complying with a command. The texts that indicate this are numerous:

• Such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let those who oppose his command beware lest a trial strike them or a painful punishment strike them﴾ [an-Nur: 63],

• and His saying: ﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice about their affair﴾ [al-Ahzab: 36], so He made the command of Him and the command of His Messenger ﷺ a barrier to choice and a requirement for compliance.

• And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], so He rebuked him with this severe rebuke for not complying with the command indicated by the imperative form "ifal" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Prostrate to Adam﴾ [Ta-Ha: 116].

The majority of the usul scholars (jama-hir al-usuliyyin) hold that the bare imperative form, free of any indicators (qara'in), implies obligation, on account of the evidences we have mentioned and others similar to them. Indicating this, the author of Maraqi as-Su'ud said in his verse:

"Perform (ifal) — for the most part it is for obligation, and it is said it is for recommendation or for what is desired."

... etc.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 94:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head. Indeed, I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not observe my word.'"﴾

In this noble verse, exalted and most high is He, mentions that Harun said this to his brother Musa: ﴿O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or my head.﴾ This indicates that, due to the intensity of his anger, he wanted to grasp his head and beard. Allah, the Exalted, has made clear in "al-A'raf" that he seized his head, dragging him toward himself. This is in His saying: ﴿And he threw down the tablets and seized his brother by the head, dragging him toward himself. He said, "O son of my mother..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 150]. His saying ﴿and did not observe my word﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94] is part of Harun's speech. That is: "I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel,' and that you would say to me, 'You did not observe my word,'" meaning: you did not act upon my instruction and obey my command.

* *

(p-92) Alert

This noble verse, together with the verse of "al-An'am" added to it, indicates the obligation of letting the beard grow, so it is a Qur'anic proof for letting the beard grow and not shaving it. The verse of al-An'am referred to is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among his descendants were Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, Yusuf, Musa, and Harun﴾, to the end of the verse [al-An'am: 84]. Then, after enumerating the noble prophets mentioned, He said: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [6]. This indicates that Harun is among the prophets whom our Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow, and his command to do so is a command to us, because the command to take an example is a command to his followers, as we have explained with Qur'anic evidence in this blessed book in surah "al-Ma'idah," where we previously mentioned that it is established in Sahih al-Bukhari that: "Mujahid asked Ibn 'Abbas: From where was the prostration in 'Sad' derived? He said: Do you not recite ﴿And among his descendants Dawud﴾ [al-An'am: 84], ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [6], so Dawud prostrated, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prostrated." When you know this, that Harun is among the prophets whom our Prophet ﷺ was commanded to follow in surah "al-An'am," and you know that his command is a command to us, because we have in it an excellent example, and you know that Harun was letting his beard grow abundantly, as evidenced by his saying to his brother: ﴿Do not seize me by my beard,﴾ because if he had been shaving, his brother would not have wanted to seize his beard. It becomes clear to you from this, with explanation, that letting the beard grow is among the manner (samt) which we were commanded in the Great Qur'an, and that it was the manner of the noble messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them. It is strange that among those whose consciences have become corrupted and whose taste has withered, to the point that they flee from the attributes of manliness and the nobility of masculinity toward the effeminacy of femininity, and who disfigure their faces by shaving their chins, imitating women, trying to eliminate one of the greatest physical distinctions between male and female, which is the beard. The Prophet ﷺ had a thick beard, and he was the most beautiful of creation and the most handsome in form. And the men who took the treasures of Kisra and Caesar, and to whom the eastern and western lands submitted, none of them was a shaver. We ask Allah to show us and our believing brothers the truth as truth, and grant us to follow it, and falsehood as falsehood, and grant us to avoid it.

As for the prophetic hadiths indicating letting the beard grow, we have no need to mention them because of their fame among people and the abundance of works authored on this. Our intention here is to show the evidence for this from the Qur'an. Harun said to his brother, ﴿He said, "O son of my mother,"﴾ because the kinship through the mother is stronger in tenderness and compassion than kinship through the father.

Its original form is "ya ibna ummi," with the suffix of the first person ya'. The deletion of the ya' and its replacement with an alif, and the deletion of the alif replacing it, as here, is regular. Ibn Malik alluded to this in the Khulasah with his saying:

"Opening or kasra, and deletion of the ya' remains constant in 'ya ibna umm' and 'ya ibna amm', there is no escape."

As for retaining the ya' of the first person, Harmalah ibn al-Mundhir says:

"O son of my mother and my full brother, ***  you have left me yourself for a harsh age"

This is a rare dialect. Some said it is for the necessity of poetry. The phrase "ya ibna umm" was read by Ibn 'Amir, Shu'bah from 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i with a kasra on the mim, and the rest read it with a fatha. Likewise His saying in "al-A'raf": ﴿He said, "O son of my mother, indeed the people..."﴾ [al-A'raf: 150].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 98:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity, He has encompassed all things in knowledge.﴾

In this verse, exalted is He, makes clear that the calf which al-Samiri fashioned from the ornaments of the Copts cannot possibly be a god. That is because He restricted divinity (al-ilah), meaning the one worshipped in truth, by means of innama (the particle of restriction, al-hasr, in its established sense), to the Creator of the heavens and the earth: ﴿other than whom there is no deity﴾. That is, there is no one worshipped in truth except Him alone, exalted is He, and He is the one who ﴿has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾. His saying "in knowledge" (ilman) is a tamyiz (specification) transferred from the subject (the agent), meaning: His knowledge has encompassed all things.

What Allah, exalted is He, mentions in this noble verse, namely that He is the God who is worshipped in truth to the exclusion of others, and that He has encompassed all things in knowledge, He mentions in many verses of His Book, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 2] to the end of the verse, and His saying: ﴿So know that there is no deity except Allah﴾ [Muhammad: 19], and other verses besides these.

And regarding the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of everything, He says: ﴿Not absent from your Lord is an atom's weight within the earth or within the heaven or anything smaller than that or greater, but it is in a clear register﴾ [Yunus: 61], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen; none knows them except Him. And He knows what is on the land and in the sea. Not a leaf falls but that He knows it, nor is there a grain within the darknesses of the earth or anything fresh or dry but that it is in a clear register﴾ [al-An'am: 59]. The verses similar to this are very many indeed.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 99:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus do We relate to you some news of what has passed before⁠﴾.

The kāf in His saying "thus" (kadhālika) is in the accusative position, as it is an adjective (na't) of a deleted verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: We relate to you the news of what has passed before, a relating like that relating, the good, true relating which We related to you concerning Mūsā and Hārūn, and concerning Mūsā and his people, and the Sāmirī. The apparent meaning of "min" (some) in His saying ﴿of the news of what has passed before﴾ is partitive (li-l-tab'īd), and from this it is understood that some of them were not related to you. This understanding is supported (p-94) by His saying in Surat al-Nisā': ﴿And messengers We have related to you before, and messengers We have not related to you⁠﴾ [al-Nisā': 164], and His saying in Surat al-Mu'min: ﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you; among them are those We related to you and among them are those We did not relate to you⁠﴾ [Ghāfir: 78], and His saying in Surat Ibrāhīm: ﴿Has there not come to you the news of those before you: the people of Nūḥ, ʿĀd, and Thamūd, and those after them, whom none knows but Allah? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs⁠﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 9]. Al-anbā' is the plural of naba', which is news that has significance.

What He, the Majestic and Exalted, mentioned in this noble verse, that He related to His Prophet ﷺ the reports of those who passed on, means: so that by this He might demonstrate the truthfulness of his prophethood, since he was unlettered, who did not write nor read books, and had not learned the reports and stories of nations. Had Allah not revealed that to him, he would not have known it. He clarified this also in other places,

such as His saying in Āl ʿImrān: ﴿That is of the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they cast their pens [to see] which of them would be the guardian of Maryam, nor were you with them when they disputed⁠﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 44], meaning: had Allah not revealed that to you, you would have had no knowledge of it.

And His saying, the Exalted, in Surat Hūd: ﴿These are of the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. Neither you nor your people knew them before this. So be patient; indeed, the best outcome is for the righteous⁠﴾ [Hūd: 49],

and His saying also in Hūd: ﴿And all [of] the news of the messengers We relate to you is that by which We strengthen your heart⁠﴾ [Hūd: 120], the verse,

and His saying, the Exalted, in Surat Yūsuf: ﴿That is of the news of the unseen which We reveal to you. And you were not with them when they agreed upon their plan while they were conspiring⁠﴾ [Yūsuf: 102],

and His saying also in Yūsuf: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, although you were before it among the unaware⁠﴾ [Yūsuf: 3],

and His saying in al-Qaṣaṣ: ﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Mūsā the commission⁠﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 44],

and His saying therein: ﴿And you were not at the side of the mount when We called⁠﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 46],

and His saying: ﴿And you were not a resident among the people of Madyan, reciting to them Our verses⁠﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 45],

and other verses besides these. That is, you were not present, O Prophet of Allah, at those events; had Allah not revealed that to you, you would not have known it. And His saying ﴿of what has passed before⁠﴾ means: the reports of what passed of the conditions of nations and messengers.

* *

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder⁠﴾.

That is: We have given you from Our presence a reminder, and it is this great Qur'an. Verses of the Book of Allah have indicated this.

Such as His saying: ﴿And this is a blessed reminder which We have sent down, so are you now rejecting it?⁠﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 50],

and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That We recite to you of the verses and the wise reminder⁠﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 58],

and His saying, the Exalted: (p-95) ﴿No new reminder comes to them from their Lord except that they listen to it while playing⁠﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 2],

and His saying: ﴿And they say, "O you to whom the reminder has been sent down, indeed you are mad!"⁠﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 6],

and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Ṣād. By the Qur'an containing reminder⁠﴾ [Ṣād: 1],

and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people⁠﴾, the verse [al-Zukhruf: 44],

and His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian⁠﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 9],

and other verses besides these.

Al-Fakhr al-Rāzī said in his tafsir of this noble verse: Then, in naming the Qur'an "reminder" there are several aspects:

The first: that it is a book in which is mentioned what people need of the affairs of their religion and their worldly life.

The second: that it mentions the kinds of Allah's blessings and favours, the Exalted. Thus in it is reminding and admonition.

The third: that in it is a reminder and honour for you and your people, as He said: ﴿And indeed, it is a reminder for you and your people⁠﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 44].

Know that Allah, the Exalted, named all His books "reminder," as He said: ﴿So ask the people of the reminder⁠﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 7]. End of what is intended from al-Rāzī's words.

What supports the second aspect in his words is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿A Book We have sent down to you, blessed, that they may ponder its verses and that those of understanding may be reminded⁠﴾ [Ṣād: 29], and His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have diversified in it from the warning that perhaps they will fear Allah, or it will produce for them a reminder⁠﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 113].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 100:

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever turns away from it, indeed he will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden, abiding therein; and evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection as a load.﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that whoever turns away from this Reminder, which is the Great Qur'an, that is, averts from it and turns his back on it, and does not act upon what it contains of the lawful, the unlawful, the good manners and the noble qualities, and does not believe in what it contains of the articles of faith, and does not take lessons from what it contains of narratives, parables and the like, then indeed he will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden. Al-Zamakhshari said in his tafsir of this noble verse: "He means by the burden the heavy, crushing punishment. He called it a burden, by way of comparison in its heaviness upon the one who is punished and the difficulty of bearing it, to a load that weighs down the bearer, breaks his back, and throws its burden upon him. Or because it is the recompense of the burden, which is sin."

The one who restricts it (i.e., the author, al-Shinqiti) — may Allah pardon him and forgive him — says: Many verses of the Book of Allah have shown that the criminals will come on the Day of Resurrection carrying their burdens, that is, the weights of their sins upon their backs.

As in His saying in surah "al-An'am" (p-96): ﴿Those have lost who denied the meeting with Allah, until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly, they say, "O our regret over what we neglected concerning it!" while they carry their burdens on their backs. Unquestionably, evil is what they carry.﴾ [al-An'am: 31],

and His saying in "al-Nahl": ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and [also] some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear.﴾ [al-Nahl: 25],

and His saying in "al-'Ankabut": ﴿And they will surely carry their burdens and burdens along with their burdens, and they will surely be questioned on the Day of Resurrection about what they used to invent.﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13],

and His saying in "Fatir": ﴿No bearer will bear the burden of another. And if a heavily laden soul calls [another] to its load, nothing of it will be carried, even if he were a close relative.﴾ [Fatir: 18].

By these verses that we have mentioned, and others like them in the Qur'an, you know that the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿indeed he will carry on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾ [Ta-Ha: 100], and His saying: ﴿and evil will it be for them on the Day of Resurrection as a load﴾ [Ta-Ha: 101], is that what is meant by the burden carried is the weight of their sins and their disbelief, which they will come to carry on the Day of Resurrection. This holds whether we say that their evil deeds take a bodily form in the most hideous and foulest shape, or otherwise, as has already been explained. And knowledge is with Allah. We have already discussed the function of "sa'a" (evil is), which is used in the sense of "bi'sa" (how evil is), several times, so that repeating it here is unnecessary.

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿abiding therein﴾. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this noble verse: "﴿Abiding therein﴾ means remaining therein, that is, in its recompense, and its recompense is Jahannam (Hell)."

Tanbih (a point of caution)

The singular pronoun in His saying: "a'rada" (turned away)

• and His saying: "fa-innahu" (indeed he)

• and His saying: "yahmilu" (carries) is in view of the wording of "man" (whoever). As for the plural "khalidina" (abiding) and the pronoun in "lahum" (for them), and "yawma al-qiyamah" (on the Day of Resurrection), they are in view of the meaning of "man".

• As in His saying: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteous deeds, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾ [Ta-Ha: 101],

• and His saying: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ and the verse [al-Jinn: 23].

Al-Zamakhshari also said in his tafsir of this noble verse: "If you say: What is the lam in 'lahum' (for them)? And what does it relate to? I say: It is the lam of clarification (lam al-bayan), as in ﴿Come, I am at your disposal﴾ [Yusuf: 23]."

(p-97) Almighty and Exalted God mentions in this noble verse that they ask him about the mountains, and He commands him to say to them: indeed, his Lord will blow them away with a blowing, by uprooting them from their foundations, then making them like sand that is loose and flows, and like carded wool that the winds scatter this way and that.

Know that Almighty and Exalted God has explained the states into which the mountains will pass on the Day of Resurrection in verses of His Book. He explained that He will remove them from their places, carry them, and crush them to dust. This is in His saying: ﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown with one blast, and the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with a single crush﴾ [al-Haqqah: 13-14].

Then He explained that He will set them moving through the air between the heaven and the earth. This is in His saying: ﴿And on the Day the Trumpet is blown, whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom God wills, and all will come to Him humbled. And you see the mountains, thinking them fixed, while they pass like clouds: the work of God who perfected everything. Indeed He is Aware of what you do﴾ [an-Naml: 87-88].

And His saying: ﴿On the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare﴾ [al-Kahf: 47].

And His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾ [at-Takwir: 3].

And His saying: ﴿And the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾ [an-Naba': 20].

And His saying: ﴿On the Day the sky will sway violently and the mountains will move with a movement﴾ [at-Tur: 9-10].

Then He explained that He will pulverize them and crush them, as in His saying: ﴿And the mountains are crushed to dust﴾, meaning they will be broken into pieces until they become like al-busaysah (a dish of flour kneaded with ghee or the like, according to that interpretation). And His saying: ﴿And the earth and the mountains are lifted and crushed with a single crush﴾ [al-Haqqah: 14].

Then He explained that He will make them like loose sand, and like carded wool. This is in His saying: ﴿On the Day the earth and the mountains quake, and the mountains become a heap of sand poured out﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 14], and His saying: ﴿On the Day the sky will be like molten brass, and the mountains will be like tufts of wool﴾ [al-Ma'arij: 9], in "al-Ma'arij" and "al-Qari'ah." Al-'ihn means dyed wool. From this is the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma in his mu'allaqah (suspended ode):

"As if the crumbs of dyed wool in every abode they alighted at were seeds of the fana' not crushed."

Then He explained that they will become like scattered dust, in His saying: ﴿And the mountains are crushed to dust and become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6]. Then He explained that they will become a mirage, in His saying: ﴿And the mountains are set in motion and become a mirage﴾ [an-Naba': 20]. He has also explained in another place that the mirage is nothing, in His saying: ﴿until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ [an-Nur: 39]. And He explained that He will blow them away with a blowing, in His saying here: ﴿They ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blowing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105].

* *

Note

(p-98) It is the custom in the Qur'an that when God says to His Prophet ﷺ "They ask you" (yas'aluunaka), He then says "Say" (qul) without a fa' (the conjunction "then").

For example:
- His saying: ﴿They ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is...﴾ [al-Isra': 85].
- His saying: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219].
- His saying: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 215].
- His saying: ﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them. Say: Lawful for you are the good things...﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 4].
- His saying: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is a great matter...﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], and others besides these verses.

But in this verse of Ta-Ha, He said: ﴿So say: He will blow them away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 105], with a fa'.

Al-Qurtubi answered this in his tafsir of this verse with the following text: "﴿They ask you about the mountains﴾, meaning: about the state of the mountains on the Day of Resurrection, then say. It came with a fa', and every question in the Qur'an is followed by 'Say' without a fa' except this one, because the meaning is: if they ask you about the mountains, then say. So the speech contains the meaning of a condition, and God knew that they would ask him about them, so He answered them before the question. Those were questions that had already occurred, which they asked the Prophet ﷺ about, and the answer came right after the question; therefore it was without a fa'. But this is a question they had not yet asked him, so understand it." End of quotation. What he mentioned needs evidence, and God knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 106:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then He will leave it a smooth, level plain, in which you will see no crookedness or elevation.﴾

Regarding the pronoun in His statement "fa-yadharuha" (then He will leave it), there are two well-known views among the scholars:

The first: it refers to the earth, although it has not been previously mentioned. A parallel to this in this verse is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿He leaves nothing upon its back of a creature﴾ [Fatir: 45], and His statement: ﴿He leaves upon it no creature﴾ [an-Nahl: 16]. In both, the pronoun refers to the earth, though no mention of it has preceded. We have explained the evidence for this from the Arabic language and the Qur'an with clarity in surah an-Nahl, so there is no need to repeat it here.

The second: it refers to the places of the mountains, which are their centres and resting places, since these are understood from the mention of the mountains.
