The meaning is: He will leave their places, which were settled in the earth, as a smooth, level plain (qa'an safsafan). The qa' (qa'): the level part of the earth. It was said: a pool of water. The safsaf (ṣafṣaf): the level, smooth ground that has no vegetation and no buildings, for it is on one level in its evenness. Sibawayh cited for this the verse of al-A'sha:

"How many a safsaf lies beyond your house, and dunes of sand and their hillocks."

And from this is the saying of another:

"A compact, white (cloud) — if they hurled with it peaks of Radwa, it would become a safsaf."

As for His statement: ﴿in which you will see no crookedness (ʿiwajan) or elevation (amtan)﴾ [Ta-Ha: 107], meaning: there is no unevenness in it, and no amt. The amt (amt): a slight protrusion. That is, there is no unevenness in it, nor one part rising above another; rather, it is level. From the use of amt in the stated sense is the saying of Labid:

"She galloped, then moved on, while idle, in a darkness in which there was no amt, nor any elevation."

And the saying of another:

"She saw a glimpse of the head of ʿIkrisha, in a darkness in which there was no amt nor ʿiwaj."

The "darkness" (kafir) in the two verses is said to be the night, and it is said to be the rain, because it prevents the eye from seeing the rise and the descent of the ground.

Al-Zamakhshari said in his interpretation of this noble verse: If you say: they have distinguished between ʿiwaj and ʿawaj, saying: ʿiwaj (with a kasra) is used for meanings, and ʿawaj (with a fatha) for physical objects. The earth is a physical object, so how is the form with the kasra in the ʿayn valid for it?

I say: the choice of this word has a fine and wondrous effect in describing the earth as level, smooth, and free of crookedness in the most eloquent way. That is because if you were to take a piece of land and level it, and exaggerate in levelling it in the eyes of yourself and of the sharp-sighted farmers, and you all agreed that no crookedness remained in it at all, then you sought the opinion of an engineer about it and asked him to test its evenness by geometric measures, he would find crookedness in it in places that cannot be perceived by the sense of sight, but only by geometric measurement. So God, mighty and majestic, negated that crookedness which is so fine and subtle as to be beyond perception, except by the measurement known to the expert in estimation and geometry. And since that crookedness is not perceived except by measurement and not by the senses, it is treated like the abstract meanings, so it is called ʿiwaj with a kasra. The amt is a slight protrusion; it is said: he stretched his rope until there was no amt in it. End of his words. We have already mentioned at the beginning of surah al-Kahf what suffices instead of this speech which he mentioned, and God knows best.

(p. 100) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿On that Day they will follow the summoner, from whom there is no deviation. And voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a faint whisper.﴾

His saying "on that Day" means: on the Day when the mountains are blown away, they will follow the summoner. The summoner (al-dā'ī) is the angel who calls them to appear for the reckoning. Some scholars of knowledge said: he will call to them, "O decayed bones, O scattered joints, O torn flesh, arise to your Lord for the reckoning and the recompense," and they will hear the voice and follow it.

The meaning of ﴿from whom there is no deviation﴾ is that they will not turn away from him, nor incline to the right or the left. It was also said: there is no deviation in the summons of the angel from anyone, i.e., he does not divert his call away from anyone, but calls them all together.

What Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned in this noble verse, namely their following the summoner to the reckoning and their not turning away from him, He explained in other places, and added that they hasten toward him, as in His saying: ﴿So turn away from them, on the Day when the caller calls them to a dreadful thing, their eyes humbled, they will come out from the graves as if they were scattered locusts, hastening toward the caller. The disbelievers will say, "This is a hard day."﴾ [al-Qamar: 6–8]. Al-ihtā' (hastening) means speeding.

And His saying: ﴿And listen, on the Day the caller calls from a near place, the Day they hear the Cry in truth. That is the Day of Coming Forth.﴾ [Qaf: 41–42].

And His saying: ﴿On the Day He calls you, and you will respond with His praise﴾ [al-Isra: 52].

And other verses besides these.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿And voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful﴾ means: they will be lowered, subdued, and become still out of awe of Allah, reverence, and fear. ﴿So you will not hear﴾ on that Day any loud voice; rather you will hear ﴿nothing but a whisper﴾, i.e., a hidden, faint sound, from the intensity of fear. Or ﴿nothing but a whisper﴾ means nothing but the sound of feet striking and moving toward the place of gathering. Al-hams (whisper) in the language is applied to concealment, so it includes lowering the voice and the sound of feet. It is like the sound of camels' soft hooves on land where dry plants are. From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"And they walk with us in a whisper; if the bird tells the truth, we will be safe and sound."

What Allah, may He be exalted, mentioned here, He indicated elsewhere, as in His saying: ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, the Most Merciful; they will not have the power to address Him. On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks, none will speak except one whom the Most Merciful permits, and he will say what is right.﴾ [al-Naba': 37].

As for His saying here: ﴿On that Day intercession will not benefit﴾ and the verse [Ta-Ha: 109], we have already presented the verses clarifying that in Surat Maryam and elsewhere, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

(p-101) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And faces will be humbled before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all; and he will have failed who carries wrongdoing﴾.

His saying: "ʿanat" means: they became humble and submissive. The Arabs say: ʿanā yaʿnū ʿunūwan wa-ʿanāʾan, meaning he became humbled, submissive, and meek. From this comes the saying that a captive is called ʿānin (a captive/one in subjection) because of his humiliation and submission to the one who captured him. From this is the verse of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt al-Thaqafi:

"A king over the throne of heaven, the Guardian; before His might, faces are humbled and prostrate."

And his saying also:

"My face and all my creation are humbled, among those who prostrate to His face, thankfully."

Know that the scholars differed regarding this noble verse. Some of them said: the intended meaning of "the faces" that became humbled and submissive before the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all, is specifically the faces of the disobedient, and that is on the Day of Resurrection. The humiliation and submission were attributed to their faces because the effects of humiliation and submission appear in the face. Among the Qur'anic verses that indicate this meaning is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But when they see it approaching, the faces of those who disbelieved will be distressed﴾ [al-Mulk: 27], and His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be dust-stained, expecting that a calamity will be inflicted upon them﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Faces that Day will be humbled, laboring and exhausted, burning in a scorching fire﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 2–4]. Al-Zamakhshari supported this opinion and cited some of the aforementioned verses as evidence for it.

Other scholars said: ﴿And faces will be humbled﴾ means: the faces of the believers became humbled and submissive to Allah in this worldly life, through prostration and bowing. The apparent meaning of the Qur'an indicates that the intended meaning is humiliation and submission to Allah on the Day of Resurrection, because the context concerns the Day of Resurrection, and on that Day all creatures will display signs of humiliation and submission to Allah, Majestic and Exalted.

As for His saying in this verse: ﴿and he will have failed who carries wrongdoing﴾, some scholars said: it means he who carries polytheism (shirk) has lost. Verses that call shirk "wrongdoing" support this view, such as:

• His saying: ﴿Indeed, shirk is a great wrongdoing﴾ [Luqman: 13],

• His saying: ﴿And it is the disbelievers who are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 254],

• His saying: ﴿And do not invoke, besides Allah, that which can neither benefit you nor harm you; for if you do, then you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ [Yunus: 106],

• His saying: ﴿Those who believed and did not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾ [al-An'am: 82], and other verses. The more apparent view is that the wrongdoing in His saying ﴿and he will have failed who carries wrongdoing﴾ [Ta-Ha: 111] is general, encompassing shirk and other sins. The failure of every wrongdoer is in proportion to the amount of wrongdoing he has committed. And knowledge is with Allah, Exalted.

(p-102) His saying in this noble verse: ﴿the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all﴾. Al-Hayy: the One characterized by life who never dies. Al-Qayyum is an intensive form (sigha mubalaghah), because He, Majestic and Exalted, is the One who manages the affairs of all creation, and He is the One who stands over every soul with what it has earned. It was also said: al-Qayyum is the Everlasting who never ceases to exist.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 112:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer, will not fear injustice or diminution.﴾

In this noble verse, He, majestic and exalted, mentions that whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer in his Lord, then he will not fear injustice (zulm) or diminution (hadm). This meaning has been explained in other places in the Qur'an,

- such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong even the weight of an atom; and if it is a good deed, He multiplies it and gives from Himself a great reward﴾ [an-Nisa': 40],

- and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not wrong the people at all, but it is the people who wrong themselves﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 44 (as cited)],

- and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ [al-Kahf: 49],

in addition to other verses, as we have previously mentioned.

Some scholars distinguished between zulm and hadm, saying that zulm is the withholding of the whole of a right, while hadm is the deficiency and withholding of part of a right. So every hadm is a zulm, but not vice versa. From the use of hadm for what has been mentioned is the saying of al-Mutawakkil al-Laythi:

؎Indeed, the humble and the base are a group whose protector is the one who is diminished and wronged (al-munhadim al-mazlum).

Al-munhadim is a passive participle (ism maf'ul) from ihtadama, meaning that he is diminished in some of his rights and wronged in them.

The majority of the Seven Readers, except Ibn Kathir, read this letter (word) ﴿fa-la yakhafu﴾ [Ta-Ha: 111], with a damma on the fa' and an alif after the kha', in the nominative, and with a negative la. That is, "so he does not fear," or "then indeed he does not fear." Ibn Kathir read it as "fa-la yakhaf" in the jussive, without an alif after the kha'. In that case, "la" is a prohibitive particle (nahiyah) governing the jussive of the imperfect verb.

Al-Qurtubi's statement in his tafsir, that on Ibn Kathir's reading it is jussive because it is an answer to the conditional "wa-man ya'mal," is an error on his part, because the fa' in His saying "fa-la yakhafu" prevents that. The verified view is what we have mentioned: that "la" is prohibitive on Ibn Kathir's reading, and the imperative clause is the apodosis of the condition, so it must be preceded by fa', because it cannot serve as a verb of the condition, as we have previously mentioned many times.

Allah's saying: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have diversified in it some of the warning,﴾ ...the verse. We have already presented the verses that clarify this in Surat al-Kahf, so that suffices and there is no need to repeat it here.

(p-103) The Prophet ﷺ, whenever Jibril came to him with the revelation, would recite along with him each verse as soon as Jibril recited it, out of his intense eagerness to memorize the Qur'an. So Allah guided him in this verse to what was fitting. He forbade him to hasten to recite the Qur'an along with Jibril, and instead commanded him to listen silently to Jibril's recitation until it was finished, and then to recite it himself afterward, for Allah would make its memorization easy for him. The meaning indicated in this verse, Allah explained in another place, as in His words in "al-Qiyamah": ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation. So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation. Then upon Us is its clarification.﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16-19]. Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: Musa ibn Isma'il narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Awana narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn Abi 'A'isha narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated to us, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His words, ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it,﴾ he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to struggle with the revelation, and he would move his lips with it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "I will move them for you as the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to move them." Sa'id said: "I will move them as I saw Ibn 'Abbas move them," and he moved his lips. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it. Indeed, upon Us is its collection and its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16-17]. He said: Its collection for you is in your breast, and its recitation: ﴿So when We have recited it, then follow its recitation﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 18]. He said: Then listen to it and be silent. ﴿Then upon Us is its clarification﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 19], then upon Us is that We recite it. After that, whenever Jibril came to the Prophet ﷺ, he would listen. And when Jibril departed, the Prophet ﷺ would recite it just as he had recited it (end of quotation).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 115:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾.

His saying: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam﴾, meaning: We enjoined upon him that he not approach that tree. This covenant with Adam, which He summarised here, He explained in other places, such as His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise and eat therefrom in abundance wherever you will, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 35]. So His saying, "do not approach this tree," is the covenant with Adam mentioned here.

And His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿"And O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise and eat from wherever you will, but do not approach this tree, or you will be among the wrongdoers."﴾ [al-A'raf: 19].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but he forgot﴾, the scholars have two well-known views concerning it:

The first: that what is meant by forgetting (nisyan) is abandonment (tark), and this does not preclude that the abandonment was deliberate. The Arabs use "forgetting" and mean by it abandonment, even if deliberate. Among this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Thus did Our signs come to you, and you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126]. So what is meant in this verse is deliberate abandonment.

Like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will forget them as they forgot the meeting of this their day, and as they used to deny Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 51];

and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So taste [the punishment] for your forgetting the meeting of this your day; indeed, We have forgotten you. And taste the everlasting punishment for what you used to do﴾ [al-Sajdah: 14];

and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be like those who forgot Allah, so He caused them to forget themselves. Those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Hashr: 19];

and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it will be said, "Today We forget you as you forgot the meeting of this your day, and your refuge is the Fire, and you have no helpers."﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 34].

Accordingly, the meaning of His saying "but he forgot" is: he abandoned fulfilling the covenant and contravened what Allah had commanded him, namely abstaining from eating from that tree, because the prohibition against a thing necessarily entails the command to its opposite.

The second view: that what is meant by forgetting in the verse is forgetting which is the opposite of remembering, because when Iblis swore to him by Allah that he was sincerely advising him in what he invited him to, namely eating from the tree which his Lord had forbidden him, he deceived him and tricked him thereby, until he caused him to forget the aforementioned covenant. This is as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you of those who give sincere advice." So he made them fall through deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 21–22]. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Man was only named insan because he was given a covenant and forgot it." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from him. End of quote. Some poet has said:

"Man was named only for his forgetting, and the heart only because it turns about."

As for the first view, there is no difficulty in His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. As for the second view, there is a well-known difficulty, because the forgetful one is excused, so how can it be said of him: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾?

The most evident answer to this, in my view, is that Adam was not excused by forgetting. I have shown in my book (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab) the evidences indicating that excuse by forgetting, error and compulsion are among the special features of this Ummah. Like His saying here, "but he forgot," along with His saying "and disobeyed," so forgetting and disobedience are both attributed to him, which shows that he was not excused by forgetting. Among what proves this is what is established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Hurairah: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], Allah said: 'Yes, I have done so.'" For if this were pardoned for all nations, its mention in the manner of bounty and the magnification of grace would have no great impact. This is supported by His saying: ﴿As You placed it upon those before us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286]. This is reinforced by the hadith: "Indeed, Allah has overlooked for me from my Ummah error, forgetting, and what they have been compelled to do." So His saying "has overlooked for me from my Ummah" indicates specificity to his Ummah, and this is not an argument from the negation of a title (mafhum laqab), because the basis of the overlooking in this is what Allah specially favoured him with over other messengers.

Although Imam Ahmad and Ibn Abi Hatim have declared the aforementioned hadith defective, it has established supporting evidences in the Book and the Sunnah, and the scholars of the Ummah, past and present, have never ceased to receive it with acceptance. Among the proofs for this is the well-known hadith of Tariq ibn Shihab concerning the one who entered the Fire over a fly, which he brought near (to an idol) while he was compelled, and his companion who refused to bring anything near the idol, even a fly, and they killed him. This indicates that the one who brought it near was compelled, for had he not brought it near they would have killed him as they killed his companion; yet despite this he entered the Fire, so his compulsion was not an excuse. Among the proofs for this is His saying, exalted is He, concerning the People of the Cave: ﴿Indeed, if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you or return you to their religion, and you will never succeed thereafter, ever﴾ [al-Kahf: 20]. His saying, "they will stone you or return you to their religion," is evidence of compulsion, and His saying, "and you will never succeed thereafter, ever," is evidence that this compulsion is no excuse. As we have explained elsewhere.

Know that in our Law there is what indicates a kind of obligation in this respect in general, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever kills a believer by mistake, [then] the freeing of a believing slave﴾ [an-Nisa': 92], the verse continuing. So the freeing of the slave here is an expiation for that killing by mistake. And expiation indicates the existence of a sin in general, as His saying concerning the expiation for killing by mistake indicates: ﴿And whoever does not find [a slave], then fasting two consecutive months as repentance to Allah. And ever is Allah Knowing and Wise﴾ [an-Nisa': 92]. So fasting two months was made a substitute for freeing a slave when one is unable to do so. And His saying after that, ﴿as repentance to Allah﴾, indicates that there is in general a taking to account for that mistake, along with His saying: ﴿And there is no blame upon you for what you have done by mistake﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5], and what we have previously mentioned from the hadith of Muslim: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: 'Do not impose blame upon us if we forget or make mistakes,' Allah said, 'Yes, I have done so.'" So the blame which is sin is lifted, and the expiation mentioned remains. Some people of knowledge have said: it is due to negligence in guarding against error and forgetting, and Allah, Majestic and Exalted, knows best.

As for His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121], this and similar verses are the basis for those among the usulis who hold that prophets are not immune from minor sins that are unconnected with conveying the message, because they make amends for them through repentance and turning back to Allah, until they become as though they had never been.

Know that all the scholars have agreed on the infallibility of the prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, in everything connected with conveying the message. They differed concerning their immunity from minor sins unconnected with conveying the message, in a well-known and established difference among the usulis. There is no doubt that they, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, if something of that sort occurs from them, they make amends for it with sincere turning back to Allah, until they reach a rank higher than the rank of one for whom that did not occur. As He said here: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾, then He followed that with His saying: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, and accepted his repentance and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 122].

His saying, exalted is He, in this noble verse: ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115], indicates that our father Adam, upon him and upon our Prophet be the prayer and peace, is not among the messengers of whom Allah said: ﴿So be patient as the messengers of resolve were patient﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. They are: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, 'Isa and Muhammad (ﷺ). It has been said: they are all the messengers. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah concerning ﴿And We found in him no resolve﴾ that it means: We found in him no patience to refrain from eating from the tree and persistence in adhering to the command.

The sayings of the scholars return to this. As for the word "found" in His saying ﴿and We found﴾, Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: it may be in the sense of knowing, with its two objects being ﴿in him resolve﴾; and it may be the opposite of non-existence, as if he said: "and at his reaching resolve." End of quote from him. The first is more evident, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot﴾.

The apparent meaning of this verse is that Adam forgot the covenant concerning the prohibition of eating from the tree, because Satan swore to him by Allah that he was sincerely advising him, until he deceived him with delusion and caused him to forget the covenant. On this basis he is excused, not disobedient.

(p-341) But another verse has come indicating otherwise, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121].

The answer to this is in two respects:

The first: what we have previously mentioned, that there is no excuse by forgetting for other than this Ummah.

The second: that "nasiya" here means "taraka" (abandoned), and the Arabs sometimes use forgetting in the sense of abandonment, among which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So today We will forget them﴾ [al-A'raf: 51], and Allah knows best.

The Almighty mentions in this noble verse that He commanded the angels to prostrate to Adam, "so they prostrated, except Iblis, who refused" (أبى). That is, he refused to prostrate. Here He mentions his refusal (الإباء) and does not mention his arrogance (الاستكبار). He also mentions his refusal in *al-Hijr*, in His words: ﴿Except Iblis; he refused to be among those who prostrated﴾ [al-Hijr: 31]. His statement in this *al-Hijr* verse, ﴿he refused to be among those who prostrated﴾, clarifies the omitted object (المعمول, the complement governed by the verb) of "أبى" in this *Ta-Ha* verse, which is His words ﴿except Iblis, who refused﴾ [Ta-Ha: 116]. That is, "he refused to be among those who prostrated," as he stated explicitly in *al-Hijr* and as he alluded to in *al-A'raf* in His words: ﴿except Iblis; he was not among those who prostrated﴾ [al-A'raf: 11]. In *Sad* He mentions only his arrogance, in His words: ﴿except Iblis; he was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [38]. In *al-Baqarah* He mentions both his refusal and his arrogance together, in His words: ﴿except Iblis, who refused and was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [2]. We have explained in *al-Baqarah* the cause of his arrogance according to his claim, and the proofs of the invalidity of his claimed justification. In *al-Kahf*, the statements of the scholars about it have been explained, namely whether his origin was one of the angels or not.

His statement in this noble verse, ﴿so they prostrated, except Iblis﴾, has been made explicit elsewhere: the prostration mentioned was performed by all the angels together, not by some of them, in His words (p. 107): ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together, except Iblis﴾ [Sad: 73–74].

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (*Adwa' al-Bayan*) on Surah 20, verse 117:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife. So let him not drive you out of the Garden and [thus] you be distressed. Indeed, it is [granted] for you that you will not be hungry therein or be naked. And indeed, you will not be thirsty therein or be exposed to the sun."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117-119]

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife﴾. We have already presented the verses that clarify this in *al-Kahf*, so their repetition here is unnecessary.

As for His saying in this noble verse, ﴿so you be distressed﴾, it means: so you become weary in seeking a livelihood through toil and earning. This is because, after leaving the Garden, one does not obtain a morsel of food in this world until he plows the land, then sows it, then tends to the crop until it ripens, then threshes it, then winnows it, then grinds it, then kneads it, then bakes it. This is the distress mentioned.

The evidence that the intended meaning of *shaqa'* (distress) in this verse is the weariness of earning a livelihood is His saying after it: ﴿Indeed, it is [granted] for you that you will not be hungry therein or be naked, and that you will not be thirsty therein or be exposed to the sun﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118-119]. That is, beware lest your enemy drive you out of the abode of comfort in which you are guaranteed satiety, quenching of thirst, clothing, and shelter. Al-Zamakhshari said: These four are the pillars upon which a person's sustenance revolves. So mentioning that they are all gathered for him in the Garden, and that he is provided for and does not need someone to suffice him or a earner to earn for him, as the people of this world need that, [shows his complete provision]. Mentioning them in the negative form, opposite to their contraries, which are hunger, nakedness, thirst, and sun-exposure, is so that his hearing is struck with the names of the categories of wretchedness from which he was warned, until he avoids the cause that leads to them, out of aversion to them. [End of quotation.]

So His saying in this noble verse, ﴿Indeed, it is [granted] for you that you will not be hungry therein or be naked﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118], is a clear indication that the distress he was warned against is the toil of this world in the labor of livelihood, by which one repels hunger, thirst, nakedness, and exposure to the sun. Hunger is well known, and *al-zama'* is thirst. *Al-'uri* (nakedness), with a *damma* on the *'ayn*, is the opposite of wearing clothes.

As for His saying, ﴿and be not exposed to the sun﴾, it means: you will not become exposed to the sun, having no shelter from its heat. The Arabs say: *dahiya yadhha*, like *radiya yarda*, and *dahha yadhha*, like *sa'a yas'a*, when one is exposed to the heat of the sun with nothing to shield him from it. From this meaning is the saying of 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah:

*She saw a widowed man, when the sun came against him, he was exposed to it, and in the evening he was confined.*

And the saying of another:

*I was exposed for his sake, so that I might find shade in his shadow, when the shadow becomes shrunk on the Day of Resurrection.*

Almost all of the seven readers, except Nafi' and Shu'bah on the authority of 'Asim, read this letter: ﴿and that you will not be thirsty therein﴾ with a *fatha* on the hamza of *'anna*. The verbal noun formed from *'anna* and its clause is conjoined to the verbal noun formed from *'anna* and its clause in His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is [granted] for you that you will not be hungry﴾. That is: and indeed, for you is that you will not be thirsty therein and will not be exposed to the sun. In the conjoined verbal noun mentioned, both the accusative and the nominative are permissible, as he indicated in the *Khulasah* with his saying:

*Your raising [of the conjoined noun] is permissible, when it follows the accusative of inna, after you complete [the phrase].*

The clarification of the estimation of the two mentioned verbal nouns is: indeed, for you is the absence of hunger therein, and the absence of thirst.

**A note (tanbih):**

Some scholars derived from this noble verse the obligation of a wife's maintenance upon her husband. Because God, when He said ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not drive you out of the Garden﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], addressed both Adam and Eve in an inclusive address, then singled out Adam with distress, excluding her, in His saying ﴿so you be distressed﴾, this indicates that he is the one charged with toil for her and with obtaining the necessary requirements of life for her: food, drink, clothing, and shelter.

Abu 'Abdullah al-Qurtubi said in his *tafsir* of this noble verse, the following text: "He singled him out with the mention of distress and did not say *fatasqa* (you two be distressed), to teach us that the maintenance of the wife is upon the husband. From that day, the maintenance of women became due upon husbands. Since Eve's maintenance was upon Adam in this manner, so too the maintenance of her daughters is upon the sons of Adam, by right of marriage. And He informed us in this verse that the maintenance that is due to a woman from her husband is these four: food, drink, clothing, and housing. So if he gives her these four, he has discharged her maintenance; if he goes beyond that, he is rewarded. But these four are indispensable, for by them the sustaining of life is achieved." [End of quotation from him.]

It is also mentioned in the story of Adam that when he was sent down to the earth, a red ox and grains from the Garden were sent down with him. He used to plow with that ox and wipe the sweat from his forehead, and that is from the distress mentioned in the verse.

It appears that what occurs in this noble verse, in the terminology of the rhetoricians, of *al-badi' al-ma'nawi* (semantic embellishment), is what is called *mura'at al-nazir* (observing the counterpart), also called *al-tanasub* (harmony), *al-i'tilaf* (concord), *al-tawfiq* (conformity), and *al-talfiq* (combination). All of these are names for this type of semantic embellishment. Its principle is: gathering a matter and what suits it, not by opposition. Like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The sun and the moon [move] by calculation﴾ [Al-Rahman: 5], for the sun and the moon are harmonious, not opposite. And like the saying of al-Buhturi describing lean, emaciated camels, or spears:

*Like bent bows, and arrows that have been straightened, and strings.*

Between the arrows, the bent bows, and the strings there is a harmony in slenderness, although some are more slender than others, and they are harmonious without opposition. And like the saying of Ibn Rashiq:

*The most sound and strongest of what we have heard regarding generosity, from the transmitted report since ancient times:*

*Narrations that the torrents transmit from the rain, from the sea, from the palm of the Amir Tamim.*

He harmonized between soundness, strength, hearing, the transmitted report, the narrations, and the transmission, and likewise harmonized between the torrent, the rain (*al-hayya*, meaning rainfall), the sea, and the palm of the Amir Tamim. And like the saying of Usayd ibn 'Anqa' al-Fazari:

*As if the Pleiades were hung on his forehead, and on his cheek Sirius, and on his face the full moon.*

He harmonized between the Pleiades, Sirius, and the full moon, just as he harmonized between the forehead, the cheek, and the face. Examples of this type are numerous and well known in the art of eloquence.

Once you know this, understand that He, may He be majestic and exalted, harmonized in this noble verse, in His saying ﴿Indeed, it is [granted] for you that you will not be hungry therein or be naked﴾, between the negation of hunger, which includes the negation of inner heat and inner pain of feeling, and the negation of nakedness, which includes the negation of outer pain from the harm of heat and cold. These are harmonious without opposition. Likewise, He, may He be exalted, harmonized in His saying ﴿and that you will not be thirsty therein or be exposed to the sun﴾, between the negation of thirst, which includes the negation of the inner pain of feeling that thirst causes, and the negation of exposure to the sun, which includes the negation of outer pain caused by the heat of the sun and the like, as is clear.

By what we have mentioned, you know that the saying of one who claimed that in this verse there is what is called *qat' al-nazir 'an al-nazir* (severing the counterpart from the counterpart), and that the purpose of severing the supposed counterpart from its counterpart is to affirm the enumeration of these blessings and to multiply them, is incorrect. For if he had linked each counterpart with its counterpart, it would have given the impression that the enumerated items were one blessing. This is why He severed thirst from hunger, and exposure to the sun from clothing, despite the harmony between them. They also said: among the examples of severing the counterpart from the counterpart mentioned is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*As if I had never ridden a horse for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets.*

*And I had never poured out the wine-skin of aged wine, nor said to horses, "Turn back a charge after a rout."*

So he severed the riding of the horse from his saying "Turn back a charge," and severed "embracing the maiden" from "drinking the aged wine-skin," despite the harmony in that. His purpose is to enumerate his delights and his glories and multiply them. All of this is speech for which there is no need, since the harmony among the items mentioned in the verse is evident, as we have clarified. And knowledge is with God, may He be exalted.
