**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 120:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾.

*Al-waswasah* (whispering) and *al-waswas* mean a faint sound. It is also said of the whisper of a hunter, of dogs, and of the sound of ornaments: *waswas*. *Al-wiswas* with a kasra on the first wa is the verbal noun (*masdar*), and with a fatha it is the noun (*ism*). It is also one of the names of Satan, as in His saying: ﴿from the evil of the whisperer, who withdraws﴾ [al-Nas: 4]. Inner speech of the self is also called *waswas* and *waswasah*. An example of using *waswas* for the sound of ornaments is the saying of al-A'sha:

*You hear the jingling of ornaments when she turns, like the sound of a rumbling reed-wind used for aid.*

An example of using it for the whisper of a hunter is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

*So he spent the night, disturbed by a sound and kept awake by the howling of the wind, the whispering, and the hills.*

And the saying of Ru'bah:

*He whispered, calling sincerely upon the Lord of the daybreak, in secret, though he had gathered like a cloud gathering, in the pen, though he chews drink and does not spit it out.*

Knowing this, understand that His saying in this noble verse, ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120], means: he spoke to him in a hidden speech, and Adam heard it from him and understood it.

The evidence that the whispering mentioned in this noble verse is a speech from Iblis that Adam heard and understood is that He explained the whispering in this verse as being speech, in His saying: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120]. So the speech mentioned is the whispering mentioned. He clarified this in surah al-A'raf and showed that he also whispered to Eve with Adam, in His saying: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both...﴾ up to His saying ﴿and he swore to them both, "Indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisers." So he brought them down by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 20–22]. This is because His explicit statement in this verse of al-A'raf, that Iblis *qasamahuma*, that is, swore to them that he was a sincere adviser to them regarding what he claimed, which was a lie, is clear evidence that the whispering mentioned is audible speech.

Know that in Satan's whispering to Adam there is a well-known problem (p-111): it may be said that Iblis had been expelled from the Garden disgraced, condemned and banished, so how was it possible for him to return to the Garden until he whispered to Adam? The commentators mention in this the story of the serpent, that he entered it and it brought him into the Garden, while the angels assigned to it were unaware. All of that is from the Israelite narrations (*isra'iliyyat*). The reality is that there is no problem in this, since it is possible that Iblis stood outside the Garden near its edge, such that Adam could hear his speech while he was in the Garden; and it is possible that God admitted him into it to test Adam and his wife, not as an honour to Iblis. So there is nothing rationally impossible in any of this. The Qur'an has come with the fact that Iblis spoke to Adam and swore to him until he deceived him and his wife by it.

His saying in this noble verse, ﴿of the tree of eternity﴾, attributed the tree to *al-khuld*, which is eternity (*al-khulud*). This is because whoever eats from it, in his false claim, will be eternal, not dying and not perishing. Likewise, he will have, in his claim, a kingdom that does not decay, that is, that does not vanish and does not end. We have already mentioned that His saying here, ﴿and a kingdom that does not decay﴾, indicates the meaning of the reading of the one who read ﴿unless you become angels﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] with a kasra on the lam. And His saying ﴿or become of the eternal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20] is the meaning of His saying in Ta-Ha: ﴿shall I direct you to the tree of eternity﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120].

The summary is that Iblis, may Allah curse him, was among what he whispered to Adam and Eve: that if they ate from the tree that Allah had forbidden them, they would attain eternity and kingdom, and become angels; and he swore to them that he was a sincere adviser to them in this, desiring for them eternity, endurance and kingdom, and so he brought them down by deception. In the story, when Adam heard him swearing by Allah, he believed, out of his intense reverence for Allah, that no one could swear by Him falsely, and so that belief made him forget the covenant regarding the prohibition of the tree.

* *

**Note**

In this noble verse there is a well-known question: how did the verb *waswasa* (to whisper) take *ila* (to) in Ta-Ha, in His saying ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾, while in al-A'raf it took *li* (for/to) in His saying ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]? The scholars have several answers to this question.

The first: prepositions may substitute for one another. So *li* can come with the meaning of *ila*, and vice versa.

Al-Jawhari said in his *Sihah*: "His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾ means *ilayhima* (to both of them), but the Arabs connect the verb with all these particles." Ibn Manzur followed him in *al-Lisan*. Among the answers to this is the intention of *tadmin* (implying one verb's meaning within another). Al-Zamakhshari said in his commentary on this verse:

(p-112) "If you say, how did *waswasa* take *li* in His saying ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾, and at another time *ila*? I say: the whispering of Satan is like the wailing of a bereaved mother, the howling of a wolf, and the clucking of a hen, in that they are imitations of sounds, and its judgement is the judgement of a sound and a jingle. From it comes *waswasa al-mubarsam* (he whispered, being delirious), and he is *muwaswis* with a kasra, and the fatha is a grammatical error." Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

*He whispered, calling sincerely upon the Lord of the daybreak...*

"So when you say *waswasa lahu*, its meaning is *li-ajlihi* (for his sake), as in his saying:

*Ajris lahā, O son of Abi Kibash, for tonight she has no dishonouring, except the night journey and a driver who drives with a cry.*

And the meaning of ﴿Then he whispered to him﴾ is that he conveyed the whispering to him, like His saying: *haddatha ilayhi* (he related to him) and *asarra ilayhi* (he confided to him)." End of his words.

This which we have pointed to is the meaning of the well-known disagreement between the Basran and the Kufan grammarians regarding the interchange of prepositions and the substitution of some of them for others: is it by way of *tadmin*, or is it because prepositions come with the meaning of one another? We will mention one example that makes the intended point clear. For instance, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We helped him against the people who denied Our signs﴾ [al-Anbiya': 77], according to the view of *tadmin*: the preposition *min* (from) is used in its own meaning, but *nasara* (to help) here implies the meaning of *al-injа'* (to rescue) and *al-takhlis* (to deliver), that is, "We rescued him and delivered him from the people who denied Our signs." Rescue, for example, takes *min*. According to the second view, *nasara* is used in its own meaning, but *min* carries the meaning of *ʿala* (against), that is, "We helped him against the people who denied Our signs," and likewise in everything similar to it.

We have already mentioned in surah al-Kahf that the scholars' disagreement over identifying the tree from which Allah forbade Adam to eat is a disagreement with no benefit in it, since there is no evidence identifying it, and no benefit in knowing its specific nature.

Some of them say it is the ear of grain (*sunbulah*). Some say it is the grapevine. Some say it is the fig tree, and other opinions besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 121 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to stitch together over themselves some leaves of the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾

The fa' (then) in His saying "fa-akalā" (so they both ate) indicates that the cause of their eating was the whispering of Satan mentioned before it, in His saying: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾. That is, they ate from it because of that whispering. Likewise, the fa' in His saying: ﴿so their private parts became apparent to them﴾ indicates that the cause of that was their eating from the tree mentioned (p. 113). So Satan's whispering was the cause of eating from that tree, and eating from it was the cause of their private parts becoming apparent. It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh), under the method of (al-Iyma' wal-Tanbih) (indication and alerting), that the fa' indicates causation, as in the saying "sahā fa-sajada" (he forgot, so he prostrated), meaning: because of his forgetfulness; "saraqa fa-quṭiʿat yaduhu" (he stole, so his hand was cut off), meaning: because of his theft. As we have mentioned many times before. Likewise His saying here: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?" So they both ate from it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120–121]. That is, because of that whispering, ﴿their private parts became apparent to them﴾, that is, because of that eating. So in the verse there is mention of the cause, and what the fa' indicates here, as we have explained, that Satan's whispering was the cause of what happened to Adam and Eve. This is explained in several places in the Book of Allah, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then Satan caused them both to slip from it and removed them from that in which they had been﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36], where He stated explicitly that it was Satan who caused them to slip. In the other reading it is "fa-azālahumā" (and he removed them), and that it was he who removed them from that in which they had been, that is, from the bounty of the Garden. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O children of Adam, let not Satan tempt you as he removed your parents from the Garden﴾, and so on, [al-A'raf: 27], and His saying: ﴿and he brought them down by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 22], along with other verses.

What He, may He be majestic and exalted, mentioned in the verse of Ta-Ha regarding the sequence of the apparent nakedness of the two upon their eating from that tree, I will clarify in other places. Such as His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿So when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 22], and His saying in the same surah: ﴿as He removed your parents from the Garden, stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 27].

The aforementioned verses indicate that Adam and Eve were under a covering from Allah by which their private parts were concealed, and that when they ate from the tree that their Lord had forbidden them, that covering was removed because of that slip. So their private parts became apparent, that is, their nakedness (ʿawrah). The nakedness was called sawʾah (that which is bad) because its exposure distresses its owner. They began trying to cover the nakedness with the leaves of the tree of the Garden, as He said here: ﴿and they began to stitch together over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121], and in al-A'raf He said: ﴿So when they tasted the tree, their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to stitch together over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾ [al-A'raf: 22].

His saying "wa-ṭafiqā" (and they began), that is, they started. These are verbs of commencement (af'al al-shuruʿ), and the predicate of verbs of commencement can only be an imperfect verb not preceded by "an" (that). Alfiyyah refers to this in its summary with his saying:

"... and the omission of 'an' with the verb of commencement is obligatory,
like 'anshaʾa al-sāʾiq yaḥdū' (the driver began to chant) and 'ṭafiq', and likewise 'jaʿaltu', 'akhadhtu' and 'ʿaliq'."

So the meaning of His saying "wa-ṭafiqā yakhṣifāni" (and they began to stitch together) is: they started to attach to themselves, one piece to another, some leaves of the Garden, in order to cover their nakedness with them. The Arabs say: "khaṣafa al-naʿl yakhṣifuhā" (he stitched the sandal), when he sewed it; and "khaṣafa al-waraq ʿalā badanihi" (he fastened the leaves over his body), when he attached them and covered himself with them, leaf by leaf. Many of the exegetes say that the leaves of the Garden from which Adam and Eve began to stitch covering for themselves were the leaves of the fig tree. And Allah knows best.

Know that the covering which Adam and Eve had, and which was removed from them when they tasted the tree, the scholars differed about its specification. A group of the people of knowledge said: they had a garment of the nature of nail (ẓufr). When they ate from the tree, Allah removed it from them except what remained on the tips of the fingers. Some people of knowledge said: their garment was light by which Allah concealed their private parts. It was also said: a garment of ruby, along with other opinions. This is from the disagreement that has no value, and there is no evidence on which the matter depends, as we have mentioned many examples of that in surah al-Kahf. The most that the Qur'an indicates is that they had a garment which Allah covered them with. When they ate from the tree, it was removed from them, and so their private parts became apparent to them. The garment mentioned may be the nail, or the light, or the garment of piety, or other opinions mentioned regarding it.

Allah, may He be exalted and majestic, attributed the exposure of what had been concealed of their private parts to Satan, in His saying: ﴿that He might show them what was concealed from them of their private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 20], just as the removal of their garment was attributed to him in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿as He removed your parents from the Garden, stripping them of their clothing to show them their private parts﴾ [al-A'raf: 27], because he was the one who caused that through his whispering and beautification, as we mentioned shortly before.

In this noble verse there is a well-known question, which is: how was the whispering of Satan, which is the cause of the slip, made specific to Adam without Eve in His saying ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾, even though He mentioned that this whispering caused the slip to both of them together, as we explained?

The answer is clear. He explained in al-A'raf that he whispered to Eve as well as Adam in the same story, in His saying: ﴿So Satan whispered to them both﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. So the verse of al-A'raf clarifies what the verse of Ta-Ha did not clarify, as you see. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.

* *

Issue

Some people of knowledge derived from this noble verse the obligation to cover the nakedness, because His saying: ﴿and they began to stitch together over themselves some leaves of the Garden﴾ indicates that the exposure of the nakedness is ugly, and that effort should be made to cover it. Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir on surah al-A'raf, with the following text: "In the verse there is evidence that exposing the nakedness is ugly, and that Allah made covering obligatory for them both. That is why they hastened to cover it. It is not impossible that they were commanded to do so in the Garden, just as it was said to them: ﴿Eat from wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree﴾ [al-A'raf: 19]." And the owner of Adwa' al-Bayan (al-Shinqiti) related from al-Shafi'i that whoever finds nothing to cover his nakedness except the leaves of a tree, it is obligatory for him to settle with that, because it is a visible covering, and he must cover himself with it, as Adam did in the Garden. And Allah knows best. End of al-Qurtubi's words.

The obligation to cover the nakedness during prayer is agreed upon among the Muslims (ijma'), that is, scholarly consensus. It is indicated by texts from the Book and the Sunnah, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ [al-A'raf: 31], and like His sending of the Prophet (ﷺ) to proclaim in the year of nine, at the time of the pilgrimage of Abu Bakr with the people: "No polytheist shall perform the pilgrimage after this year, and no naked person shall circumambulate the House." Likewise, there is no disagreement among the scholars on prohibiting the exposure of the nakedness in front of people. Some of what relates to this will come, if Allah wills, in surah al-Nur.

If it is said: why did He use the plural "sawʾātuhumā" (their private parts) in His saying, when they are only two private parts? The answer is from three aspects:

The first aspect: Adam and Eve each had two private parts: the front (qubul) and the rear (dubur). So there are four. Each of them sees their own front and the other's front, and their own rear. According to this there is no problem with the plural.

The second aspect: when a dual noun is annexed to it two things which are its parts, the annexed noun which is two things may take the plural, the dual, or the singular, and the most eloquent of them is the plural, then the singular, then the dual, according to the most correct view, whether the annexation is by form (lafẓ) or by meaning (maʿnā). An example of the form: "shawaytu ruʾūsa al-kabshayn" (I roasted the heads of the two rams), or "ra'sahumā" (their head), or "ra'sayhimā" (their two heads). An example of meaning: "qaṭaʿtu min al-kabshayn al-ruʾūs" (I cut the heads from the two rams), or "al-ra's", or "al-ra'sayn". If the annexed dual is separated, the preferred form for the annexed noun is the singular, such as: "ʿalā lisān Dāwūd wa-ʿĪsā ibn Maryam" (on the tongue of David and Jesus son of Mary).

An example of the preferred plural of the aforementioned annexed dual is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. An example of the singular is the poet's saying:

"O dove of the valley between the two valleys, sing,
may the bright, passing clouds water you with their rain."

An example of the dual is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"And two deserts, wide and far,
whose backs are like the backs of two shields."

The pronouns referring back to the aforementioned annexed noun, which is plural in form but dual in meaning, may be plural in consideration of the form, and dual in consideration of the meaning. From the first is his saying:

"My two friends, do not let your souls perish in grief,
for they have, in what I was afflicted with, grief."

From the second is his saying:

"Your hearts are habitually covered by security,
when, among you, the brave are covered by terror."

The third aspect: what Malik ibn Anas held, that the least of the plural is two. In Maraqi al-Su'ud it is said:

"The least meaning of the plural in what is well known
is two, according to the view of the Imam al-Humayri."

And if the two annexed things are separate from the dual annexed noun, meaning they are not its two parts, then the analogical rule is the plural, in agreement with al-Farra', such as your saying: "mā akhrajakumā min buyūtikumā" (what brought you out of your houses), "wa-idhā āwaytumā ilā maḍājiʿikumā" (when you two retire to your beds), "wa-ḍarabāhu bi-asyāfihimā" (and they both struck him with their swords), "wa-saʾalatā ʿan infāqihimā ʿalā azwājihimā" (and they both asked about their spending on their wives), and similar.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾

Disobedience (maʿṣiyah) is the opposite of obedience (ṭāʿah). So His saying ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray﴾ means: he did not obey Him in avoiding what He had forbidden him, namely approaching that tree.

As for His saying "fa-ghawā" (and so he went astray): al-ghayy is misguidance, which is departing from the path of what is right. So the meaning of the verse: Adam did not obey his Lord, and so he erred from the path of what is right because of not obeying. This disobedience and ghayy, which Allah, may He be majestic and exalted, explained in several places in His Book, means that Allah permitted him and his wife to eat from the Garden freely wherever they wished, and forbade them to approach a particular tree of its trees. Satan continued to whisper to them, and he swore to them by Allah that he was truly a sincere adviser to them, and that if they ate from it they would attain eternity and a kingdom that does not decay. So he deceived them with that, as Allah stated in His saying: ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisers." So he brought them down by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 21], and so they ate from it. Some of the people of knowledge used to say: "Whoever deceives us by Allah, deceives us," and this is narrated from Umar. In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah in Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Hakim: "The believer is naive and generous, and the wicked person is cunning and base." Nafṭawayh recited for this:

"If you deceive a generous person, you will find him,
and you will see the base person, tested, cannot be deceived."

So Adam, upon him be prayer and peace, did not commit the slip except because of the deception of Iblis towards him. We have already mentioned the saying of some people of knowledge: that Adam, out of his intense exaltation of Allah, believed that no one could swear by Him while lying, so Iblis's oath by Allah made him forget the covenant regarding the prohibition of the tree. And the saying of some people of knowledge: that the meaning of His saying "fa-ghawā" is: his life was spoiled for him by his descent to this world.

They said: al-ghayy means corruption. This is contrary to what is apparent, even though al-Naqqash related it, al-Qushayri preferred it, and al-Qurtubi approved it.

Likewise is the saying of one who said "fa-ghawā" means: he was overfull from much eating. Al-bashm is over-satiation (tukhmah), so this is a false saying. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf about it: "This, even if it is valid according to the dialect of those who change a kasra'd ya' preceded by a letter into an alif, saying in fanī and baqiya: fanā and baqā, namely the Banu Ṭayyi', it is a corrupt interpretation." End of his words. What al-Zamakhshari pointed to regarding the dialect of Ṭayyi' is well known. They say to the girl "jārāh" (jāriyah), for "nāṣiyah" "nāṣāh", and they say in baqiya "baqā", like "karamā". And from this dialect is the poet's saying:

"By your life, I do not fear poverty as long as
there remains on the earth a Qaysi driving camels."

This dialect that al-Zamakhshari mentioned is not needed for the false interpretation mentioned, because the Arabs say: "ghawā al-faṣīl" (the weaned camel colt went astray), like "raḍiya" and "karamā", when it is overfull from milk.

And His saying, exalted is He, in this verse: ﴿And Adam disobeyed﴾ indicates that the meaning of "ghawa" (went astray) is that he departed from the path of rectitude, as we have mentioned. We have already noted that this noble verse and similar verses in the Qur'an are the proof for those who say that the prophets are not protected from minor sins. The infallibility ('ismah) of the prophets, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon them, is a question of legal theory (usul al-fiqh) on which the scholars of usul have much discussion and well-known disagreement. Here we will mention a portion of what the people of usul have said on this. Ibn al-Hajib said in his Mukhtasar fi al-Usul:

* *

Question:
The majority hold that it is not rationally impossible for the prophets to commit disobedience (ma'siyah). The Rafidah (Rafidites) disagreed, and the Mu'tazilah disagreed except regarding minor sins. Their reliance is on rational good and evil (al-taqbih al-'aqli). There is consensus (ijma') on their infallibility after prophethood from deliberately lying in the rulings, because of the proof of the miracle for truthfulness. Al-Qadi allowed it by mistake and said: the miracle indicates truthfulness only as a belief. As for other sins, there is consensus on their infallibility from major sins and from base minor sins (saghair al-khissah). The majority hold that the others are permissible. End of his words verbatim.

The essence of his words: they are protected from major sins and from base minor sins, but not from other minor sins.

Al-'Allamah al-'Alawi al-Shinqiti said in (Nashr al-Bunud Sharh Maraqi al-Su'ud), in discussing his words:

"And the prophets are protected from what they forbade, and there is no enjoyment of it
Permissible, rather that is for legislation, or for intent of nearness from the Exalted."

His text reads: The people of the religions and all the sacred laws agree on the obligation of their infallibility from deliberately lying regarding what the decisive miracle indicates of their truthfulness, such as the claim of prophethood and what they convey from Allah Most High to creation. Lying from them regarding what was mentioned, whether through forgetfulness or heedlessness, was prohibited by most scholars, as was anything other than lying in conveying. If it were disbelief, the Ummah has agreed on their protection from it before prophethood and after it. If it were other than that, the majority hold their protection from major sins committed deliberately. The opponent of the majority is the Hashwiyyah.

The people of truth differed: is what prevents major sins from them deliberately reason or revelation (al-sam')? As for the Mu'tazilah, it is reason. And if it is through heedlessness, the preferred view is their protection from them. As for minor sins, whether deliberately or through heedlessness, the majority have permitted them rationally. However, they do not occur from them except for base minor sins, so their occurrence from them is not permissible, neither deliberately nor through heedlessness. End of his words.

The essence of his words: their protection from lying in what they convey from Allah, and from disbelief, major sins, and base minor sins. And the majority hold that other minor sins may occur from them rationally, except that this has not actually happened.

Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr in (Surat al-Baqarah), and in al-Muntakhab of the Imam Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Abi al-Fadl al-Mursi, the gist of which is: The Ummah has prevented the occurrence of disbelief from the prophets, peace be upon them, except the Fudayliyyah of the Khawarij, who said: sins have occurred from them, and sin for them is disbelief. The Imamiyyah permitted their manifesting disbelief by way of taqiyyah (dissimulation). The Ummah has agreed on their protection from lying and distortion in what relates to conveying, so it is not permissible deliberately or through error. Some people permitted that through error. They agreed on the impossibility of their erring in giving rulings deliberately, and differed regarding error through heedlessness. As for their actions, the Hashwiyyah said: major sins may occur from them deliberately. Most of the Mu'tazilah said: minor sins are permissible deliberately, except in speech such as lying. Al-Juba'i said: both are impossible for them except by way of interpretation. It was said: both are impossible for them except through forgetfulness and error, and they are held accountable for that, even if it is lifted from their nation. The Rafidah said: this is impossible from every standpoint.

The time of infallibility has been disputed. The Rafidah said: from the time of their birth. Many of the Mu'tazilah said: from the time of prophethood. Our preferred view is that no sin at all proceeded from them during prophethood, neither a major sin nor a minor one, because if sin proceeded from them they would be of lower rank than the disobedient of the Ummah, given their great honour, and that is impossible; and so that they would not be unacceptable as witnesses; and so that they would not have to be rebuked and harmed; and so that they would not be followed in that; and so that they would not be deserving of punishment; and so that they would not do the opposite of what they were commanded, because they are chosen; and because Iblis excepted them in misguidance. End of what we have summarized from (al-Muntakhab), and the discussion of the evidences for these positions and the refutation of what should be refuted are mentioned in books of the principles of religion (usul al-din). End of Abu Hayyan's words.

The essence of the words of the usuliyyun on this question: their protection from disbelief and from everything related to conveying, and from major sins and base minor sins such as stealing a morsel or cheating by a grain. Most usul scholars hold that minor sins other than base ones may occur from them. But a large group of later usul scholars chose that although that is rationally permissible, it has not occurred in fact, and they said: what came in the Book and the Sunnah of that is that what they did was by interpretation, or forgetfulness, or heedlessness, or the like.

The one who annotates it, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: What appears to us to be correct on this question is that the prophets, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon them, did not commit anything that would detract from their lofty ranks and exalted positions, and no error or deficiency attributed to them arises, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon them. Even if we suppose that some sins did occur from them, they make up for what occurred from them by repentance, sincerity, and true turning back to Allah, until through that they attain their highest ranks, so that their ranks become higher than the rank of one who committed none of that. What clarifies this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he erred﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, so He turned to him in forgiveness and guided him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. Consider what effect remains of disobedience and error after Allah's turning to him in forgiveness, His choosing him, that is, His selecting him, and His guiding him. There is no doubt that one who repents from some lapses attains through repentance a rank higher than his rank before committing that lapse. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 122:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then his Lord chose him, and accepted his repentance, and guided him﴾.

Al-ijtiba' (choosing, singling out) means al-istifa' (selection) and al-ikhtiyar (preference). That is, after what came from Adam, after a delay, his Lord selected him and preferred him, accepted his repentance, and guided him to what pleases Him. He does not specify here the reason for this, but He specified in another place that he received words from his Lord, and these words were the cause of his Lord's acceptance of his repentance. This is in His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37], meaning: because of those words, as the particle *al-fa'* (الفاء, "then/so") indicates. We have already mentioned in surah "al-Baqarah" that the words referred to are those mentioned in surah "al-A'raf" in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers"﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. (p-120) The best way to explain the Qur'an is by the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 123 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said, "Go down from it, all of you, some of you being enemies to others."﴾

The apparent meaning is that the alif of the dual in His saying "ihbita" (go down, two of you) refers back to Adam and Hawwa' (Eve), who are mentioned in His saying ﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. This is contrary to those who claim that it refers to Iblis and Adam. His command to them both to descend from the Garden, mentioned in this verse of Ta-Ha, has been made clear in other places,

such as His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And We said, "Go down, some of you being enemies to others, and for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36],

and His saying in the same surah: ﴿We said, "Go down from it, all of you. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance – there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 38],

and His saying in al-A'raf: ﴿He said, "Go down, some of you being enemies to others, and for you on the earth is a dwelling place and provision for a time."﴾ [al-A'raf: 24]. Regarding these verses there is a well-known question, namely: why is the plural form used in His saying ﴿ihbitu﴾ [al-Baqarah: 36, 38; al-A'raf: 24] in al-Baqarah and al-A'raf, while the dual form is used in Ta-Ha, in His saying ﴿ihbita﴾, even though in Ta-Ha He follows the dual form with the plural form in His saying ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me⦆? The most evident answer to this, in my view, is that the dual refers to Adam and Hawwa' only, while the plural refers to them together with their descendants. This is contrary to those who claim that the dual refers to Adam and Iblis, and the plural refers to them together with their descendants; and contrary to those who claim that the plural in His saying ﴿ihbitu﴾ is intended to include Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent. The evidence that the serpent is not intended in this is that it does not enter into His saying ﴿And when guidance comes to you from Me﴾, because it is not morally accountable.

Know that the exegetes mention the story of the serpent, that it had four legs like the Bactrian camel, the finest creature Allah created, and that Iblis entered into its mouth and it brought him into the Garden, so he whispered to Adam and Hawwa' after presenting himself to many animals, and none admitted him except the serpent. Then he was sent down to the earth, and the serpent was cursed, its legs were drawn back into its belly, and enmity was placed between it and the children of Adam, and for this reason they were commanded to kill it. On this occasion, al-Qurtubi in his tafsir, in the surah of al-Baqarah, mentioned several rulings on killing snakes. He mentioned from Saкinah bint al-Ja'd that she narrated from Suraiy bint Nabhan al-Ghanawiyyah that she heard the Prophet (ﷺ) command the killing of snakes, small and large, black and white, and encourage it. Then he mentioned from Ibn Jurayj, from 'Amr ibn Dinar, from Abu 'Ubaydah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, a hadith in which: "The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded his companions to kill a snake, but it outran them to its hole. So he commanded them to set fire to it (p-121)." He also mentioned from the scholars of the Malikiyyah that they restricted by this the prohibition against burning with fire and against punishing anyone with the punishment of Allah. Then he mentioned from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i that he disliked burning a scorpion with fire, and said: it is mutilation. He answered this by saying that it is possible that the report mentioned had not reached him. Then he mentioned the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, which is established in the two Sahihs, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a cave, and Surat al-Mursalat ("By those sent forth in gusts") had been revealed to him [77], and we were taking it from his mouth while it was fresh. Then a snake came out at us, and he said, 'Kill it!' We rushed to kill it, but it outran us. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Allah has protected you from its evil as you have protected yourselves from its evil,' and he did not set fire to it, nor did he devise a means to kill it." He answered this too, by saying that it is possible that he did not find fire at that time, or that the hole was not of a form in which fire could be used there, along with the harm of the smoke and its not reaching the snake. Then he mentioned that the command to kill snakes is part of guidance toward repelling a harm that causes fear from snakes. Then he mentioned that the command to kill snakes is general in all its kinds, if they are not house snakes. Then he mentioned what Abu Dawud recorded from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud: "Kill all snakes, and whoever fears their vengeance is not of me." Then he mentioned that house snakes are not killed until they are warned for three days, because of the hadith: "Indeed in Madinah there are jinn who have accepted Islam; so when you see anything of them, warn them for three days." Then he mentioned that some scholars restricted that to Madinah alone, not to other places, because of the hadith: "Indeed in Madinah there are jinn who have accepted Islam." They said: "We do not know whether any of the jinn outside Madinah have accepted Islam or not." This was said by Ibn Nafi'. Then he mentioned from Malik the prohibition against killing house jinn in all lands. Then he said: "And this is the correct view, because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And when We turned to you a company of jinn listening to the Qur'an﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], and so on." In Sahih Muslim, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with them, and I recited the Qur'an to them," and in it: "they asked him for provision, and they were jinn of al-Jazirah." It will come in full in Surat al-Jinn, Allah willing. Since this is established, none of them is to be killed until it has been warned, as its explanation will come, Allah willing.

(Then he said): The imams narrated from Abu al-Sa'ib, client of Hisham ibn Zahrah: "He entered upon Abu Sa'id al-Khudri in his house. He said: I found him praying, so I sat waiting for him until he finished his prayer. I heard a rustling in the palm-stalks in a corner of the house, so I turned and saw a snake, and I leapt up to kill it, but he gestured to me to sit, so I sat. When he finished, he pointed to a room in the house and said: Do you see this room? I said: Yes. He said: In it there was a young man of ours, recently married. We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the Trench, and that young man used to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) permission at midday to go back to his family. He asked him permission one day (p-122), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Take your weapon, for I fear for you from Quraydah.' The man took his weapon and then returned, and found his wife standing between the two doors. He raised the spear at her to stab her, and jealousy overcame him. She said to him: 'Hold back your spear, and enter the house until you see what it was that brought me out.' He entered, and there was a huge snake coiled on the bed. He raised the spear at it and pierced it through, then came out and planted the spear in the courtyard, and the snake writhed upon it. They did not know which of them died first, the snake or the young man. He said: We came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him of that, and we said: Pray to Allah that He revive him for us. He said: 'Ask forgiveness for your brother.' Then he said: 'Indeed in Madinah there are jinn who have accepted Islam; so when you see anything of them, warn them for three days. If they appear to you after that, kill them, for it is a devil.'" In another route, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed these houses have inhabitants; so when you see something of them, admonish it three times. If it goes, well and good; otherwise kill it, for it is a disbeliever," and he said to them: "Go and bury your companion."

Then he said: Our scholars, may Allah have mercy on them, said: It is not understood from this hadith that this jinn which the young man killed was a Muslim, and that the jinn killed him in retaliation for it. For even if it were granted that retaliation (qisas) is prescribed between us and the jinn, it would only apply to deliberate murder, and this young man did not intend or deliberately kill a Muslim soul, since he had no knowledge of that; he only aimed at killing a creature whose kind is lawfully permitted to be killed, so this is accidental killing, and there is no retaliation in it. The better view is that the disbelieving jinn, or their wicked ones, killed the young man in revenge for their companion, by enmity and vengeance. And they did kill Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, may Allah be pleased with him, for he was found dead in his bathing place, his body turned green, and they did not perceive his death until they heard a speaker saying, while they saw no one:

"We have killed the lord of the Khazraj, Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah,
and we shot him with two arrows, and did not miss his heart."

The Prophet (ﷺ) only said: "Indeed in Madinah there are jinn who have accepted Islam," to explain a means by which one may guard against killing a Muslim among them, and by which one may be empowered to kill the disbeliever among them. It is related by many routes that 'A'ishah, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), killed a jinn. Then she was shown in a dream that a speaker said to her: "You have killed a Muslim." She said: "Had he been a Muslim, he would not have entered upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)." He said: "He entered upon you only while you were wearing your clothes." So in the morning she ordered twelve thousand dirhams to be spent in the way of Allah. In another narration: "He entered upon you only while you were covered," so she gave in charity and freed slaves.

Al-Rabi' ibn Badr said: The jinn among the snakes whose killing the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade are those that walk and do not coil. This is also reported from 'Alqamah.

Then he mentioned the manner of warning house snakes, and said: Malik said: "I prefer that they be warned for three days." 'Isa ibn Dinar said the same: (p-123) even if it appears many times in a day, one should not limit the warning to three times in a single day, until it has been three days. It was also said: three times suffice, based on his saying (ﷺ): "Let him warn it three times," and his saying "Admonish it three times," and because "thalatha" (three) is used for the feminine plural, so it is evident that what is meant is three times. But Malik's view is better, based on his saying (ﷺ): "three days," which is a sound explicit text restricting those unrestricted reports, and "three" is understood as referring to the nights of the three days, since the Arabs in matters of dating give precedence to the night, as the feminine form predominates in their usage. Malik said: It suffices in the warning to say: "I adjure you by Allah and the Last Day not to appear to us, nor harm us." Thabit al-Bunani narrated from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla that house snakes were mentioned in his presence, and he said: "If you see any of them in your dwellings, say: I adjure you by the covenant which Noah, peace be upon him, took from you, and I adjure you by the covenant which Solomon, peace be upon him, took from you. If you see any of them after that, kill it." Then he said: Ibn Habib has related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that it is said: "I adjure you by the covenant which Solomon, peace be upon him, took from you, that you not harm us, nor appear against us." This ends the words of al-Qurtubi, summarized closely to his wording.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him and forgive him, says: The verified view on this matter is that whatever snakes are not in houses are killed, like those found in the wilderness, and house snakes are not killed except after warning. The stronger of the two opinions in my view is the generality of warning in Madinah and elsewhere, and that warning for three days is necessary, and three times within one day or two days does not suffice, as the evidences for this were given earlier in al-Qurtubi's words. And that the "abtar" (short-tailed) and the "dhu al-tufyatayn" (two-striped) are killed in houses without warning, because of what is established in some narrations of Muslim, in the wording: Abu Lubabah said: "Indeed they have been forbidden from them" (meaning the inhabitants of houses), "and it was commanded to kill the abtar and dhu al-tufyatayn." And in a narration in Sahih al-Bukhari from Abu Lubabah: "Do not kill the jinn except every abtar dhu tufyatayn, for it causes miscarriage and takes away sight, so kill it."

The evidence for killing snakes and warning house snakes is established in the two Sahihs and elsewhere.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 123 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: "Abdullah ibn Muhammad narrated to us, Hisham ibn Yusuf narrated to us, Ma'mar narrated to us from al-Zuhri, from Salim, from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) delivering a sermon on the minbar (pulpit), saying: 'Kill the snakes, and kill the one with two stripes (dhu'l-tufyatayn) and the short-tailed one (al-abtar), for they blind the sight and cause miscarriage.' Abdullah said: 'While I was pursuing a snake to kill it, Abu Lubabah called out to me: "Do not kill it!" I said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has ordered the killing of snakes?" He said: "He later forbade (killing) the dwelling-snakes (dhawat al-buyut), which are the 'awamir.'"'" Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar: "Abu Lubabah or Zayd ibn al-Khattab saw me." Yunus, Ibn Uyaynah, Ishaq al-Kalbi and al-Zubaydi followed him (in this narration), while Salih, Ibn Abi Hafsah and Ibn Mujammi' said, from al-Zuhri, from Salim, from Ibn Umar: "Abu Lubabah and Zayd ibn al-Khattab saw me." End of quotation from Sahih al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him.

Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj said in his Sahih: "Amr ibn Muhammad al-Naqid narrated to me, Sufyan ibn Uyaynah narrated to us from al-Zuhri, from Salim, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Kill the snakes, and the one with two stripes and the short-tailed one, for they cause miscarriage and seek out the sight.'" He said: "Ibn Umar would kill every snake he found. Abu Lubabah ibn Abd al-Mundhir, or Zayd ibn al-Khattab, saw him pursuing a snake and said: 'He has forbidden the dwelling-snakes.'" Then he mentioned it through multiple chains. In all of them there is explicit prohibition of killing the dwelling-jinn snakes, that is, except after warning them three times. From Malik: whatever of them is found in mosques is to be killed.

The words of the Prophet (ﷺ) in this hadith, "dhu'l-tufyatayn," are with a dammah on the unmarked ta' and a sukun on the fa' followed by a ya'. The root of tufyah is the frond of the muql, which is the doum palm tree. It was said: the muql is the fruit of the doum palm tree. Its plural is tufa, with a dammah then a fatah, according to analogy. What is meant by "al-tufyatayn" in the hadith is two white lines. It was said: two black marks on the back of the aforementioned snake, resembling in their form the fronds of the aforementioned muql. The abtar is the short-tailed snake. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: it is a kind of blue snake with a cut-off tail; no pregnant woman looks at it without miscarrying what is in her womb. Al-Dawudi said: it is the viper which is about a span or a little more in length. As for his words in this hadith, "they cause miscarriage" (yastaskitani al-habal), its meaning is that a pregnant woman who looks at them and is frightened generally miscarries her fetus. Muslim has also reported from al-Zuhri what indicates that the miscarriage mentioned is a property of these two due to their venom. The most apparent meaning of "they seek out the sight" (yaltamisani al-basar) is that Allah placed in them, because of the intensity of their venom, a property by which they snatch away sight and blind it merely by looking at it. The view that its meaning is that they target the sight by biting and stinging is weak. And knowledge is with Allah, the Exalted.

His words, may peace and blessings be upon him, in the hadith agreed upon (muttafaq alayhi): "Kill the snakes," indicate the obligation of killing them, due to what we have previously mentioned, that the bare imperative form free of indicators denotes obligation.

The majority hold that the command to that killing mentioned is for recommendation (nadb) and desirability (istihbab). And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

His statement, the Exalted, in this noble verse: "Some of you are enemies to others" (Ta-Ha: 123), according to what we have mentioned that it is most apparent, means: some of the children of Adam are enemies to some of them, as the Exalted said: "Or He will confuse you with factions and make you taste the violence of one another" (al-An'am: 65), and similar verses. And according to the view that what is meant by his statement "descend" (ihbitu) is Adam and Iblis, the meaning is that Iblis and his offspring are enemies to Adam and his offspring, as the Exalted said: "Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me while they are an enemy to you?" (al-Kahf: 50), and similar verses.

The apparent view is that what al-Qurtubi mentioned, of burning a snake with fire, is not established, and that it is not fitting to punish with the punishment of Allah, so it is not fitting that it be killed by fire. And Allah knows best.

If it is said: the aforementioned hadith indicates that dhu'l-tufyatayn is other than the abtar, since it is conjoined to it in the hadith, while the narration of al-Bukhari we previously cited from Abu Lubabah, "Do not kill the jinn-snakes except every abtar with two stripes," implies that they are one. The answer: Ibn Hajar in al-Fath answered this, saying that the narration mentioned apparently indicates their unity, but it does not negate their distinctness. The apparent meaning of his statement that it "does not negate distinctness" is that the abtar, even if it has two stripes, does not preclude the existence of a two-striped snake other than the abtar. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

* *

His statement, the Exalted: "Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor suffer."

The apparent view is that the address is to the children of Adam. That is: if guidance comes to you from Me, that is, a messenger whom I send to you, and a scripture brought by a messenger, then whoever among you follows My guidance, that is, whoever believes in My messengers and affirms My scriptures, complies with what I have commanded, and avoids what I have forbidden through the tongues of My messengers, then he will not go astray in this world, that is, he will not deviate from the path of truth, because he holds firmly to the most trustworthy handhold; and he will not suffer in the Hereafter, because in this world he was acting in accordance with what necessitates happiness, namely obedience to Allah, the Exalted, and obedience to His messengers. This meaning mentioned here has been mentioned in other places, such as His statement in al-Baqarah: "Then if there comes to you guidance from Me, whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve" (al-Baqarah: 38), and similar verses. In these verses there is evidence that Allah, after expelling our two parents from the Garden, does not return any of us to it except after trial and testing through obligations, namely commands and prohibitions, and then He obeys Allah in what He has tested him with. As the allusion to this was previously made in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 124:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed for him is a constricted living﴾.

We have already discussed, in surah "al-Kahf," in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the verses of his Lord but turns away from them﴾ [al-Ra'd: 57], the verses that clarify the dire consequences of turning away from the remembrance of God, may He be exalted. That makes repeating it here unnecessary. We also mentioned there that among these consequences is the constricted living. (p-126) Know that *al-danku* (الضَّنْكُ) in the language means narrowness. From it is the saying of 'Antara:

*"If they overtake me, I will charge back; if they seize me in the fight, I will press on; and if they find me in a narrow place, I will descend."*

And his saying also:

*"Were death to be given a form, it would take my form when they descend into a narrow abode."*

The origin of *al-danku* is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as a description, so it is the same for the masculine and feminine, the singular and the plural. From this you know that the meaning of His saying ﴿constricted living﴾ is a narrow life, and we seek refuge in God, may He be exalted.

The scholars differed about the meaning of this narrow life, giving sayings that are close in meaning and do not contradict one another. We have mentioned many times that the better approach in such cases is for the verse to encompass all the sayings mentioned. Among these sayings: the meaning is that God, mighty and majestic, placed with religion submission, contentment, reliance upon God, and acceptance of His allotment; so its possessor spends from what God has provided him with generosity and ease, and he lives a pleasant life. Evidence for this meaning from the Qur'an is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [al-Nahl: 97], and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that you seek forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will let you enjoy a good provision for a specified term﴾ [Hud: 3]. The explanation of all this has preceded.

As for the one who turns away from religion, greed takes control of him, a greed that never ceases to drive him toward increasing worldly gain. Stinginess is imposed upon him, which holds back his hand from spending. So his living is constricted and his state is darkened. Among the disbelievers are those upon whom God imposed humiliation and wretchedness because of their disbelief, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And humiliation and misery were struck upon them, and they returned with anger from God. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God﴾ [al-Baqarah: 61], and the verses that follow. This is part of the constricted living, caused by turning away from the remembrance of God. In other places God has explained that if they abandoned turning away from the remembrance of God and obeyed Him, exalted is He, their living would become broad and abundant, not constricted,

such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they had established the Torah and the Gospel and what was revealed to them from their Lord, they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 66],

and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed and been mindful of God, We would have opened upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 96],

and as His saying, may He be exalted, about Noah: ﴿So I said, "Seek forgiveness of your Lord; indeed, He is ever Forgiving. He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain, and provide you with wealth and children, and make for you gardens and make for you rivers"﴾ [Nuh: 10–12],

and His saying, may He be exalted, about Hud: ﴿And O my people, seek forgiveness of your Lord and then repent to Him; He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain and increase you in strength upon your strength﴾ [Hud: 52], (p-127)

and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that if they had remained steadfast upon the way, We would have given them abundant water to test them therein﴾ [al-Jinn: 16–17],

and other verses besides these.

It is reported from al-Hasan that the constricted living is the food of *al-ḍarī'* and *al-zaqqūm* on the Day of Resurrection, and this is mentioned in verses of the Book of God, such as His saying: ﴿They have no food except from *ḍarī'*﴾ [al-Ghashiyah: 6], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, the tree of *al-zaqqūm* is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43–44], and similar verses. It is reported from 'Ikrimah, al-Dahhak and Malik ibn Dinar that the constricted living is unlawful earnings and evil deeds. It is reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah that the constricted living is the punishment of the grave and its squeezing. God, may He be exalted, has indicated the trial of the grave and its punishment in His saying: ﴿God keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in the worldly life and in the Hereafter, and God leads astray the wrongdoers, and God does what He wills﴾ [Ibrahim: 27].

The one who restricts this (i.e., the author) — may God pardon him and forgive him — says: It has come from the Prophet (ﷺ), through a hadith of Abu Hurayrah, that the constricted living in the verse is the punishment of the grave. Some of its chains are sound, as Ibn Kathir said in his *tafsir* (interpretation) of this verse. This does not contradict the constricted living including his livelihood in this world and the food of *al-ḍarī'* and *al-zaqqūm*. So his living will be constricted in this world, in the *barzakh* (intermediate state), and in the Hereafter, and we seek refuge in God, may He be exalted.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾.

In this noble verse, God, may He be exalted, mentions that whoever turns away from His remembrance will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection in a state of blindness. Mujahid, Abu Salih and al-Suddi said: "Blind" means he has no proof. 'Ikrimah said: "Everything is blinded to him except Hell." We have mentioned in the introduction to this blessed book that among the kinds of clarification it contains is that some scholars give a saying about a verse, while within the same verse there is an indication contradicting that saying. We have given many examples of this. Knowing this, understand that in this noble verse there is an indication contradicting the sayings of Mujahid, Abu Salih and 'Ikrimah, and that the intended meaning of His saying "blind" is blind in sight, seeing nothing. The indication mentioned is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind when I was seeing?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125]. So He has explicitly stated that his blindness is the blindness opposite to sight, which is blindness of the eye, because the disbeliever in the world was blind of heart, as many verses of the Book of God indicate. In surah "Bani Isra'il," God, may He be exalted, added that along with that blindness he will also be gathered deaf and mute, in His saying: (p-128) ﴿And whomever God guides, he is the guided; and whomever He leads astray, you will not find for them allies besides Him. And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf; their refuge is Hell; whenever it subsides, We increase for them the blaze﴾ [al-Isra': 97].

* *

A NOTE

In this verse of "Ta-Ha" and the verse of "al-Isra'" there is a well-known difficulty. It may be said: both indicate that the disbeliever will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection blind, and the verse of "al-Isra'" adds that he will also be gathered mute and deaf, while verses of the Book of God indicate that the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection will see, hear and speak.

Such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿How clearly they will hear and see on the day they come to Us﴾ [Maryam: 38],

and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the criminals will see the Fire and will be certain that they are going to fall into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53],

and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, we have seen and heard, so return us; we will do righteousness﴾ [al-Sajdah: 12],

and other verses besides these. We have mentioned in our book (*Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab*) the answer to this difficulty from three aspects:

The first aspect, which Abu Hayyan favored, is that what is mentioned of blindness, deafness and muteness is meant literally. It occurs at the beginning, then God returns to them their sight, speech and hearing, so they see the Fire and hear its roaring, and they speak as God related of them in more than one place.

The second aspect: they will not see anything that pleases them, nor hear it, nor speak with a proof, just as they were in the world, not seeing with insight, not speaking the truth, and not hearing it. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported this from Ibn 'Abbas, and it is also reported from al-Hasan, as al-Alusi and others mentioned. According to this saying, what they say, hear and see is treated as nonexistent, because they gain no benefit from it, as we explained in other places. It is known that the Arabs use "nothing" for what has no benefit in it. Do you not see that God says about the hypocrites: ﴿Deaf, mute, blind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 18], although He also says about them: ﴿But when fear departs, they will lash you with sharp tongues﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19], and He says about them: ﴿And if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4], meaning for their eloquence and sweetness of tongue. He says about them: ﴿And if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾ [al-Baqarah: 20]. This is only because speech and the like that has no benefit in it is like nothing, so it is true of its owner that he is blind, deaf and mute. Among this is the saying of Qa'nab ibn Umm Sahib:

*"They are deaf when they hear good said about them, but when evil is mentioned about them in their presence, they perk up their ears."*

And the saying of another:

*"I am deaf to the matter I do not want, and I hear the creation of God when I want."*

And the saying of another:

*"Say whatever lies and falsehood you wish; my forbearance is deaf, and my ear is not deaf."*

Similar examples are many in the speech of the Arabs, applying deafness to hearing that has no benefit. Likewise speech that has no benefit, and sight that has no benefit.

The third aspect: when God says to them: ﴿Be silent therein, and do not speak to Me﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 108], that blindness, deafness and muteness befalls them from the intensity of distress and despair of relief. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the word will be fulfilled against them for what they did wrong, so they will not speak﴾ [al-Naml: 85]. According to this saying, the five states are as follows: His saying in "Ta-Ha": ﴿And We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ [Ta-Ha: 125], His saying in the same surah: ﴿Why have You gathered me blind?﴾, and His saying in "al-Isra'": ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf﴾ [al-Isra': 97]. The first of these is, in my view, the most apparent, and God, may He be exalted, knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted, in this noble verse: ﴿He said, "Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; likewise today you are forgotten"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126]. "Forgetting" here means deliberate abandonment, as we previously mentioned the verses that clarify this in this noble surah, in the commentary on His saying: ﴿But he forgot, and We found in him no determination﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 127:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And thus We recompense those who commit excess﴾.

In this noble verse, He—majestic and exalted—mentioned that He recompenses those who commit excess (al-musrifin) with that recompense mentioned. The method of allusion and alerting has indicated that this recompense is due to the cause of their excess against themselves, through rebellion (al-tughyan) and sins (al-ma'asi). In another place He made clear that the recompense for excess is the Fire, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, the transgressors are the companions of the Fire﴾ [Ghafir: 43]. And in another place He made clear that this applies when they do not turn back (yunibu) to Allah and repent to Him, as in His saying: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah..."﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And turn back to your Lord and submit to Him before the punishment comes upon you﴾ [Az-Zumar: 52–54].

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾.

(p-130) In this noble verse, He—majestic and exalted—mentioned that the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting. That is: more painful and more enduring than the punishment of this world, and than the constricted life (al-ma'ishah al-dank), which is the punishment of the grave. This meaning has been clarified in other places.

• As in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe, and they will have no protector from Allah﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 34],

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more humiliating, and they will not be helped﴾ [Fussilat: 16],

• And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, if only they knew﴾ [Al-Qalam: 33],

and other verses besides these.
His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Has it not guided them?﴾ Some of the verses clarifying this were given earlier in Surah Maryam, and more clarification of it will come after this, God willing.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 133:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord? Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?"﴾.

The most apparent of the opinions in my view regarding the meaning of this noble verse is that the disbelievers, according to their habit of obstinacy, proposed a sign for prophethood, such as the staff and the hand from the signs of Musa, and the she-camel of Salih, and their proposal for that was with the particle of urging (ḥarf al-taḥḍīḍ, the particle of exhortation), which indicates intense insistence in demanding that, in His saying: ﴿Why does he not bring us﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133], i.e., "Why does Muhammad not bring us a sign such as the she-camel of Salih and the staff of Musa?", meaning: we demand that from him with urging and insistence. So Allah answered them with His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133], and it is this great Qur'an; for it is a sign that is the greatest of signs and the most indicative of its inimitability. The reason this great Qur'an is described as "the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures" is that the Qur'an is a decisive proof of the correctness of all the books sent down from Allah, exalted is He. It is therefore a clear evidence of their truthfulness and soundness, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Book and as a guardian over it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. He, exalted is He, also said: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of that over which they differ﴾ [an-Naml: 76]. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say, "Then bring the Torah and recite it, if you should be truthful"﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 93], and other verses besides these.

This meaning which this verse indicates according to this interpretation, which is the most apparent, was clarified by Him, majestic and exalted, in Surah al-'Ankabut in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why were not signs sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "The signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner."﴾ ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them? Indeed in that is mercy and a reminder for a people who believe﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 50-51]. So His saying in al-'Ankabut: ﴿Is it not sufficient for them that We have sent down to you the Book which is recited to them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 51] is the meaning of His saying in Ta-Ha: (p-131) ﴿Has there not come to them the clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾, as we have clarified. And Allah knows best. This is further clarified by the agreed-upon hadith: "There is not a prophet among the prophets except that he was given what mankind believed in because of its like, and what I was given was revelation which Allah revealed to me, so I hope that I will be the most numerous of them in followers on the Day of Resurrection." And there are other opinions regarding the verse besides what we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 134:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we could follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?"﴾.

We have already mentioned in Surat an-Nisa' that this verse of Ta-Ha indicates its meaning is the verse of al-Qasas, which is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if not that a misfortune would strike them for what their hands have put forth, they would say, "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we could follow Your signs and be among the believers."﴾ [al-Qasas: 47]. And that this argument, which they would present had no warner come to them, is the one mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that mankind will not have any argument against Allah after the messengers﴾ [an-Nisa': 165].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 20, verse 135:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Each of us is waiting, so wait."﴾

In this noble verse, Allah, may He be exalted, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to say to the disbelievers who were demanding signs from him out of obstinacy and stubborn defiance: "Each of us and you is waiting (mutarabbis), that is, awaiting what will befall the other of the turns of fortune, such as death and defeat." He has made clear in other places that what the Prophet ﷺ, his Companions and the Muslims await is entirely good, contrary to what the disbelievers await and wait for. As in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "Do you await for us anything but one of the two best things? And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Himself or at our hands. So wait; indeed, we are with you among those who wait."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52], and His saying: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who consider what they spend as a loss and await misfortunes for you. Upon them is the misfortune of evil﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98], and other verses besides these. Al-tarabbus (waiting) means al-intizar (expectation).

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So you will know who are the companions of the right path and who is guided.﴾

In this noble verse, He, may He be exalted, mentioned that the disbelievers will know, at a later time, who are the companions of the right path and who is guided, that is, who has been granted success on the path of truth and steadfastness upon it. He commanded His Prophet to say this to the disbelievers. The meaning is: "It will become clear to you that we are rightly guided and upon a straight path, and that you are in error and falsehood." This will become manifest to them on the Day of Resurrection when they witness the reality, and it becomes manifest to them in this world through what they see of the victory of Allah for His Prophet ﷺ.

(p-132) This meaning that he mentioned here he has explained in other places as well:

• As in His saying: ﴿And they will know, when they see the punishment, who is further astray in way﴾ [al-Furqan: 42],

• and His saying: ﴿They will know tomorrow who is the liar, the insolent﴾ [al-Qamar: 26],

• and His saying: ﴿And you will surely know its news after a time﴾ [Sad: 88],

and other verses besides these. Al-sirat (the path) in the language of the Arabs is the clear road. Al-sawiyy means the straight, which has no crookedness in it. From it is the saying of Jarir:

"The Commander of the Believers is upon a path that is straight when the watering-places are crooked."

As for "man" in His saying "man ashab" (who are the companions), some scholars said: it is a relative pronoun, object of "ta'lamun" (you will know). Others said: it is an interrogative, suspending the verb of knowledge, as we have already clarified in the commentary on Surat Maryam. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.
